ocr-aaq-it-da.title: OCR Cambridge Advanced National Level 3 AAQ
ocr-aaq-it-da.subtitle: OCR IT: Data Analytics (H119)

f200.title: Fundamentals of data analytics
f200.notice: Covers all five OCR F200 topic areas (specification v6, October 2026). Original practice includes recall, applied questions and six-mark evaluations. Written feedback is indicative. The OCR exam is 75 minutes and 60 marks.

questions.q: A sensor logs 18.4. Which addition turns that reading into usable information?
o: Water temperature was 18.4 °C at Pier 2 at 09:00.
questions.e: Units, place and time supply context for interpreting the reading.

questions.q: Which is an example of knowledge derived from maintenance records?
o: A supervisor concludes that pump checks should be more frequent on cold nights.
The ID printed on a pump
A table of dated breakdown counts
questions.e: Knowledge applies interpreted information to understanding or action.

questions.q: Which is a social risk of using past service records to allocate new services?
o: Every record becomes inaccurate when grouped.
The records can no longer be used to identify trends.
Groups whose needs were under-recorded may receive too little support.
questions.e: Historical records can reflect unequal access and reinforce it in later decisions.

questions.q: A leisure centre has timestamped turnstile readings. Explain how it could use them to make a staffing decision.

pts.p: Group entry counts by hour and day to identify periods of high demand.
Schedule more staff during regularly busy periods to reduce queues.

questions.model: Group entry counts by hour and day to identify periods of high demand. Schedule more staff during regularly busy periods to reduce queues.

questions.q: Which collection best illustrates big data from multiple sources?
o: A short list of depot addresses
Continuous vehicle positions, journey transactions and passenger comments across a region
A weekly total typed by one driver
questions.e: The collection combines large, rapidly arriving datasets in different formats.

questions.q: Which source adds unstructured data to a supermarket's big-data analysis?
o: A fixed set of till totals
A list of product IDs in a database column
questions.e: Free text lacks the fixed fields of a structured table.

questions.q: Why might more data fail to improve a flood forecast?
o: Sensors may be concentrated in well monitored areas.
Forecasts become exact once more records arrive.
questions.e: A large volume can still leave geographical gaps or contain poor quality readings.

questions.q: Explain one benefit and one limitation of a delivery firm analysing live GPS records from thousands of vans.

pts.p: Live GPS patterns can reveal congestion so dispatchers can reroute vans and reduce delays.
Location records can reveal individual movements, so access and retention need controls.

questions.model: Live GPS patterns can reveal congestion so dispatchers can reroute vans and reduce delays. Location records can reveal individual movements, so access and retention need controls.

questions.q: Which format represents basic English letters and digits using standard numeric character codes?
questions.e: ASCII maps a limited character set to numeric codes.

questions.q: Which format uses named tags to identify elements?
questions.e: XML tags give explicit structure to the data.

questions.q: Which representation is valid JSON?
questions.e: A JSON object uses braces and quoted property names.

questions.q: Which plain-text format defines fields by their character positions?
questions.e: Fixed width uses agreed positions and lengths, so padding or truncation may be needed.

questions.q: Which pair consists of audio formats?
questions.e: Both AIFF and WAV are audio containers often used for high quality recordings.

questions.q: A designer needs an image with a transparent background for a website. Which format is suitable?
questions.e: PNG supports transparency. JPEG does not.

questions.q: Which format is commonly used to retain high quality scanned page images for archiving?
questions.e: TIFF is common in scanning workflows, though files can be large and browser support varies.

questions.q: Which format is a common choice for photographs displayed on a public website?
questions.e: JPEG is widely supported and usually provides a practical file size for photographs.

questions.q: Which format suits a plain, human-readable note with no formatting requirements?
questions.e: TXT stores plain text. It carries no standard rich formatting or table schema.

questions.q: A venue exports ticket counts as CSV. Explain one benefit and one limitation of CSV for this transfer.

pts.p: Spreadsheet tools can open the comma-separated rows as columns for analysis.
CSV does not enforce numeric data types, so the importer must interpret ticket counts correctly.

questions.model: Spreadsheet tools can open the comma-separated rows as columns for analysis. CSV does not enforce numeric data types, so the importer must interpret ticket counts correctly.

questions.q: A finance system exchanges monetary values in an agreed numeric representation. Why should both systems agree how many decimal places it carries?
o: Precision settings determine which currency is used automatically.
Every numeric representation preserves all fractions exactly.
Decimal places identify which staff can view a file.
They need to preserve the intended precision and interpret each amount consistently.
questions.e: A numeric representation has rules for precision and range. The systems must also agree units or currency where relevant.

questions.q: Which type suits the number of seats sold?
questions.e: Counts are whole numbers.

questions.q: Which type suits a measured depth of 12.75 metres?
questions.e: A real value supports a fractional part.

questions.q: Which type is appropriate for whether a delivery has been signed for?
questions.e: A Boolean represents a true or false condition.

questions.q: Which type is best for a postcode such as AB1 2CD?
questions.e: A postcode is an identifier containing text and digits.

questions.q: Which type suits a single letter indicating a boarding zone?
questions.e: A character holds one symbol.

questions.q: Which type supports sorting bookings in calendar order and finding the interval between them?
questions.e: A date type represents calendar values and supports date operations.

questions.q: Which item is qualitative?
o: An interviewee's explanation of why a trip felt unsafe
questions.e: A descriptive explanation conveys qualities rather than a numerical measurement.

questions.q: A clinic stores appointment times in a table and recordings of patient calls. Classify each as structured or unstructured and explain why.

pts.p: Appointment rows follow defined fields and types, so the table is structured.
Audio recordings have no fixed row and column schema for their spoken content, so they are unstructured.

questions.model: Appointment rows follow defined fields and types, so the table is structured. Audio recordings have no fixed row and column schema for their spoken content, so they are unstructured.

questions.q: Which sequence represents the five lifecycle phases?
questions.e: Lifecycle management follows the record from creation through active use and retention to disposal.

questions.q: A completed claim must be retained for a defined period but is seldom accessed. Which phase fits?
questions.e: Archival keeps inactive records retrievable for a legitimate retention need.

questions.q: A claim is reopened and its archived record is retrieved for investigation. What does this show?
o: Retrieval creates a different legal record automatically.
Every record can be used only once.
A record can return from archival to usage.
questions.e: Lifecycle phases can interact and repeat.

questions.q: Explain two benefits of applying lifecycle management to a housing provider's repair records.

pts.p: A retention schedule keeps records available while they are needed for disputes or repeat repairs.
Planned secure destruction reduces exposure of personal data after the retention period ends.

questions.model: A retention schedule keeps records available while they are needed for disputes or repeat repairs. Planned secure destruction reduces exposure of personal data after the retention period ends.

questions.q: Which pipeline phase receives new events from a booking system?
questions.e: Capture or ingestion brings source data into the pipeline.

questions.q: Which stage converts inconsistent date representations into one agreed representation?
questions.e: Transformation prepares data for storage or analysis.

questions.q: Which stage identifies a recurring cancellation pattern in processed records?
questions.e: Analysis turns prepared records into findings.

questions.q: Which stage communicates the findings on a dashboard?
questions.e: Visualisation is a way of using analysis to communicate information.

questions.q: A dashboard shows an apparent fall in weekday tickets. The analyst suspects one machine stopped sending records. Explain why the team should revisit capture and analysis.

pts.p: Check ingestion from the machine to find gaps that could make the recorded totals incomplete.
Restore missing records where possible and rerun the analysis before acting on the trend.

questions.model: Check ingestion from the machine to find gaps that could make the recorded totals incomplete. Restore missing records where possible and rerun the analysis before acting on the trend.

questions.q: Which check is verification?
o: Allow only digits in a numeric field.
Check that a serial number has eight characters.
Compare a typed serial number with the original label.
questions.e: Verification checks that a value was copied correctly from its source.

questions.q: Which example is a validation rule?
o: Ask an operator to confirm a reading matches the gauge.
Compare each typed value with a paper sheet.
Reject an occupancy value outside the permitted range.
Recount every person in a room.
questions.e: Validation checks whether an input meets specified rules.

questions.q: A recorded age of 31 passes the range check but the actual age is 13. What does this demonstrate?
o: Valid data always matches the real world.
A valid entry can still be inaccurate.
Timeliness is the only measure of quality.
questions.e: The range rule cannot tell whether a plausible value is true.

questions.q: A stock screen shows yesterday's count during a flash sale. Which concern is most direct?
questions.e: Accurate historical data can be too old for a current decision.

questions.q: What problem can redundant copies of a customer record cause?
o: Copies automatically verify the original value.
An update in one copy may leave inconsistent addresses elsewhere.
All duplicate data is needed for analysis.
questions.e: Unmanaged duplication makes it harder to maintain consistent data.

questions.q: A station relies on automated passenger counts. Explain one check for reliability and one for accuracy.

pts.p: Repeat counts under similar conditions and compare results to check consistency.
Compare the automatic count against a trusted manual count of the same passengers.

questions.model: Repeat counts under similar conditions and compare results to check consistency. Compare the automatic count against a trusted manual count of the same passengers.

questions.q: Which method lets an interviewer ask follow-up questions about a vague response?
questions.e: An interview allows probing for clarification.

questions.q: Which method captures products and prices at checkout?
questions.e: Transaction logs record details of completed transactions.

questions.q: Which method is most appropriate for seeing how people actually navigate an exhibition?
o: A focus group discussing a different exhibition
questions.e: Direct observation captures behaviour in context.

questions.q: Which source is best for first-hand accounts of how a depot operated decades ago?
questions.e: Verbal histories preserve personal recollections, which may need corroboration.

questions.q: Which method collects click paths and abandonment events on a booking website?
questions.e: Online tracking records browsing behaviour subject to privacy requirements.

questions.q: What is a limitation of using public social media posts to estimate overall satisfaction?
o: Public posts always give a representative random sample.
Every post identifies the author accurately.
Social media monitoring cannot capture opinions.
People who post may differ systematically from those who do not.
questions.e: Platform participation and willingness to post can bias the results.

questions.q: A theatre wants to understand why first-time visitors struggled to find their seats. Explain one benefit and one limitation of using a focus group.

pts.p: Participants can build on each other's accounts and identify shared signage problems.
Dominant participants can influence answers, so quieter visitors' experiences may be missed.

questions.model: Participants can build on each other's accounts and identify shared signage problems. Dominant participants can influence answers, so quieter visitors' experiences may be missed.

questions.q: A council wants representative feedback on a new cycle route. Explain two improvements to a survey shared only with a cycling club.

pts.p: Recruit from several user and non-user groups to reduce selection bias.
Use neutral questions about specific journeys so wording does not push respondents toward approval.

questions.model: Recruit from several user and non-user groups to reduce selection bias. Use neutral questions about specific journeys so wording does not push respondents toward approval.

questions.q: A station is redesigning ticket machines for infrequent passengers. It has transaction logs and a budget for one additional data gathering method. Evaluate using observation or a survey and recommend one.

pts.p: Transaction logs show successful purchases and their times, but may omit people who abandon a purchase before paying.
Observation can reveal where infrequent users hesitate or request help without requiring them to remember each step later.
An observer may misinterpret behaviour and people can act differently when they know they are being watched.
A survey can ask users why a task felt difficult and gather comparable responses across many journeys.
People who complete surveys may differ from those who leave quickly, and self-reporting can introduce bias.
Choose structured observation across peak and quiet periods because locating abandonment points is the first design priority.

questions.model: Transaction logs show successful purchases and their times, but may omit people who abandon a purchase before paying. Observation can reveal where infrequent users hesitate or request help without requiring them to remember each step later. An observer may misinterpret behaviour and people can act differently when they know they are being watched. A survey can ask users why a task felt difficult and gather comparable responses across many journeys. People who complete surveys may differ from those who leave quickly, and self-reporting can introduce bias. Choose structured observation across peak and quiet periods because locating abandonment points is the first design priority.
questions.marking_guidance: Use the points to review your reasoning. For a high-level answer, apply both sides to the scenario, develop their consequences and support your judgement. The practice score is a keyword estimate.

questions.q: Which source is most direct for checking the date and terms of a purchase made last year?
o: A focus group guessing when it happened
A survey of current customer preferences
questions.e: Existing records can supply evidence of the actual transaction. Check their completeness and provenance.

questions.q: A report is crossing a network from a sensor gateway to a server. Which state applies?
questions.e: Data in transit is moving between systems.

questions.q: Which is data at rest?
o: A video packet moving through a router
A backup file stored on an unplugged drive
Records currently being sorted in memory
A live upload to cloud storage
questions.e: Stored data that is not currently being transferred or processed is at rest.

questions.q: Identify the data state while a report is being filtered in memory and while the saved report sits on disk.

pts.p: While filtered in memory the report is data in use.
The saved report on disk is data at rest.

questions.model: While filtered in memory the report is data in use. The saved report on disk is data at rest.

questions.q: Which best describes a data store in a pipeline?
o: A location or service that holds data so another stage can retrieve it
A presentation style for discussing findings
A rule that destroys a drive
questions.e: A store makes captured, prepared or derived data available later.

questions.q: Why might a pipeline use separate raw and prepared data stores?
o: Raw records must be destroyed before every analysis.
Separate stores prevent any access between systems.
Analysts can use prepared data while retaining original records for reprocessing.
questions.e: Keeping originals can aid replay and traceability.

questions.q: Explain how a raw event store and reporting database can interact in a visitor-count pipeline.

pts.p: A process reads events from the raw store and prepares consistent records or totals.
Prepared totals are written to the reporting database for dashboards to retrieve.

questions.model: A process reads events from the raw store and prepares consistent records or totals. Prepared totals are written to the reporting database for dashboards to retrieve.

questions.q: Which storage type presents fixed-size blocks that a host can use like a disk?
questions.e: Block storage supports direct block addressing, useful for many database workloads.

questions.q: Which storage type organises documents in a shared hierarchy of folders?
questions.e: File storage provides named files in directories.

questions.q: Which storage type addresses a stored photo by a key and can attach metadata to it?
questions.e: Object storage associates data with a unique key and metadata.

questions.q: Recommend a storage type for millions of photographs accessed individually by an application and explain a trade-off.

pts.p: Object storage suits large collections accessed by key and can scale as photographs accumulate.
Applications may need object-aware access and cannot assume normal shared-folder editing.

questions.model: Object storage suits large collections accessed by key and can scale as photographs accumulate. Applications may need object-aware access and cannot assume normal shared-folder editing.

questions.q: Which device exposes shared files over the office network?
questions.e: Network attached storage provides shared file access over a network.

questions.q: What does a SAN typically present to servers?
questions.e: A SAN supplies shared block storage over a specialised storage network.

questions.q: Why might an SSD suit a workstation that frequently opens many small files?
o: It requires a motor to locate data.
It has low access latency and no moving heads.
It is always cheaper per gigabyte than an HDD.
It can be sanitised by degaussing.
questions.e: SSD access does not require mechanical movement.

questions.q: Why might an HDD suit a large local archive with infrequent reads?
o: It always reads faster than an SSD.
High capacity can be available at a lower cost per gigabyte.
questions.e: Cost and capacity may matter more than read latency for infrequent access.

questions.q: Explain one advantage and one risk of using a portable drive to move a dataset between sites.

pts.p: A portable drive can transfer a large dataset when network bandwidth is limited.
The drive can be lost in transit, exposing records unless protected by encryption.

questions.model: A portable drive can transfer a large dataset when network bandwidth is limited. The drive can be lost in transit, exposing records unless protected by encryption.

questions.q: A small design studio has eight staff editing shared project files. It has a fast office network, unreliable internet and no dedicated IT administrator. Discuss whether it should use a NAS or a cloud file service. Recommend an approach.

pts.p: A NAS offers a shared folder on the office network so staff can reach project files during internet outages.
Local transfer speeds can suit large project files if network capacity and simultaneous access are adequate.
The studio must manage updates, access and backup itself, which takes staff time without an administrator.
A cloud file service can simplify off-site access and transfer some maintenance to the provider.
Poor internet connectivity may interrupt access or leave collaborators working on conflicting versions.
Use a NAS for active office files with tested off-site backups, unless reliable remote access becomes the priority.

questions.model: A NAS offers a shared folder on the office network so staff can reach project files during internet outages. Local transfer speeds can suit large project files if network capacity and simultaneous access are adequate. The studio must manage updates, access and backup itself, which takes staff time without an administrator. A cloud file service can simplify off-site access and transfer some maintenance to the provider. Poor internet connectivity may interrupt access or leave collaborators working on conflicting versions. Use a NAS for active office files with tested off-site backups, unless reliable remote access becomes the priority.
questions.marking_guidance: Use the points to review your reasoning. For a high-level answer, apply both sides to the scenario, develop their consequences and support your judgement. The practice score is a keyword estimate.

questions.q: Several councils share a cloud environment restricted to members with similar governance requirements. Which model fits?
questions.e: A community cloud serves organisations with shared requirements.

questions.q: An insurer combines a private cloud for identifiable records with public cloud capacity for de-identified reporting. Which model fits?
questions.e: Hybrid combines distinct cloud environments used together.

questions.q: Which model supplies cloud services from a provider to many customers with isolated accounts?
o: Community cloud restricted to one sector
questions.e: Public cloud capacity is sold to many customers. Their data need not be public.

questions.q: Which feature is characteristic of a private cloud?
o: Its cloud environment is dedicated to one organisation.
It can only be built with removable drives.
All files must be visible to the public.
questions.e: Private refers to exclusive use, not necessarily physical location.

questions.q: Explain one advantage and one limitation of a managed cloud database for a seasonal ticketing service.

pts.p: The service can scale database capacity during ticket releases without buying permanent hardware.
Reliance on connectivity or the provider can disrupt access during outages.

questions.model: The service can scale database capacity during ticket releases without buying permanent hardware. Reliance on connectivity or the provider can disrupt access during outages.

questions.q: What is the purpose of data wrangling in a pipeline?
o: Make source data suitable for consistent use and analysis.
questions.e: Wrangling prepares data so analysis can use it meaningfully.

questions.q: Two branches send records that are not directly comparable. Explain why wrangling matters before combining them for reporting.

pts.p: Wrangling makes the records consistent so equivalent values can be compared.
Without preparation, differences in the way data is represented could distort the totals or conclusions.

questions.model: Wrangling makes the records consistent so equivalent values can be compared. Without preparation, differences in the way data is represented could distort the totals or conclusions.

questions.q: Why maintain data after its first use?
o: Keep records accurate, relevant and useful as circumstances change.
Ensure every record remains unchanged forever.
questions.e: Maintenance sustains quality across the useful life of the records.

questions.q: Explain why maintaining a food bank's stock records matters after a report has been published.

pts.p: Stock changes as supplies arrive and leave, so old records can become inaccurate.
Reliable current records help staff plan orders and avoid shortages.

questions.model: Stock changes as supplies arrive and leave, so old records can become inaccurate. Reliable current records help staff plan orders and avoid shortages.

questions.q: Which activity is data analytics?
o: Copy a file without examining it.
Store an unlabelled recording for later.
Examine delivery records to identify when delays occur.
questions.e: Analytics examines data to derive insights for decisions.

questions.q: Explain why a museum analyses timed-entry data rather than simply keeping the records.

pts.p: Analysis identifies busy periods or recurring patterns from the entries.
Staff can use the findings to plan opening slots or staffing levels.

questions.model: Analysis identifies busy periods or recurring patterns from the entries. Staff can use the findings to plan opening slots or staffing levels.

questions.q: Which question is descriptive?
o: How many cancellations are expected next month?
How many cancellations occurred last month?
What change should we make to minimise cancellations?
questions.e: Descriptive analytics summarises what happened.

questions.q: Which activity is diagnostic?
o: Recommend a timetable that minimises delays.
Investigate whether a new timetable explains an increase in missed connections.
Report the count of missed connections.
questions.e: Diagnostic analytics investigates why an observed outcome occurred.

questions.q: Which activity is predictive?
o: Estimate next week's demand from previous booking patterns.
Identify why last week's service ran late.
questions.e: Predictive analytics estimates future outcomes.

questions.q: Which activity is prescriptive?
o: Recommend staffing levels based on forecast demand and budget.
Estimate next month's number of enquiries.
Count the number of workers on site today.
Explain the cause of a past outage.
questions.e: Prescriptive analytics proposes actions under goals or constraints.

questions.q: Which is a use of cognitive analytics?
o: Interpret free-text incident reports to help identify recurring concerns.
Count rows in an attendance table only.
Archive reports after their retention period.
Sort a folder by name without analysing it.
questions.e: Cognitive analytics can use AI to interpret less structured inputs such as language.

questions.q: A venue uses historic ticket sales to forecast attendance. Explain one advantage and one limitation of the prediction.

pts.p: A forecast helps allocate staff before an event so queues can be managed.
Unexpected changes in events or customer behaviour can make historic patterns unreliable.

questions.model: A forecast helps allocate staff before an event so queues can be managed. Unexpected changes in events or customer behaviour can make historic patterns unreliable.

questions.q: A community health service wants to reduce missed appointments. Evaluate how descriptive, diagnostic and predictive analytics could inform its decision about reminder calls.

pts.p: Descriptive analysis can summarise missed appointments by time and clinic, showing where the problem is concentrated.
Those summaries show patterns but cannot alone explain why people missed their appointments.
Diagnostic analysis could compare appointment lead times and patient feedback to investigate possible reasons for missing appointments.
An observed association may reflect transport or work schedules, so a comparison alone cannot establish causation.
Predictive analysis can help prioritise calls, but incomplete records may misclassify people or disadvantage underrepresented groups.
Use these findings to design a small trial and compare attendance before expanding the reminder policy.

questions.model: Descriptive analysis can summarise missed appointments by time and clinic, showing where the problem is concentrated. Those summaries show patterns but cannot alone explain why people missed their appointments. Diagnostic analysis could compare appointment lead times and patient feedback to investigate possible reasons for missing appointments. An observed association may reflect transport or work schedules, so a comparison alone cannot establish causation. Predictive analysis can help prioritise calls, but incomplete records may misclassify people or disadvantage underrepresented groups. Use these findings to design a small trial and compare attendance before expanding the reminder policy.
questions.marking_guidance: Use the points to review your reasoning. For a high-level answer, apply both sides to the scenario, develop their consequences and support your judgement. The practice score is a keyword estimate.

questions.q: Which presentation is best when staff need exact daily totals for many branches?
questions.e: A table supports precise lookup by branch and date.

questions.q: Which presentation suits a brief explanation of why an unusual result occurred?
o: A bare number in a cell
questions.e: Text provides context, causes and qualifications.

questions.q: Explain why a chart and a table might both be included in a manager's monthly report.

pts.p: A chart makes trends or contrasts easier to see quickly.
A table provides exact values for checking or decisions.

questions.model: A chart makes trends or contrasts easier to see quickly. A table provides exact values for checking or decisions.

questions.q: Which chart best shows how average wait time changes over a year?
o: Bubble chart with no time axis
questions.e: A line chart shows trends over ordered time.

questions.q: Which chart best compares counts across five transport modes?
o: Scatter plot of two unknown measures
questions.e: Bars compare separate categories on a common scale.

questions.q: Which chart shows the relationship between engine temperature and fuel use for individual journeys?
questions.e: A scatter plot positions paired measurements to reveal a relationship or outliers.

questions.q: Which chart adds a third numerical variable through marker size?
questions.e: Bubble size encodes an additional quantity.

questions.q: Which chart can emphasise the magnitude of a quantity across time by filling the space under its line?
questions.e: Area shading can communicate magnitude or composition over time.

questions.q: Which chart can show each category's share of a single total when there are few categories?
questions.e: Each slice represents part of a whole.

questions.q: Which method is most suitable for monitoring several metrics that update during a shift?
questions.e: A dashboard brings key measures together and can update as data changes.

questions.q: A charity wants to share campaign results with volunteers and trustees. Explain why an infographic and a report may serve different audiences.

pts.p: An infographic can show key figures quickly using simple visuals for volunteers.
A report can give trustees detailed figures, methodology and limitations for scrutiny.

questions.model: An infographic can show key figures quickly using simple visuals for volunteers. A report can give trustees detailed figures, methodology and limitations for scrutiny.

questions.q: Explain one advantage of a shared document and one advantage of presenting charts on slides in an online meeting.

pts.p: A shared document supports comments and joint review before decisions are made.
Slides focus attention on selected charts while the presenter explains and answers questions live.

questions.model: A shared document supports comments and joint review before decisions are made. Slides focus attention on selected charts while the presenter explains and answers questions live.

questions.q: A bus operator needs to brief dispatchers on delays during the shift and trustees on quarterly performance. Evaluate the use of a dashboard and a written report for these audiences.

pts.p: A dashboard can show current delay measures by route so dispatchers know where an intervention is needed.
Frequent updates make it useful during a shift provided incoming records are timely and missing feeds are flagged.
Too many indicators or unclear scales can hide urgent changes, so the dashboard should prioritise a small set of measures.
A written report can give trustees quarterly trends, explain causes and set out limitations of the available evidence.
A static report takes time to prepare and is less useful for responding immediately to individual disruptions.
Use the dashboard for operational decisions and the report for oversight, with consistent definitions so the audiences can compare measures.

questions.model: A dashboard can show current delay measures by route so dispatchers know where an intervention is needed. Frequent updates make it useful during a shift provided incoming records are timely and missing feeds are flagged. Too many indicators or unclear scales can hide urgent changes, so the dashboard should prioritise a small set of measures. A written report can give trustees quarterly trends, explain causes and set out limitations of the available evidence. A static report takes time to prepare and is less useful for responding immediately to individual disruptions. Use the dashboard for operational decisions and the report for oversight, with consistent definitions so the audiences can compare measures.
questions.marking_guidance: Use the points to review your reasoning. For a high-level answer, apply both sides to the scenario, develop their consequences and support your judgement. The practice score is a keyword estimate.

questions.q: What distinguishes an archive from ordinary active storage?
o: It retains less frequently used data for later retrieval.
It is always permanently offline and unrecoverable.
It always destroys the original records immediately.
It must contain only current edits.
questions.e: Archiving keeps inactive records accessible when needed.

questions.q: Why test restoring an archived dataset?
o: To confirm records remain retrievable and usable.
questions.e: Restoration testing can reveal unreadable files or missing dependencies.

questions.q: Compare one advantage of cloud archival with one advantage of keeping an archive on site.

pts.p: Cloud archival can keep a copy away from a local disaster and scale capacity.
On-site archival can provide direct control of physical access or retrieval without internet connectivity.

questions.model: Cloud archival can keep a copy away from a local disaster and scale capacity. On-site archival can provide direct control of physical access or retrieval without internet connectivity.

questions.q: A research group needs to retain completed survey data for several years. Compare cloud archival with a network archive at its premises and recommend an approach.

pts.p: Cloud archival can hold a copy away from the building, reducing the risk that a single local incident destroys the data.
The group should check provider retrieval costs and delays, especially if several large datasets must be restored together.
An on-site network archive may offer fast access over the local network without waiting for internet connectivity.
It requires local administration and protection against failures, unauthorised access and physical damage at the premises.
Either option needs an agreed retention period, access controls and a restoration test to show files remain readable.
Choose a controlled off-site copy alongside local access where justified, and test recovery before relying on either copy.

questions.model: Cloud archival can hold a copy away from the building, reducing the risk that a single local incident destroys the data. The group should check provider retrieval costs and delays, especially if several large datasets must be restored together. An on-site network archive may offer fast access over the local network without waiting for internet connectivity. It requires local administration and protection against failures, unauthorised access and physical damage at the premises. Either option needs an agreed retention period, access controls and a restoration test to show files remain readable. Choose a controlled off-site copy alongside local access where justified, and test recovery before relying on either copy.
questions.marking_guidance: Use the points to review your reasoning. For a high-level answer, apply both sides to the scenario, develop their consequences and support your judgement. The practice score is a keyword estimate.

questions.q: Which is a limitation of relying on a network archive at the same site as active storage?
o: The archive automatically stops all access to active files.
The network archive cannot retain more than one record.
A local incident could affect both copies.
questions.e: Shared location creates a common risk even when the archive is on separate equipment.

questions.q: Which method uses a strong magnetic field to sanitise suitable magnetic media?
questions.e: Degaussing targets magnetic media. It is unsuitable for SSD flash cells.

questions.q: What does overwriting aim to do?
o: Replace stored data with other patterns so the original cannot readily be recovered.
Move the file to another folder.
questions.e: Overwriting must suit the medium and reach the intended storage locations.

questions.q: Which method physically fragments retired storage media?
questions.e: Shredding destroys the physical media. The process must suit the device and confidentiality needs.

questions.q: A firm plans to reuse SSDs internally. Explain why it should use a verified device-appropriate erasure process rather than degaussing.

pts.p: SSDs store data in flash memory, so a magnetic field does not remove the stored data.
A suitable secure erasure process can sanitise the SSD and verification confirms completion before reuse.

questions.model: SSDs store data in flash memory, so a magnetic field does not remove the stored data. A suitable secure erasure process can sanitise the SSD and verification confirms completion before reuse.

questions.q: An encrypted drive has reached the end of its life. Why might a firm choose verified physical drive destruction?
o: It allows the same drive to be reused immediately.
It proves every backup copy was also destroyed.
It makes the medium unusable and reduces recovery risk when reuse is unnecessary.
It preserves the stored files for a later audit.
questions.e: Physical destruction targets the specific medium. Other copies need their own disposal decisions.

questions.q: Why does a ticketing website use a payment API?
o: To grant the website direct ownership of the payment database.
To guarantee that no network can fail.
To exchange requests and responses through a defined interface.
To remove the need to handle failed payments.
questions.e: An API specifies how systems interact while keeping their implementations separate.

questions.q: Which API category restricts access to approved external organisations?
questions.e: Partner APIs allow selected external parties under agreed access terms.

questions.q: Which API category is designed for use within the organisation?
questions.e: Internal and private commonly overlap. Their intended consumers are inside the organisation.

questions.q: What does a composite API let a caller do?
o: Remove every dependency on other systems.
Use only one data format for all APIs.
Combine related operations in a single interaction.
questions.e: A composite API combines operations, potentially reducing repeated requests.

questions.q: Which format does SOAP use for its messages?
questions.e: SOAP uses XML envelopes.

questions.q: Which API style often sends JSON representations of resources but does not require JSON?
questions.e: REST is an architectural style and can use multiple representation formats.

questions.q: Which approach sends remote procedure calls represented in JSON?
questions.e: JSON-RPC represents method calls and responses in JSON.

questions.q: Which approach sends a remote procedure call represented in XML?
questions.e: XML-RPC encodes procedure calls and results in XML.

questions.q: A city provides a public bus-arrival API. Explain a benefit for developers and one limitation they should plan for.

pts.p: Developers can reuse consistent live arrival data in independent travel apps.
An outage or rate limit can make an app's live updates unavailable or stale.

questions.model: Developers can reuse consistent live arrival data in independent travel apps. An outage or rate limit can make an app's live updates unavailable or stale.

questions.q: Access is based on whether someone is a payroll clerk or a team manager. Which control fits?
o: ABAC based solely on device location
questions.e: Role-based access control assigns permissions according to job roles.

questions.q: Which control lets a document owner choose who receives access?
questions.e: Discretionary access control allows an owner to grant access within applicable rules.

questions.q: Which control compares fixed security labels with a user's clearance?
questions.e: Mandatory access control enforces central security classifications.

questions.q: A decision combines the user's department, document sensitivity and device status. Which model fits?
o: RBAC using one job role alone
questions.e: Attribute-based decisions evaluate attributes of the subject, resource and environment.

questions.q: Which is a typical rule-based access control example?
o: Let every owner share a file at will.
Block logins outside an approved time window.
Allow users solely because they are payroll clerks.
questions.e: Rule-based access applies predefined conditions, such as time restrictions.

questions.q: Explain why using RBAC might simplify access management for a support team and what should happen when an employee changes role.

pts.p: Permissions can be assigned to the support role once and inherited by its members.
Remove the old role and assign the new role so unneeded access does not persist.

questions.model: Permissions can be assigned to the support role once and inherited by its members. Remove the old role and assign the new role so unneeded access does not persist.

questions.q: A care provider gives visiting staff access to records on managed tablets. Access depends on both their job duties and which patients they are visiting that day. Evaluate role-based and attribute-based controls and justify an approach.

pts.p: RBAC assigns standard permissions to job roles, which makes repeated staff onboarding and review easier.
A role alone may grant access to too many patient records because assignments change daily within the same role.
ABAC can combine staff role, patient assignment and managed device status for a more specific decision.
This depends on accurate and timely assignment data, or staff might be denied access when they need it.
Complex rules require testing and auditing because conflicting conditions could allow inappropriate access or block legitimate work.
Use role permissions as a baseline and apply attribute checks for patient assignment and device, with an escalation process for exceptional access.

questions.model: RBAC assigns standard permissions to job roles, which makes repeated staff onboarding and review easier. A role alone may grant access to too many patient records because assignments change daily within the same role. ABAC can combine staff role, patient assignment and managed device status for a more specific decision. This depends on accurate and timely assignment data, or staff might be denied access when they need it. Complex rules require testing and auditing because conflicting conditions could allow inappropriate access or block legitimate work. Use role permissions as a baseline and apply attribute checks for patient assignment and device, with an escalation process for exceptional access.
questions.marking_guidance: Use the points to review your reasoning. For a high-level answer, apply both sides to the scenario, develop their consequences and support your judgement. The practice score is a keyword estimate.

questions.q: Which permission is needed to view a report without modifying it?
questions.e: Read permits inspection without changing the stored report.

questions.q: Which permission allows a staff member to alter an existing entry?
questions.e: Editing modifies an existing record. Systems may bundle it under write.

questions.q: Which task typically belongs to an administrator?
o: Enter a booking as a standard user.
View a read-only chart as a guest.
questions.e: Administrators allocate or manage user and group access.

questions.q: A records clerk must create new files but should not remove old ones. Explain a suitable permission setup.

pts.p: Grant write or create permission for the required folder so the clerk can add files.
Withhold delete permission and test the effective user or group privileges.

questions.model: Grant write or create permission for the required folder so the clerk can add files. Withhold delete permission and test the effective user or group privileges.

4.1.title: 4.1 Legislation and the role of the ICO

questions.q: Which law addresses deliberate unauthorised access to a computer system?
questions.e: The Computer Misuse Act includes offences involving unauthorised access.

questions.q: A member of the public requests a recorded council procurement policy. Which law is most relevant?
questions.e: FOIA provides access to recorded information held by relevant public authorities, subject to exemptions.

questions.q: Which legislation is most specifically concerned with electronic direct marketing and rules on accessing information on a device?
questions.e: PECR addresses electronic communications and device storage or access, with conditions and exceptions.

questions.q: Which is a data minimisation decision for a room booking service?
o: Collect contact details needed for booking and omit unrelated information.
Collect all possible personal details in case they become useful.
questions.e: Personal data should be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary.

questions.q: Which Act supplements the UK's general data protection framework?
o: Privacy and Electronic Communications Regulations alone
questions.e: The DPA 2018 sits alongside the UK GDPR. Both have been amended.

questions.q: Which organisation investigates data protection complaints and can take enforcement action in the UK?
questions.e: The ICO provides guidance and regulates information rights and data protection.

questions.q: A sports centre collects contact details for bookings. Explain two actions that support UK GDPR compliance.

pts.p: Identify an appropriate lawful basis and explain why the contact details are collected in a privacy notice.
Limit access to staff who need the details and remove records when the retention purpose ends.

questions.model: Identify an appropriate lawful basis and explain why the contact details are collected in a privacy notice. Limit access to staff who need the details and remove records when the retention purpose ends.

questions.q: An employee discovers a way to bypass a supplier's login. Explain why testing it without permission could have consequences.

pts.p: Knowingly gaining unauthorised access to the supplier's system can be an offence under the Computer Misuse Act.
The incident may lead to investigation and criminal penalties if an offence is proved.

questions.model: Knowingly gaining unauthorised access to the supplier's system can be an offence under the Computer Misuse Act. The incident may lead to investigation and criminal penalties if an offence is proved.

questions.q: A council receives an information request for a contract containing third-party personal data. Explain how it should respond.

pts.p: Identify the recorded information held and assess the request under FOIA.
Check applicable exemptions and consider redacting protected personal data before releasing disclosable parts.

questions.model: Identify the recorded information held and assess the request under FOIA. Check applicable exemptions and consider redacting protected personal data before releasing disclosable parts.

questions.q: A venue wants to reuse contact details from ticket purchases for promotional emails and install optional advertising trackers. Discuss the legislation it should consider and recommend a responsible approach.

pts.p: UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018 govern the processing of identifiable customer contact details.
The venue should identify a lawful basis and clearly explain its marketing purpose and retention in a privacy notice.
PECR has specific requirements for unsolicited electronic marketing, so check whether consent or a permitted exception applies before emailing.
For optional advertising trackers, obtain valid consent where required before accessing or storing information on a device.
Make refusal and withdrawal practical, and restrict access to contact records to staff with a defined need.
Introduce marketing and tracking only after checking these conditions because complaints can trigger ICO investigation and enforcement.

questions.model: UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018 govern the processing of identifiable customer contact details. The venue should identify a lawful basis and clearly explain its marketing purpose and retention in a privacy notice. PECR has specific requirements for unsolicited electronic marketing, so check whether consent or a permitted exception applies before emailing. For optional advertising trackers, obtain valid consent where required before accessing or storing information on a device. Make refusal and withdrawal practical, and restrict access to contact records to staff with a defined need. Introduce marketing and tracking only after checking these conditions because complaints can trigger ICO investigation and enforcement.
questions.marking_guidance: Use the points to review your reasoning. For a high-level answer, apply both sides to the scenario, develop their consequences and support your judgement. The practice score is a keyword estimate.

questions.q: Which statement describes the relationship between the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 and UK data protection rules?
o: It replaced them all with the Computer Misuse Act.
It removed data protection requirements for organisations.
It amended the UK GDPR, DPA 2018 and PECR.
It made FOIA the only law covering personal data.
questions.e: The existing regimes continue to apply as amended by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025.

5.1.title: 5.1 Job roles in the data pipeline

questions.q: Who designs how datasets and data stores should fit together across a business?
questions.e: A data architect designs data structures and how systems share and manage data.

questions.q: Who typically builds and maintains the flow from event capture to prepared data stores?
questions.e: A data engineer implements and maintains pipelines and their integrations.

questions.q: Who typically interprets recurring performance reports and explains results to managers?
questions.e: A data analyst turns data into findings that inform decisions.

questions.q: Who typically manages database access, backups and recovery?
questions.e: A database administrator helps keep database services secure, available and recoverable.

questions.q: Who is most directly responsible for putting a trained model into a reliable live prediction service?
questions.e: The machine learning engineer focuses on operational deployment and monitoring of models.

questions.q: Who would most typically test statistical models to predict demand from a range of datasets?
questions.e: A data scientist experiments with models and assesses their suitability.

questions.q: Who would most typically research and evaluate a new AI approach for interpreting incident reports?
questions.e: AI scientists investigate and evaluate AI methods. Responsibilities can overlap with adjacent roles.

questions.q: A transport operator needs a reliable data feed and a weekly explanation of delays. Explain the contributions of a data engineer and a data analyst.

pts.p: The engineer builds and monitors the ingestion and processing pipeline so records arrive reliably.
The analyst examines the records for delay patterns and communicates findings to managers.

questions.model: The engineer builds and monitors the ingestion and processing pipeline so records arrive reliably. The analyst examines the records for delay patterns and communicates findings to managers.

questions.q: A ferry operator wants to forecast demand using booking and weather records. Explain how a data engineer, data scientist and machine learning engineer would work together. Justify a handover check.

pts.p: The data engineer builds ingestion for booking and weather feeds and monitors whether expected records arrive on time.
The engineer makes prepared data available with consistent meanings and documents gaps that could affect modelling.
The data scientist explores patterns and compares forecasts using held-out observations to estimate model quality.
The scientist explains uncertainty and known limitations so the operator can judge how far to rely on predictions.
The machine learning engineer deploys the selected model and monitors its live performance when booking patterns change.
Before handover, compare the model inputs in testing and production, because mismatched definitions could make the operational predictions unreliable.

questions.model: The data engineer builds ingestion for booking and weather feeds and monitors whether expected records arrive on time. The engineer makes prepared data available with consistent meanings and documents gaps that could affect modelling. The data scientist explores patterns and compares forecasts using held-out observations to estimate model quality. The scientist explains uncertainty and known limitations so the operator can judge how far to rely on predictions. The machine learning engineer deploys the selected model and monitors its live performance when booking patterns change. Before handover, compare the model inputs in testing and production, because mismatched definitions could make the operational predictions unreliable.
questions.marking_guidance: Use the points to review your reasoning. For a high-level answer, apply both sides to the scenario, develop their consequences and support your judgement. The practice score is a keyword estimate.

questions.q: Which attribute helps a data engineer find the source of a failed import by testing possible causes?
questions.e: Problem solving involves diagnosing causes and testing fixes.

questions.q: Which attribute is most directly shown when a team lead sets priorities and coordinates work across roles?
questions.e: Leadership guides the team and coordinates its efforts.

questions.q: Which behaviour best shows self-motivation?
o: A team member avoids checking an unexplained result.
An analyst starts investigating a known quality issue without repeated prompting.
An analyst waits for repeated reminders before starting.
questions.e: Self-motivation is the drive to begin and sustain work.

questions.q: Which behaviour shows analytical skill?
o: Draw a conclusion without looking at data.
Ignore an unexpected value because the report is due.
Break down a surprising total and compare its component records.
Accept any graph with a professional appearance.
questions.e: Analytical skill includes examining evidence systematically.

questions.q: An analyst has two reporting deadlines and needs records from another team. Explain how planning and teamwork help.

pts.p: Plan milestones and allocate time to check the data before each deadline.
Agree responsibilities and share requirements early with the other team to avoid delays.

questions.model: Plan milestones and allocate time to check the data before each deadline. Agree responsibilities and share requirements early with the other team to avoid delays.

questions.q: Explain how independence and effective communication can both help a database administrator during an incident.

pts.p: Work independently through diagnostic checks without waiting for every instruction.
Communicate impact and recovery progress clearly to affected staff or managers.

questions.model: Work independently through diagnostic checks without waiting for every instruction. Communicate impact and recovery progress clearly to affected staff or managers.

questions.q: Which behaviour shows time management when a report is due by midday?
o: Wait until the deadline to estimate the workload.
Reserve time for quality checks and finish urgent tasks before lower-priority work.
Skip checks whenever the team receives new work.
Start every task at the same time without prioritising.
questions.e: Time management involves prioritising work and allowing enough time to finish it accurately.

questions.q: Which is an open question that encourages detail during data gathering?
o: Did you complete the form, yes or no?
What difficulties did you encounter when booking?
questions.e: Open questions invite description. Neutral wording reduces leading.

questions.q: Which is an example of non-verbal communication during a discussion?
o: Nodding to acknowledge a speaker's point
questions.e: Gesture and facial expression are non-verbal signals.

questions.q: Which approach suits a written briefing for managers unfamiliar with data engineering?
o: Copy the entire pipeline log into the executive summary.
Use only code and no interpretation.
Explain findings in plain language and define essential technical terms.
questions.e: Audience-appropriate wording makes findings and actions understandable.

questions.q: A data engineer is gathering requirements for a dashboard. Explain how verbal questioning and written follow-up can improve the capture stage.

pts.p: Use open verbal questions and follow-ups to clarify which data and decisions users need.
Send a written summary for stakeholders to confirm agreed definitions and requirements.

questions.model: Use open verbal questions and follow-ups to clarify which data and decisions users need. Send a written summary for stakeholders to confirm agreed definitions and requirements.

f201.title: Big Data and Machine Learning
f201.coming: Topic Areas 3+ will be added when the notes are finished.
f201.notice: Work in progress: F201 currently only covers Topic Areas 1 and 2. More topics will be added as the notes are completed.

1.title: Topic Area 1: The Scope of Managing Big Data
1.blurb: The 6Vs, the six stages of analysing big data, the evolution of big data and big data analytics.

questions.q: Which characteristic of big data refers to the amount of data being generated and stored?
questions.e: Volume is the sheer amount of data collected every day.

questions.q: A company collects customer reviews, photos, videos and voice recordings. Which characteristic is demonstrated?
questions.e: Variety means many different types of data from many different sources.

questions.q: Which characteristic is concerned with the reliability and accuracy of data?
questions.e: Veracity: data can be messy, noisy and incorrect, making it hard to trust and control.

questions.q: A stock trading platform processes thousands of transactions per second. Which characteristic is most relevant?
questions.e: Velocity is the speed at which data is generated and collected.

questions.q: Which characteristic relates to changing trends and inconsistencies in the meaning of data over time?
questions.e: Variability: changes in the meaning of data lead to inconsistencies, e.g. social media trends during a major event.

questions.q: Netflix stores billions of viewing records every day. Which V is most relevant?
questions.e: Billions of records is a huge amount of data, so Volume.

questions.q: An organisation checks whether its data is accurate. Which V does this address?
questions.e: Checking accuracy deals with Veracity, as data can be incorrect.

questions.q: Which V describes how useful the data is to an organisation?
questions.e: Value is the worth / usefulness of the data, e.g. supporting decisions.

questions.q: Which stage of big data analysis involves gathering raw information from sources such as sensors?
questions.e: Data Collection is the first stage of the pipeline: data has to enter the system.

questions.q: Which stage removes duplicate records and corrects errors?
questions.e: Data Cleaning sanitises data and transforms it into a usable format.

questions.q: Which stage identifies hidden trends and relationships in data?
questions.e: Data Mining finds and extracts patterns to reveal key information.

questions.q: Storing data in a data warehouse belongs to which stage?
questions.e: Data Storage moves data to high-availability storage so it is not lost.

questions.q: Presenting results to managers to drive decisions is which stage?
questions.e: Data Consumption is where data is utilised to drive decision making.

questions.q: What is the correct order of the six stages?
o: Collection, Cleaning, Storage, Mining, Analysis, Consumption
Collection, Storage, Cleaning, Mining, Analysis, Consumption
Storage, Collection, Mining, Cleaning, Analysis, Consumption
Collection, Storage, Mining, Cleaning, Consumption, Analysis
questions.e: Collection → Storage → Cleaning → Mining → Analysis → Consumption.

questions.q: Why should data cleaning happen before analysis?
o: Duplicates and errors would otherwise skew the results
questions.e: Dirty data (duplicates, wrong formats) produces inaccurate analysis.

questions.q: Which development lets users Create, Read, Update and Delete (CRUD) data efficiently while maintaining consistency?
questions.e: A DBMS provides the infrastructure for CRUD operations and data integrity (ACID).

questions.q: The Internet of Everything (IoE) connects which of the following?
o: Only servers in a data centre
questions.e: IoE extends beyond computers to people, processes, data and things, generating massive volumes of data.

questions.q: Which is a limitation of a DBMS?
o: High cost for hardware and personnel
questions.e: DBMSs carry high hardware/personnel costs and performance overhead.

questions.q: Which is a key benefit of web-based storage such as Amazon S3 or Google Drive?
questions.e: Web-based storage is cost efficient and scalable, but relies on a third party.

questions.q: How did the proliferation of devices contribute to big data?
o: It reduced the amount of data
Billions of sensors and smartphones each generate data
It removed the need for storage
questions.e: The widespread growth of devices means huge amounts of data are produced.

questions.q: Which is a limitation of search engines as a source of data?
questions.e: Search results can be manipulated (SEO), saturated with ads and contain misinformation.

questions.q: Which sector would use analytics mainly to detect fraud in transactions?
questions.e: Banks analyse transaction data to detect and prevent fraud.

questions.q: Netflix "Because you watched…" suggestions are an example of analytics in which sector?
questions.e: Recommendation systems are a classic Media & Entertainment application.

2.title: Topic Area 2: Big Data Processing
2.blurb: Types of data, data preparation, data mining, infrastructure, data science and analytic techniques.

questions.q: A supermarket till records product code, quantity, price, date and time. What type of data is this?
questions.e: It fits predefined fields, making it easy to store, search and analyse.

questions.q: Customer emails have a sender, recipient, date and subject but free-form message text. What type of data are they?
questions.e: Some organisational properties (headers) but the body does not fit a rigid table.

questions.q: Photographs, videos and comments about a product on social media are…
questions.e: No predefined format; often text or multimedia.

questions.q: Two organisations exchange customer information using XML tags. XML is…
questions.e: Tags give a flexible structure, but free-form text can sit inside them.

questions.q: A weather station records temperature throughout the day. This data is…
questions.e: Continuous data is measured; discrete data is counted.

questions.q: A cinema records the number of people attending each showing. This data is…
questions.e: Attendance is counted, so it is discrete.

questions.q: Which is a limitation of structured data?
o: Strict format is inflexible to additional data
questions.e: Structured data is easy to analyse but its strict format is inflexible.

questions.q: Which is a limitation of unstructured data?
o: Very hard to analyse and expensive to process
questions.e: Unstructured data gives rich insights but is hard and costly to analyse.

questions.q: Zipped files are an example of semi-structured data. What is their main limitation?
o: They must be extracted before analysis
questions.e: Compression reduces size, but files must be extracted before analysis.

questions.q: What is data preparation?
o: Getting raw data ready for analysis by organising, formatting and transforming it
questions.e: Preparation organises, formats and transforms raw data so it is ready for analysis.

questions.q: Which is a preparation method for numeric data?
questions.e: Numeric preparation: remove obvious errors, ensure consistent units, normalise values.

questions.q: Removing exclamation marks from reviews during text preparation risks…
questions.e: Textual preparation can lose context, e.g. changing how a sentence is read.

questions.q: Data wrangling is best described as…
o: Transforming and structuring raw data, e.g. merging datasets and reformatting fields
questions.e: Wrangling combines data from different sources and reshapes it. Benefit: usability; limitation: time-consuming.

questions.q: Prices stored as text instead of numbers should be fixed by…
questions.e: Converting data types enables correct analysis (risk: conversion errors).

questions.q: Dates recorded in different formats across stores should be fixed using…
questions.e: Consistent formatting improves consistency but requires clear standards.

questions.q: What is a limitation of fixing missing data with estimated values?
o: Estimated values may reduce accuracy or add bias
questions.e: It prevents data loss, but estimates may not represent the real values.

questions.q: What is a risk of removing duplicates?
questions.e: It prevents double counting, but genuine repeat records could be removed.

questions.q: Validating data before analysis has which limitation?
o: It can reject large volumes of data
questions.e: Validation ensures data meets required rules but may reject a lot of data.

questions.q: Which storage area holds large amounts of raw/unstructured data and risks becoming a "data swamp"?
questions.e: Data lakes store raw data from many sources; poorly organised ones become swamps.

questions.q: Which storage area stores structured data so analytic tools can be applied immediately?
questions.e: Data warehouses hold structured data but cannot store unstructured data.

questions.q: A government department storing secure citizen records should choose…
questions.e: Private cloud gives greater control and security (but higher cost).

questions.q: A social media platform storing millions of photos daily that must scale quickly fits best with…
questions.e: Distributed clusters scale to handle huge volumes of unstructured data.

questions.q: A small local business with limited, rarely changing data is best suited to…
questions.e: A single dedicated server is enough for small, stable data.

questions.q: Which is a limitation of SSD storage?
o: High cost per GB and limited capacity
questions.e: SSDs are fast with no moving parts but cost more per GB and are harder to scale.

questions.q: Microsoft Project Silica stores data on glass. What is its main limitation?
o: It only lasts a few years
It can only be written once
questions.e: Lasers engrave the glass, so it is write-once, read-many. Ideal for archives.

questions.q: Which software platform stores non-relational, unstructured or semi-structured data and scales well?
questions.e: NoSQL is flexible and scalable but less suitable for complex queries.

questions.q: Which is a limitation of open-source big data software?
questions.e: Open source is highly adaptable but needs technical expertise.

questions.q: Data science is mainly…
o: Forward looking: discovering patterns and building predictive models
questions.e: Data science explores large varied datasets to predict and innovate.

questions.q: Data analytics is mainly…
o: Understanding current and past performance to support operational decisions
questions.e: Analytics is descriptive/diagnostic, working with existing (often structured) data.

questions.q: Fraud prediction in banking is an example of…
questions.e: Predicting fraud with ML models is data science; transaction reporting would be analytics.

questions.q: Forecasting next quarter's sales from historical data is best done with…
questions.e: Time series analyses data points over time to forecast future values.

questions.q: Grouping customers with similar buying behaviour uses…
questions.e: Cluster analysis groups similar data points (e.g. by Euclidean distance).

questions.q: Tracking users grouped by signup month to measure retention is…
questions.e: Cohort analysis groups by shared characteristics and tracks behaviour over time.

questions.q: Estimating the relationship between a dependent variable and independent variables is…
questions.e: Regression shows how variables affect an outcome; it may oversimplify.

questions.q: Modelling the probability of outcomes affected by random variables is…
questions.e: Monte Carlo models uncertainty and risk but has high computational cost.

questions.q: Explaining correlations between many survey variables using a small number of underlying factors is…
questions.e: Factor analysis uncovers hidden factors; needs a large sample and careful interpretation.

questions.q: Which is a limitation of cluster analysis?
o: A cluster existing does not prove a relationship
It only works on time data
questions.e: Clusters can be ambiguous and sensitive to noise.

questions.q: Which is a limitation of time series analysis?
questions.e: Outliers and irregular data can heavily skew time series results.

1-1-1.group: 1.1 Characteristics of contemporary processors, input, output and storage devices
1-1-1.title: 1.1.1 Structure and function of the processor
1-1-1.blurb: CPU components, buses, the fetch-decode-execute cycle, performance factors, pipelining and Von Neumann vs Harvard.

questions.q: Which register holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched?
questions.e: The PC points to the next instruction. During fetch its value is copied to the MAR.

questions.q: Which register holds the address of the memory location that is about to be read from or written to?
questions.e: The MAR holds the address, which is sent to main memory along the address bus.

questions.q: All data travelling to and from main memory passes through which register, acting as a buffer?
questions.e: The MDR temporarily holds data that has been read from, or is about to be written to, memory.

questions.q: Which register holds the instruction that is currently being decoded and executed?
questions.e: The fetched instruction is copied from the MDR to the CIR, ready to be split into opcode and operand.

questions.q: What is the main job of the Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU)?
o: Sending control signals to the other components
Carrying out arithmetic and logical (Boolean) operations
Storing the address of the next instruction
Holding data fetched from main memory
questions.e: The ALU performs calculations (add, subtract...) and logic operations (AND, OR, NOT...). Control signals come from the Control Unit.

questions.q: What does the accumulator (ACC) store?
o: The result of the last calculation carried out by the ALU
The address of the next instruction
questions.e: The ACC holds intermediate results of ALU calculations.

questions.q: Which component coordinates the other parts of the CPU using control signals?
questions.e: The CU sends signals along the control bus, e.g. read/write signals to memory and signals to increment the PC.

questions.q: Which bus carries memory addresses in ONE direction only, from the CPU to memory?
questions.e: The address bus is unidirectional. The data and control buses carry signals in both directions.

questions.q: What does the width of the address bus determine?
o: How many bits can be transferred at once between CPU and memory
The number of memory locations that can be addressed
The clock speed of the CPU
questions.e: More address lines means more unique addresses. The width of the data bus decides how many bits move at once.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly describes the FETCH stage?
o: PC copied to MDR, read signal sent along address bus, contents travel to MAR, copied to ALU, PC reset to zero
CIR copied to MAR, address sent along data bus, instruction travels to PC, copied to ACC, MDR incremented
PC copied to MAR, address sent along address bus, read signal sent on control bus, contents travel along data bus to MDR, copied to CIR, PC incremented
MAR copied to PC, instruction decoded by ALU, result stored in MDR, read signal sent along data bus, CIR cleared
questions.e: Fetch: PC to MAR, address bus to memory, read signal on the control bus, instruction returns along the data bus to the MDR, then to the CIR, and the PC is incremented.

questions.q: What does the opcode part of an instruction specify?
o: The operation to be carried out
The width of the data bus
The address of the next instruction
The data or address the operation acts on
questions.e: The opcode says what to do. The operand says what to do it to (a value or an address).

questions.q: A CPU has a clock speed of 3 GHz. What does this mean?
o: It can transfer 3 billion bytes per second along the data bus
It can carry out up to 3 billion fetch-decode-execute cycles per second
It can store 3 GB of data in cache
questions.e: Clock speed is measured in hertz: cycles per second. 1 GHz = one billion cycles per second.

questions.q: Why does doubling the number of cores NOT usually double the speed of a program?
o: Each core runs at half the clock speed
The ALU can only be shared by two cores
Not all programs can be split up to use every core, and cores need to communicate
Extra cores can only be used for graphics
questions.e: Software must be written to use multiple cores, and there is an overhead in coordinating cores.

questions.q: Which level of cache is the fastest but has the smallest capacity?
o: They are all the same speed
questions.e: L1 is closest to the core, fastest and smallest. L3 is larger and slower.

questions.q: What is pipelining?
o: Compressing instructions to make them shorter
Running one instruction on several cores at once
Overlapping the fetch, decode and execute stages of different instructions
Storing instructions in cache before they are needed
questions.e: While one instruction is executed, the next is decoded and the one after is fetched, so less of the CPU sits idle.

questions.q: What happens to a pipeline when a branch (e.g. an IF statement) means the next instruction is not the one already fetched?
o: The clock speed is automatically increased
The pipeline is flushed and refilled with the correct instructions
The instructions are executed in reverse
questions.e: The wrongly fetched instructions are discarded (flushed), which wastes cycles.

questions.q: Which statement describes the Von Neumann architecture?
o: Program instructions and data share the same memory and buses
Only the ALU can access memory
Instructions and data use completely separate memories and buses
questions.e: Von Neumann uses one shared memory and bus, which is cheaper and simpler but creates a bottleneck.

questions.q: What is the main advantage of the Harvard architecture over Von Neumann?
o: Instructions and data can be fetched at the same time using separate buses
It only needs one memory chip
questions.e: Separate buses remove the bottleneck, at the cost of extra complexity and expense.

questions.q: How do contemporary processors typically use these architectures?
o: Von Neumann-style shared main memory, with Harvard-style separate instruction and data caches
Neither - they use a completely different design
Von Neumann for the ALU and Harvard for the registers
questions.e: Contemporary CPUs combine both: main memory is shared, but the cache is split into instruction and data caches.

questions.q: Describe the role of the Memory Address Register (MAR) and the Memory Data Register (MDR) in the fetch-decode-execute cycle.

pts.p: MAR holds the address of the memory location to be read from / written to
The address in the MAR is sent along the address bus to main memory
MDR holds data / instructions that have been read from memory or are to be written to memory
All data to and from memory passes through the MDR (it acts as a buffer)

questions.model: The MAR holds the address of the memory location that is to be read from or written to; this address is sent to main memory along the address bus. The MDR temporarily holds the data or instruction that has been fetched from memory, or that is about to be written to it. All data going to or from main memory passes through the MDR, so it acts as a buffer.

questions.q: Explain how the Control Unit interacts with other components during the execution of an instruction.

pts.p: Sends control signals to coordinate the other components
Sends read / write signals to main memory (along the control bus)
Increments the PC / tells the ALU which operation to do / controls data movement between registers

questions.model: The control unit coordinates the CPU by sending electrical control signals to other components. For example, it sends a read or write signal along the control bus to main memory, it makes the PC increment, and it tells the ALU which operation to carry out.

questions.q: Compare the Von Neumann and Harvard architectures. Include one advantage and one disadvantage of each.

pts.p: Von Neumann: shared memory / bus for instructions and data
Von Neumann advantage: cheaper / simpler / smaller circuitry
Von Neumann disadvantage: bottleneck / cannot fetch instruction and data at the same time / slower
Harvard: separate memory / buses for instructions and data
Harvard advantage: instruction and data can be fetched at the same time / faster
Harvard disadvantage: more complex / more expensive / more circuitry

questions.model: Von Neumann uses a single shared memory and bus for both instructions and data. This makes it cheaper and simpler to build, but creates a bottleneck because an instruction and data cannot be fetched at the same time. Harvard uses separate memories and buses for instructions and data, so they can be fetched simultaneously, making it faster; however it is more complex and more expensive to manufacture.

questions.q: Describe how pipelining improves the performance of a CPU.

pts.p: Stages of different instructions overlap (e.g. one is fetched while another is decoded / executed)
Less of the CPU is idle / each component is kept busy
More instructions completed in a given time (higher throughput)
