questions.model: Pipelining overlaps the stages of different instructions: while one instruction is being executed the next is decoded and the one after is fetched. This keeps every part of the CPU busy rather than idle, so more instructions are completed in a given time (higher throughput).

questions.q: Describe the fetch-decode-execute cycle. Refer to the registers and buses used in your answer.

pts.p: PC holds the address of the next instruction
The address is copied from the PC to the MAR
The address is sent along the address bus to main memory
The control unit sends a read signal (control bus)
The instruction travels along the data bus to the MDR
The instruction is copied from the MDR to the CIR
The PC is incremented
Decode: the instruction is split into opcode and operand
Execute: the instruction is carried out (e.g. the ALU performs a calculation / data is fetched using the operand address)
The result is stored (e.g. in the accumulator or written back to memory)

questions.model: Fetch: the address in the program counter (PC) is copied to the memory address register (MAR). The address is sent along the address bus to main memory and the control unit sends a read signal along the control bus. The instruction at that address is sent along the data bus to the memory data register (MDR) and then copied to the current instruction register (CIR). The PC is incremented to point at the next instruction. Decode: the instruction in the CIR is split into its opcode (what to do) and operand (the data or address to act on). Execute: the instruction is carried out, e.g. the ALU performs a calculation, or the operand address is sent to the MAR so that data can be read into the MDR and copied to the accumulator. The result is stored in the accumulator or written back to memory.

1-1-2.group: 1.1 Characteristics of contemporary processors, input, output and storage devices
1-1-2.title: 1.1.2 Types of processor
1-1-2.blurb: CISC vs RISC, GPUs and co-processors, multicore and parallel systems.

questions.q: Which statement best describes a RISC processor?
o: A very large set of complex instructions that each take many cycles
A small set of simple instructions, most of which complete in one clock cycle
A processor that can only run one program at a time
A processor designed only for graphics
questions.e: RISC = Reduced Instruction Set Computer: fewer, simpler instructions, typically one cycle each.

questions.q: Which statement best describes a CISC processor?
o: A processor with exactly one core
A large set of complex instructions, some of which take several clock cycles
A small set of identical single-cycle instructions
questions.e: CISC = Complex Instruction Set Computer.

questions.q: A program written for a CISC processor usually needs fewer lines of code than the same program on a RISC processor. Why?
o: Each complex instruction can do the work of several simple instructions
CISC processors have a faster clock speed
questions.e: One CISC instruction can load, calculate and store in a single step; RISC needs several simple instructions.

questions.q: Why are RISC processors well suited to pipelining?
o: They do not need a control unit
Instructions are simple and take the same time, so the stages overlap predictably
questions.e: Uniform, single-cycle instructions keep the pipeline flowing. Variable-length CISC instructions can cause delays.

questions.q: Why are RISC processors commonly found in smartphones and tablets?
o: They are always faster than CISC processors
They can run more cores than any other design
They use less power and generate less heat
questions.e: Simpler circuitry with fewer transistors means lower power consumption, important for battery-powered devices.

questions.q: Which of these is a disadvantage of CISC compared to RISC?
o: The compiler must do much more work
More complex circuitry, so higher cost and power use
It cannot be used in desktop computers
questions.e: CISC needs more transistors and more complex hardware.

questions.q: Which statement about compilers is correct?
o: The compiler does the same work for both
RISC does not need a compiler
The compiler has more work to do for RISC because each instruction does less
The compiler has more work to do for CISC because it has fewer instructions
questions.e: With only simple instructions available, the compiler has to build complex operations from several RISC instructions.

questions.q: What is a GPU?
o: A device that connects a monitor to a computer
The part of the CPU that stores pixels
A specialised co-processor with many cores that performs many calculations in parallel
A type of RAM used for graphics only
questions.e: A GPU supplements the CPU and has hundreds or thousands of simple cores.

questions.q: Why is a GPU suited to rendering graphics?
o: It has a higher clock speed than any CPU
It has more cache than a CPU
Pixels and vertices can be calculated at the same time on many cores
It runs the operating system more efficiently
questions.e: Graphics involves repeating the same maths on huge amounts of data - ideal for parallel processing.

questions.q: Which of the following non-graphics tasks is well suited to a GPU?
o: Running the operating system's file manager
questions.e: Machine learning involves large matrix calculations that can be done in parallel. Others include cryptocurrency mining and scientific simulation.

questions.q: What is a multicore processor?
o: A CPU with a very large cache
Two separate computers connected by a network
A processor that can only run one core at a time
A single chip containing two or more cores, each able to run its own fetch-decode-execute cycle
questions.e: Each core can process instructions independently, improving throughput.

questions.q: What is meant by parallel processing?
o: Splitting a task into parts which are carried out at the same time on multiple cores or processors
Processing instructions in a random order
questions.e: Parallel processing divides the work between processors/cores so parts run simultaneously.

questions.q: A program has not been written to use multiple cores. What is the likely result of running it on an 8-core CPU?
o: It automatically rewrites itself to be parallel
It runs mostly on one core, so it is not much faster
questions.e: Software has to be designed for parallel processing to benefit from multiple cores.

questions.q: What is a co-processor?
o: The second core in a dual-core CPU
A processor that only works when the CPU is switched off
A secondary processor designed to supplement the main CPU for particular tasks
A memory chip that holds the BIOS
questions.e: Examples include GPUs, and maths or sound co-processors.

questions.q: Explain the difference between a CISC processor and a RISC processor.

pts.p: CISC has a large set of complex instructions
RISC has a small set of simple instructions
RISC instructions take one clock cycle / CISC instructions can take several cycles
RISC programs are longer / need more instructions (CISC programs are shorter)
RISC has simpler hardware / lower power; CISC has more complex hardware

questions.model: A CISC processor has a large set of complex instructions, some of which take several clock cycles, so programs are shorter. A RISC processor has a small set of simple instructions, each normally taking one clock cycle, so programs are longer and the compiler does more work, but the hardware is simpler and uses less power.

questions.q: Explain why RISC processors are better suited to pipelining than CISC processors.

pts.p: RISC instructions are simple / the same length / take one clock cycle
So each stage takes the same time and the stages of different instructions can overlap smoothly
CISC instructions take varying numbers of cycles, causing delays / stalls / idle pipeline stages

questions.model: RISC instructions are simple and each normally takes one clock cycle, so every stage of the pipeline takes the same time and the next instruction can be fed in without waiting. CISC instructions take a variable number of cycles, which causes delays and leaves pipeline stages idle.

questions.q: Explain two reasons why a GPU is suitable for graphics rendering.

pts.p: A GPU has a large number of cores
The cores work in parallel / carry out many calculations at the same time
Rendering involves repeating the same calculation on many pixels / vertices / polygons
A GPU is optimised for the maths (vector / matrix calculations) used in graphics

questions.model: A GPU has hundreds or thousands of cores that work in parallel, so many calculations can be carried out at the same time. Rendering graphics means performing the same maths on millions of pixels, vertices and polygons, and the GPU is optimised for this kind of matrix and vector calculation.

questions.q: A quad-core processor does not usually run a program four times faster than a single-core processor. Explain why.

pts.p: The program may not be written to use multiple cores / cannot be split into parallel parts
Some instructions depend on the results of others so must wait
Overheads of coordinating / communicating between cores (or sharing memory / cache)

questions.model: Not all programs can be split into parts that run in parallel, and some instructions depend on the results of others so have to wait. There is also an overhead in coordinating and communicating between the cores, so the speed-up is less than four times.

questions.q: A company is designing a new games console. Discuss the processor features it should include.

pts.p: A multicore CPU lets different tasks (e.g. game logic, AI, operating system) run on separate cores at the same time
Parallel processing speeds up work, but only if the game software is written to use multiple cores
A GPU / co-processor with many cores renders graphics in parallel
This frees up the CPU for other tasks / gives smoother frame rates
A RISC-style design uses less power / produces less heat, which suits a small enclosed case
Pipelining and cache increase instruction throughput / reduce waiting for RAM
Higher clock speed gives more cycles per second but produces more heat / uses more power
A trade-off is needed between performance, cost and heat / power (e.g. more cores cost more)

questions.model: The console should use a multicore CPU so that the operating system, game logic and AI can run on different cores at the same time, though the games must be written to use parallel processing to benefit. A powerful GPU with thousands of cores should handle graphics rendering in parallel, which frees up the CPU and gives smooth frame rates. A RISC-based design would use less power and produce less heat, which matters in a small enclosed case. Pipelining and cache reduce the time the CPU waits for instructions and data, and a higher clock speed gives more cycles per second but generates more heat. Overall there is a trade-off between performance, cost, power use and cooling.

1-1-3.group: 1.1 Characteristics of contemporary processors, input, output and storage devices
1-1-3.title: 1.1.3 Input, output and storage
1-1-3.blurb: Input/output devices, magnetic, flash and optical storage, RAM and ROM, and virtual storage.

questions.q: Which of these is an INPUT device?
questions.e: A barcode scanner sends data into the computer. Speakers, projectors and printers are outputs.

questions.q: Why is a touchscreen described as both an input and an output device?
o: It displays information and also accepts touch input
It connects to the internet and the CPU
It stores data and processes it
questions.e: The screen outputs images and senses touch as input.

questions.q: A supermarket uses barcode scanners at the checkout. Which is the main reason this is better than typing in product codes?
o: It is faster and more accurate
It does not need a database
It is cheaper than any other input device
questions.e: Scanning avoids typing errors and speeds up each transaction; the code is used to look up the price and update stock.

questions.q: How is data stored on a magnetic hard disk?
o: As magnetised (polarised) areas on a spinning platter
As holes punched in a surface
As pits and lands burned by a laser
As trapped electrical charge in memory cells
questions.e: Read/write heads change and detect the magnetic polarity of tiny regions of the platter.

questions.q: How is data read from an optical disc?
o: A laser detects how light is reflected from pits and lands
A voltage is applied to flash cells
A camera scans the disc surface
A read head senses magnetic polarity
questions.e: Reflected light is interpreted as binary data.

questions.q: How does flash storage store data?
o: Using pits and lands read by a laser
Using magnetised areas on a platter
Using electrical charge trapped in transistor cells (no moving parts)
questions.e: Flash (e.g. SSDs, SD cards) is solid state: data is held as charge in cells arranged in blocks and pages.

questions.q: Which storage technology has no moving parts?
questions.e: HDDs and optical drives have moving parts; SSDs do not, which makes them quieter, faster and more robust.

questions.q: Why is an SSD more suitable than an HDD for a laptop used outdoors?
o: It is more robust because it has no moving parts
It always has a bigger capacity
It is much cheaper per gigabyte
questions.e: HDDs are vulnerable to vibration and knocks; SSDs are not.

questions.q: A data centre needs to store very large quantities of archive data as cheaply as possible. Which is the most suitable?
questions.e: Magnetic storage gives very high capacity at low cost per gigabyte.

questions.q: Which storage type is cheap, light and easy to post, making it suitable for distributing films?
questions.e: DVDs and Blu-rays are cheap to produce and portable, but have limited capacity and are slower.

questions.q: Which type of memory is volatile?
questions.e: RAM loses its contents when the power is turned off.

questions.q: What is ROM typically used to store?
o: Start-up (boot) instructions such as the BIOS
The programs the user currently has open
questions.e: ROM is non-volatile and read-only, so start-up instructions are not lost when power is off.

questions.q: What is meant by 'virtual storage'?
o: Storing data on remote servers that are accessed over a network such as the internet
Storage that only exists inside a virtual machine
Using part of the hard disk as extra RAM
A section of RAM reserved for the operating system
questions.e: Cloud storage such as OneDrive or Google Drive. Do not confuse with virtual MEMORY.

questions.q: Which is a disadvantage of virtual (cloud) storage?
o: The data can only be accessed from one device
It cannot be used for backups
It has no capacity limit and is always free
An internet connection is needed to access the data
questions.e: Other drawbacks: ongoing subscription fees and relying on the provider.

questions.q: Which of these correctly compares RAM and ROM?
o: RAM stores the BIOS; ROM stores open programs
RAM can be read and written; ROM can only be read
RAM is non-volatile; ROM is volatile
RAM is slower than ROM and is used for backups
questions.e: RAM is volatile read/write memory. ROM is non-volatile and read-only.

questions.q: Describe how data is stored on, and read from, an optical disc.

pts.p: Data is stored as pits and lands on the surface of the disc
A laser is shone onto the disc
Reflections / scattering of the light are detected and interpreted as binary 1s and 0s

questions.model: Data is stored as a spiral track of tiny pits and lands on the disc. A laser is shone onto the surface and the difference in how light is reflected (or scattered) by pits and lands is detected and interpreted as binary 1s and 0s.

questions.q: Compare magnetic storage and flash (solid state) storage in terms of speed, durability and cost.

pts.p: Flash storage is faster to read / write than magnetic
Magnetic storage has moving parts (spinning platters / heads) so is more fragile / affected by vibration
Flash has no moving parts so is more durable / robust
Magnetic storage is cheaper per gigabyte / has larger capacity than flash

questions.model: Flash storage is faster to read and write than magnetic storage because there is no need to wait for a disk to spin or a head to move. Magnetic drives have moving parts, so they are more fragile and affected by vibration, whereas flash has no moving parts and is more robust. However, magnetic storage is cheaper per gigabyte and is available in larger capacities.

questions.q: Explain why a barcode scanner is suitable for use at a supermarket checkout.

pts.p: It is fast to input the product code (quicker than typing)
It is accurate / reduces errors
The code is used to look up the price / update stock levels in the database

questions.model: A barcode scanner reads the product code quickly, which speeds up the checkout. It is more accurate than typing the code by hand, so fewer errors occur. The code is then used to look up the price and update the stock levels in the database.

questions.q: Explain two differences between RAM and ROM.

pts.p: RAM is volatile - contents are lost when power is off
ROM is non-volatile - contents are kept when power is off
RAM can be read from and written to; ROM is read only
RAM stores programs and data currently in use; ROM stores start-up instructions (e.g. BIOS / bootstrap)

questions.model: RAM is volatile, so its contents are lost when the power is switched off, whereas ROM is non-volatile and keeps its contents. RAM can be read from and written to, whereas ROM is read only. RAM stores the programs and data currently in use, whereas ROM stores permanent start-up instructions such as the BIOS.

questions.q: Describe one advantage and one disadvantage of using virtual (cloud) storage to back up files.

pts.p: Advantage: accessible from anywhere / any device; no hardware to buy; off-site backup protects against loss, theft or disaster
Disadvantage: needs an internet connection / subscription cost / relies on the provider / security risk

questions.model: An advantage is that the files can be accessed from anywhere on any device, and an off-site copy is safe from fire or theft of the user's own computer. A disadvantage is that an internet connection is required to access or restore the files, and there may be a subscription cost.

questions.q: A professional photographer works on location with a laptop and needs to store about 2 TB of photographs. She wants fast access to current work and safe backups. Recommend suitable storage and justify your choices.

pts.p: SSD (flash) in the laptop: fast read/write for editing current work
No moving parts so robust / withstands knocks when travelling; low power use helps battery life
External HDD (magnetic) for bulk storage because of high capacity / low cost per gigabyte
High capacity / cheaper per GB makes 2 TB affordable
Cloud (virtual) storage gives an off-site backup protected from loss or theft, accessible anywhere
Cloud needs an internet connection / subscription / upload takes time with large files
Optical discs are too small a capacity / too slow for this amount of data
SD cards / flash memory used in the camera are portable and fast to transfer

questions.model: I would recommend a solid state drive in the laptop for the current project. Flash storage is fast for opening and editing large images, has no moving parts so it is robust when travelling outdoors, and uses little power. For the bulk of the 2 TB I would use an external magnetic hard disk drive, because magnetic storage has a high capacity and is cheaper per gigabyte than flash. For backups I would use cloud (virtual) storage, giving an off-site copy that is safe from theft or damage and can be accessed anywhere, although it needs an internet connection, a subscription and a long time to upload large files. Optical discs would not be suitable because their capacity is too small and they are slow.

1-2-1.title: 1.2.1 Systems software
1-2-1.blurb: Operating systems, memory management, interrupts, scheduling, OS types, BIOS, drivers and virtual machines.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the purpose of an operating system?
o: It translates source code into machine code
It stores all of a user's files permanently
It protects the computer from viruses only
It manages the hardware and provides an interface between the user, applications and the hardware
questions.e: The OS manages memory, processor time, files, devices and security, and provides the user interface.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a function of an operating system?
o: Translating high-level source code into machine code
questions.e: Translating code is the job of a compiler, interpreter or assembler (translators).

questions.q: In paging, how is memory divided?
o: Into blocks of different sizes decided by the programmer
questions.e: Pages are equal-sized physical divisions that do not take program structure into account.

questions.q: What is a key difference between segmentation and paging?
o: Segments are logical divisions of variable size; pages are fixed-size
Segments are always the same size
Segmentation only works on the hard disk
Pages are logical divisions; segments are physical
questions.e: A segment might hold a whole procedure or array, so related code stays together.

questions.q: What is virtual memory?
o: Part of secondary storage used as an extension of RAM when RAM is full
Memory that is only available in virtual machines
Extra RAM that is installed by the operating system
A fast cache inside the CPU
questions.e: Pages not currently needed are moved from RAM to virtual memory, freeing RAM for other programs.

questions.q: What is 'thrashing'?
o: Excessive swapping of data between RAM and virtual memory, which slows the computer
Deleting files that are no longer needed
questions.e: The CPU spends more time swapping pages than running programs.

questions.q: What is an interrupt?
o: A signal that tells the processor something needs its immediate attention
A request to the user for input
A fault that stops the computer
A type of program stored in ROM
questions.e: Interrupts can come from hardware (keyboard, printer) or software (errors, requests).

questions.q: When does the CPU normally check for interrupts?
o: At the end of each fetch-decode-execute cycle
Only when the user presses a key
Only when the computer starts up
At the start of each program
questions.e: After each FDE cycle the interrupt register is checked.

questions.q: What happens to the current register contents when the CPU decides to service an interrupt?
o: They are saved on a stack so the original task can resume later
They are sent to the printer
questions.e: After the Interrupt Service Routine finishes, the registers are restored from the stack.

questions.q: What is an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR)?
o: A register that stores interrupt priorities
The code that is run to handle a particular interrupt
A utility that blocks all interrupts
questions.e: Each type of interrupt has an ISR. The CPU runs it, then returns to the interrupted task.

questions.q: Why do interrupts have priorities?
o: So that more urgent interrupts are handled before less urgent ones
questions.e: An interrupt only pre-empts the current task if its priority is higher.

questions.q: In round robin scheduling, what happens to a job that does not finish within its time slice?
o: It is moved to the front of the queue
It is given an unlimited time slice
It is moved to the back of the queue
questions.e: Each job gets a fixed slice in turn, which is fair, but longer jobs take longer to finish.

questions.q: Which scheduling algorithm processes jobs strictly in the order they arrive and is non-pre-emptive?
questions.e: FCFS is simple, but a long job at the front delays everything behind it.

questions.q: What is a disadvantage of Shortest Job First (SJF) scheduling?
o: It needs no information about the jobs
Long jobs may be starved if short jobs keep arriving
Every job gets exactly the same time
It is the slowest algorithm for short jobs
questions.e: SJF also needs to know how long jobs will take, and ignores priority.

questions.q: Which scheduling algorithm is the pre-emptive version of Shortest Job First?
questions.e: SRT always runs the job with the least time remaining, pre-empting a longer one when a shorter job arrives.

questions.q: How does a multi-level feedback queue work?
o: Jobs are run in a random order
Only the shortest job is ever run
Several queues of different priority are used, and jobs can move between queues
All jobs are placed in one queue in arrival order
questions.e: Higher-priority queues are served first and jobs can be promoted or demoted.

questions.q: Which type of operating system guarantees a task will be completed within a set time and is used in safety-critical systems?
questions.e: A real-time OS is used for e.g. anti-lock brakes, aircraft control and medical equipment.

questions.q: Which operating system type is used on devices like washing machines, with limited processing power and memory, to do one dedicated job?
questions.e: Embedded OSs run on dedicated low-power devices.

questions.q: Which type of operating system appears to run several programs at once by switching rapidly between them?
questions.e: Each process gets a small time slice, so it seems they all run at the same time.

questions.q: Which type of OS spreads work across several networked computers that act together as one system?
questions.e: A distributed OS shares tasks across multiple computers.

questions.q: What is the first program that runs when a computer is switched on?
questions.e: The BIOS (stored in ROM/flash) runs POST, then starts the bootloader.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the Power-On Self-Test (POST)?
o: To check that the hardware is connected and working
To load the operating system into RAM
questions.e: POST is run by the BIOS before the bootloader loads the OS.

questions.q: What is the role of a device driver?
o: To make a device run faster
To allow the operating system to communicate with a hardware device
questions.e: Drivers translate OS commands into signals the specific device understands.

questions.q: What is a virtual machine?
o: A hardware device for storing bytecode
Software that emulates a computer system, allowing programs (or another OS) to run inside it
questions.e: VMs are used for testing, safe use of untrusted software and running software for a different OS.

questions.q: What is bytecode?
o: A platform-independent intermediate code that is run by a virtual machine
The source code of a program written in Java
The machine code for a specific CPU
questions.e: Java source is compiled to bytecode, which any machine with a JVM can run.

questions.q: Describe three functions of an operating system.

pts.p: Memory management (allocating / managing RAM, paging, virtual memory)
Processor / resource management (scheduling processes)
File management (creating, organising, deleting, saving files)
Peripheral / input-output management (drivers)
Provides a user interface (GUI / CLI)
Security / user accounts / access rights / firewall
Handles interrupts

questions.model: The operating system manages memory by allocating RAM to programs and using paging or virtual memory. It manages the processor by scheduling which process runs and for how long. It manages files, allowing users to create, organise and delete them. It manages peripherals using device drivers, provides a user interface, and provides security through user accounts and access rights.

questions.q: Explain the difference between paging and segmentation.

pts.p: Paging divides memory / programs into fixed-size (equal) blocks called pages
Pages are physical divisions that do not consider the structure of the program
Segmentation divides memory into variable-sized segments
Segments are logical divisions (e.g. a procedure, function or data structure kept together)

questions.model: Paging divides memory into equal, fixed-size physical blocks called pages, regardless of what the program contains, so related code may be split across pages. Segmentation divides memory into variable-sized logical segments, such as a procedure or an array, so related code stays together.

questions.q: Explain what is meant by virtual memory and describe one problem it can cause.

pts.p: Part of secondary storage (hard disk / SSD) is used as an extension of RAM
When RAM is full, pages / data not currently needed are moved out to it and swapped back when required
Problem: it is much slower than RAM / thrashing slows the computer when swapping is excessive

questions.model: Virtual memory is part of the secondary storage that is used as an extension of RAM. When RAM is full, pages that are not currently needed are moved out to it and swapped back in when required. A problem is that secondary storage is much slower than RAM, so excessive swapping (thrashing) slows the computer down.

questions.q: Describe how the round robin scheduling algorithm works.

pts.p: Each process / job is given a fixed time slice (quantum)
If a job is not finished when its time slice ends it is paused and moved to the back of the queue
The next job in the queue then gets the processor; this repeats until all jobs are complete (each job gets a fair share)

questions.model: Each job is given a fixed time slice in turn. If a job is not finished when its time slice ends, it is paused and moved to the back of the queue, and the next job in the queue is given the processor. This repeats until all jobs are complete, so every job gets a fair share of processor time.

questions.q: Describe the role of the BIOS when a computer is switched on.

pts.p: It is the first program run (held in ROM / non-volatile memory)
It runs the Power-On Self-Test (POST) to check the hardware is present and working
It finds the boot device (boot order) and starts the bootloader, which loads the operating system into RAM

questions.model: The BIOS is the first program to run when the computer is switched on and is stored in non-volatile memory. It runs the Power-On Self-Test to check that the hardware is connected and working. It then finds the boot device and starts the bootloader, which loads the operating system into RAM.

questions.q: A car's anti-lock braking system uses a real-time operating system. Explain why.

pts.p: It is a safety-critical system - a delay could cause an accident / harm
A real-time OS guarantees a response / task is completed within a fixed time limit
Tasks must respond immediately to sensor input (e.g. wheel locking) with no unpredictable delays

questions.model: Braking is safety-critical, so a delay in the system's response could cause an accident. A real-time operating system guarantees that tasks are completed within a fixed time limit, so the system reacts to sensor input (such as a wheel locking) without unpredictable delays.

questions.q: Explain how a CPU handles an interrupt. Your answer should refer to when interrupts are checked, how the current task is preserved and how priority is used.

pts.p: An interrupt signal is generated by hardware or software
Interrupts are stored in a queue / register and have a priority
The CPU checks for interrupts at the end of each fetch-decode-execute cycle
The interrupt is only serviced if its priority is higher than the current task; otherwise the current task continues
The contents of the registers (including the PC) are saved to a stack
The PC is set to the address of / the CPU runs the Interrupt Service Routine (ISR)
When the ISR finishes the CPU checks for further interrupts
The saved register contents are restored from the stack and the original task resumes

questions.model: An interrupt is a signal from hardware or software that is placed in the interrupt queue with a priority. At the end of every fetch-decode-execute cycle the CPU checks the interrupt register. If an interrupt has a higher priority than the current task, the contents of the registers, including the program counter, are saved on a stack so that the task can be resumed later. The program counter is then set to the address of the Interrupt Service Routine, which handles the interrupt. When the ISR has finished, the CPU checks for any further interrupts. If there are none of higher priority, the saved register values are restored from the stack and the original task resumes.

questions.q: A university server is used by hundreds of staff and students at the same time. Discuss the scheduling algorithms its operating system could use.

pts.p: Scheduling decides which process gets the CPU and for how long, to use the processor efficiently and fairly
Round robin gives each job a time slice, so every user gets a share and response times are good for interactive users
If the time slice is too short there is too much overhead from switching; too long and users wait
FCFS is simple, but one long job delays all the jobs behind it
FCFS (and SJF) are non-pre-emptive
SJF minimises the average waiting time because short jobs finish quickly
SJF can starve long jobs if short jobs keep arriving / needs the run time to be known in advance
SRT is the pre-emptive version, always running the job with the least time left
A multi-level feedback queue uses several priority queues and moves jobs between them
It favours short / interactive jobs and can prevent starvation, but is complex to implement
A justified conclusion, e.g. a multi-level feedback queue or round robin is most suitable for many interactive users

questions.model: Scheduling decides which process gets the CPU and for how long, so that the processor is used efficiently and every user is treated fairly. First come first served is simple but non-pre-emptive, so a single long job delays everything behind it, which would be poor for hundreds of users. Shortest job first minimises the average waiting time because short jobs finish quickly, but long jobs can be starved if short jobs keep arriving and the run time must be known in advance. Shortest remaining time is the pre-emptive version of this. Round robin gives each job a time slice, so every user gets a share of the processor and response times are good for interactive use; however if the slice is too short there is a lot of overhead from switching, and if it is too long users wait. A multi-level feedback queue uses several priority queues and moves jobs between them, favouring short and interactive jobs while preventing starvation, but it is more complex to implement. Overall, I would recommend a multi-level feedback queue (or round robin) because the server mainly runs interactive jobs for many users.

1-2-2.title: 1.2.2 Applications generation
1-2-2.blurb: Application types, utilities, open vs closed source, translators, stages of compilation, linkers, loaders and libraries.

questions.q: Which of these is application software?
questions.e: Application software does tasks for the user. Utilities, drivers and the BIOS are system software.

questions.q: A bank has software written specially for its own needs, by a software company, to its exact requirements. What is this called?
questions.e: Bespoke software is custom-made for one organisation, which is expensive but matches their needs.

questions.q: Which statement describes general-purpose software?
o: It can be used for a wide variety of tasks
It can only be used on one computer
It is written for one specific organisation
questions.e: A spreadsheet is general purpose. Special-purpose software does one specific job (e.g. CAD).

questions.q: What does a defragmentation utility do?
o: Rearranges file fragments on a hard disk so that files are stored contiguously
questions.e: Fragmented files slow down a magnetic hard disk because the read head has to move around more.

questions.q: Which utility is used to reduce the size of files?
questions.e: Compression allows files to be stored in less space and sent faster.

questions.q: What is the purpose of antivirus software?
o: To increase the speed of the CPU
To scan for, detect and remove or quarantine malicious software
To back up the operating system
questions.e: Antivirus compares files against known malware signatures and detects suspicious behaviour.

questions.q: What does 'open source' software mean?
o: The software can only be run online
The source code is available for anyone to view, modify and distribute
The software must be compiled before it is run
The software is free but the code is secret
questions.e: Open source encourages collaboration, but support may be limited.

questions.q: Which is an advantage of open source software?
o: The community can inspect, fix and improve the code
It is always more reliable than closed source
The code is kept secret so it is more secure
questions.e: Many developers can find bugs and add features. There is no guarantee of formal support.

questions.q: Which is an advantage of closed source software?
o: Users can modify the code to suit them
The vendor is responsible for support and updates, and the code is not available to attackers
The code can be redistributed by anyone
questions.e: Closed source software is typically licensed, with a company providing support.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a translator?
o: To convert source code into machine code the processor can execute
questions.e: The CPU can only execute machine code.

questions.q: What is the key difference between how a compiler and an interpreter work?
o: An interpreter produces an executable file
A compiler runs line by line; an interpreter translates the whole program first
A compiler only works on assembly code
A compiler translates the whole program before it runs; an interpreter translates and runs it line by line
questions.e: Compiling produces an executable that can be run without the compiler.

questions.q: Which is an advantage of a compiled program over an interpreted one?
o: The source code is needed to run it
It generally runs faster because translation has already been done
It can run on any processor
It is easier to debug line by line
questions.e: An interpreter must translate each line every time the program runs.

questions.q: Which is an advantage of an interpreter during development?
o: The program does not need an interpreter to run
The source code is hidden from users
Errors are reported as the program runs, so it is easy to test and debug small changes
questions.e: Interpreters can stop at the line with the error and need no separate compile step.

questions.q: What does an assembler do?
o: Translates a high-level language line by line
Translates assembly language into machine code
questions.e: Each line of assembly is translated to (roughly) one machine code instruction.

questions.q: What happens in the LEXICAL ANALYSIS stage of compilation?
o: Whitespace and comments are removed and the code is broken into tokens
The tokens are checked against the grammar rules
questions.e: Tokens (keywords, identifiers, operators, separators) are stored in a symbol/token table.

questions.q: What happens in the SYNTAX ANALYSIS stage of compilation?
o: The program is loaded into memory
The tokens are checked against the grammar rules and an abstract syntax tree is built
questions.e: Syntax errors are reported at this stage.

questions.q: What is produced during CODE GENERATION?
o: Machine (object) code, built from the abstract syntax tree
The final executable with libraries linked
questions.e: The AST is traversed to generate the object code.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the OPTIMISATION stage?
o: To make the code faster or smaller without changing what it does
To translate the code to a different language
questions.e: Examples: removing unused variables and subroutines, and redundant instructions.

questions.q: What is a code library?
o: A folder of source code backups
A collection of pre-written, pre-tested routines that can be used in other programs
questions.e: Libraries save development time and are reliable because they are already tested.

questions.q: What does a linker do?
o: Combines object code and library routines into a single executable file
questions.e: The linker resolves references to library routines.

questions.q: What does a loader do?
o: Loads an executable program (and any dynamic libraries) into main memory so it can run
questions.e: The loader is part of the operating system.

questions.q: What is a benefit of DYNAMIC linking compared with static linking?
o: The executable is smaller and libraries can be shared between programs
The library code is copied into every program
The program never fails if a library changes
questions.e: A risk: if the library is changed or missing, the program may stop working.

questions.q: Explain two differences between a compiler and an interpreter.

pts.p: A compiler translates the whole program before it runs, an interpreter translates line by line
A compiled program can run without the compiler / translator; an interpreter is needed every time it is run
Compiled code runs faster / interpreted code runs slower because it is translated each time
An interpreter reports errors as it reaches them, so debugging is easier; a compiler reports all errors after compiling

questions.model: A compiler translates the whole program into machine code before it is run, whereas an interpreter translates and executes the program one line at a time. The compiled executable can be run without the compiler and runs faster, but an interpreter is needed every time an interpreted program is run, and it runs more slowly because lines are translated each time. An interpreter stops at the line with an error, making debugging easier.

questions.q: Describe what happens during the lexical analysis and syntax analysis stages of compilation.

pts.p: Lexical: comments and whitespace are removed
Lexical: the code is broken into tokens (keywords, identifiers, operators...) stored in a table
Syntax: the tokens are checked against the grammar / syntax rules of the language
Syntax: an abstract syntax tree is produced / syntax errors are reported

questions.model: In lexical analysis the comments and whitespace are removed and the code is broken into tokens such as keywords, identifiers and operators, which are stored in a table. In syntax analysis the tokens are checked against the grammar rules of the language; if they are valid an abstract syntax tree is produced, and any syntax errors are reported.

questions.q: Describe the purpose of a linker and a loader.

pts.p: The linker combines the object code with library routines / other modules into one executable
The linker resolves / replaces references to library routines with their addresses
The loader loads the executable (and any dynamic libraries) into main memory ready to be run

questions.model: The linker combines the object code with the library routines it needs into a single executable file, resolving references to the routines. The loader then loads the executable (and any dynamic libraries) into main memory so that it can be run.

questions.q: Describe one advantage and one disadvantage of using library routines when developing a program.

pts.p: Advantage: pre-written and pre-tested so reliable / saves development time / reusable / fast to use
Disadvantage: may be difficult to modify / may include unneeded code (larger program) / depends on the library being maintained / unknown efficiency

questions.model: A library routine is already written and tested, so it saves development time and is reliable. A disadvantage is that it may not do exactly what is required and cannot easily be modified, and the programmer has to depend on the library being maintained.

questions.q: A company is deciding whether to release its software as open source or closed source. Compare the two approaches.

pts.p: Open source: source code available for others to view / modify
Open source: community help finds bugs and adds improvements / usually free
Closed source: code is kept secret, which protects intellectual property / prevents copying
Closed source: company controls updates and provides support / makes money from licences

questions.model: With open source, the source code is available for anyone to view and modify, so the community can find bugs and add improvements, and it is usually free, though there may be no formal support. With closed source, the code is kept secret, which protects the company's intellectual property and prevents copying. The company can sell licences, control updates and provide professional support.

questions.q: Describe the stages of compilation of a high-level language program.

pts.p: Compilation translates the source code (high-level) into machine / object code
Lexical analysis: comments and whitespace are removed
Lexical analysis: the code is broken into tokens (keywords, identifiers, operators, etc.) held in a table
Syntax analysis: the tokens are checked against the grammar / syntax rules and syntax errors are reported
Syntax analysis: an abstract syntax tree is built
Code generation: the AST is used to produce the machine / object code
Optimisation: the code is made more efficient (faster / smaller) without changing what it does

questions.model: Compilation translates a high-level program into machine code in four stages. In lexical analysis the comments and whitespace are removed and the code is broken into tokens such as keywords, identifiers and operators, which are stored in a table. In syntax analysis the tokens are checked against the grammar rules of the language, any syntax errors are reported, and an abstract syntax tree is built. In code generation the abstract syntax tree is used to produce the object (machine) code. Finally, in optimisation the code is made more efficient, for example by removing unused variables, unused subroutines and redundant instructions, so that it runs faster or uses less memory without changing what it does.

1-2-3.title: 1.2.3 Software development
1-2-3.blurb: Waterfall, agile, extreme programming, spiral and RAD; alpha, beta, white box and black box testing; algorithms.

questions.q: Which describes the waterfall model?
o: Short repeating cycles where a working version is released each time
A model where all stages happen at the same time
Development stages completed one after another in a fixed order
A model based on repeated prototypes with risk analysis in each loop
questions.e: Analysis, design, implementation, testing and evaluation follow in sequence.

questions.q: Which is a disadvantage of the waterfall model?
o: It is inflexible, so changes to requirements are costly and difficult
There is too much user involvement
questions.e: No working software appears until late, and users see little until the end.

questions.q: For which type of project is waterfall MOST suitable?
o: One with clear, fixed requirements that are unlikely to change
One where the requirements are not yet known
A project that needs a working version every week
A project where risks are unclear
questions.e: Waterfall works well for well-understood, stable requirements.

questions.q: Which is a feature of agile development?
o: Users only involved at the start
Detailed documentation completed before any coding
A single release at the end of the project
Short iterations with frequent working releases and regular user feedback
questions.e: Agile adapts to changing requirements, but can lead to less documentation.

questions.q: Which of these is associated with Extreme Programming (XP)?
o: Pair programming and frequent small releases
A formal risk analysis in every loop
questions.e: XP is an agile approach. Pair programming means two developers work at one computer.

questions.q: What is the key feature of the spiral model?
o: Risk analysis and prototyping repeated in each loop of development
Writing all the code before any design
Strictly one pass through the stages
questions.e: Each loop identifies and reduces risks, so it suits large, high-risk projects.

questions.q: Which methodology is MOST suitable for a large, complex and high-risk project?
questions.e: Early prototypes and continual risk analysis reduce the chance of expensive failure.

questions.q: What is a feature of Rapid Application Development (RAD)?
o: A full specification is written first and never changed
Testing only takes place at the end
Prototypes are developed quickly with high user involvement and reuse of existing components
Long development phases with no user contact
questions.e: RAD suits projects where requirements are unclear or time is limited.

questions.q: What is a disadvantage of RAD?
o: Code quality or documentation may suffer because of the speed
It is too slow for small projects
questions.e: Quick prototypes can leave the product 'good enough' but less robust.

questions.q: What is alpha testing?
o: Testing the inputs and outputs only
Testing after the software has been released
Testing done by a small group of external users before release
Testing done in-house by the development team
questions.e: Alpha testing happens within the developer's organisation.

questions.q: What is beta testing?
o: Testing by the programmers who wrote the code
Testing by a selected group of real end users before full release
Testing of every path through the code
questions.e: Beta testers give feedback on bugs and usability in real conditions.

questions.q: What is white box testing?
o: Testing based on knowledge of the code, making sure every path is tested
Testing only the inputs and outputs without seeing the code
questions.e: The tester can see the internal structure of the program.

questions.q: What is black box testing?
o: Testing carried out by the programmer who wrote the code
Testing inputs and expected outputs without knowledge of the internal code
questions.e: The tester does not need to know how the code works.

questions.q: Which of these is a quality of a good algorithm?
o: It uses as many variables as possible
It relies on the user guessing what to do
It always reaches a stopping condition
questions.e: Algorithms should have clear inputs, produce correct output, handle invalid inputs and terminate.

questions.q: Why is it useful to design an algorithm before writing the program code?
o: It makes the program run faster automatically
It lets the logic be planned and checked independently of a programming language
It removes the need for testing
It is required by the compiler
questions.e: Errors are cheaper to find and fix at the design stage.

questions.q: A development team knows only a rough idea of what the client wants and expects the requirements to change. Which methodology is most suitable?
o: None - a plan cannot be made
questions.e: Agile copes with changing requirements by delivering working versions and getting frequent feedback.

questions.q: Describe the waterfall model of software development.

pts.p: Stages (e.g. analysis, design, implementation, testing, evaluation) are carried out one after another / in sequence
Each stage must be completed before the next begins
It is difficult to go back / change requirements; stages have to be repeated

questions.model: In the waterfall model the stages of development (such as analysis, design, implementation, testing and evaluation) are carried out in a fixed linear sequence, and each stage is completed before the next begins. It is difficult to go back, so any change to the requirements means revisiting every stage.

questions.q: Explain two differences between the agile and waterfall approaches to software development.

pts.p: Agile develops in short iterations / increments; waterfall is a single linear sequence
Agile copes well with changing requirements; waterfall is inflexible
Agile has frequent user involvement / feedback; waterfall users are only involved at the start and end
Agile gives working software early / often; waterfall only at the end (agile has less documentation)

questions.model: Agile works in short iterations, delivering a working version each time, whereas waterfall is a single linear sequence of stages. Agile copes well with changing requirements, whereas waterfall is inflexible and changes are costly. Agile involves users and gets feedback throughout, whereas in waterfall users are only involved at the start and the end.

questions.q: Explain the differences between white box testing and black box testing.

pts.p: White box: the tester knows / can see the internal code or structure
White box: tests every path / branch / statement through the code
Black box: tests inputs and expected outputs only
Black box: the tester does not need to know how the code works

questions.model: In white box testing the tester knows the internal structure of the code and designs tests to cover every path through the program. In black box testing the tester only considers the inputs and the expected outputs, and does not need to know how the code works.

questions.q: Explain how the spiral model helps to manage risk.

pts.p: Development is carried out in repeated loops / iterations
Risk analysis is carried out in each loop
Prototypes are produced / users give feedback early, so problems are found and fixed before large costs are incurred (or the project is stopped)

questions.model: The spiral model repeats the stages of development in a series of loops. In each loop the risks are identified and analysed, and a prototype is produced and evaluated with the user. Problems are therefore found early, before large amounts of money have been spent, and a very risky project can be stopped or changed.

questions.q: Compare the waterfall and agile methodologies, referring to flexibility, user involvement and documentation.

pts.p: Waterfall is a linear sequence of stages, each finished before the next starts
Waterfall is inflexible - changing requirements means going back / is expensive
Agile develops in short iterations / increments with working versions delivered frequently
Agile is flexible and copes with changing requirements
Waterfall has little user involvement (mainly at the start and end)
Agile has frequent user involvement and feedback
Waterfall produces thorough documentation; agile tends to have less
Waterfall suits fixed, well-understood requirements; agile suits projects where requirements may change

questions.model: The waterfall model is a linear sequence of stages, each completed before the next begins, whereas agile develops the software in short iterations, delivering a working version each time. Waterfall is inflexible: if the requirements change, earlier stages must be revisited, which is costly. Agile is flexible and copes well with changing requirements. In waterfall the users are only involved at the start and end, but in agile there is frequent user involvement and feedback. Waterfall produces thorough documentation, while agile tends to produce less. Waterfall therefore suits projects with fixed, well-understood requirements, whereas agile suits projects where the requirements may change.

questions.q: A hospital is developing a new patient-records system. The requirements are complex and likely to change, and errors could put patients at risk. Discuss which software development methodology (or methodologies) should be used.

pts.p: Waterfall: sequential and well documented, but inflexible, and users see nothing until the end - unsuitable if requirements will change
Waterfall would be too risky / costly if errors found late, or requirements change
Agile: short iterations with frequent working releases and user feedback - copes with changing requirements
Agile may lead to poor documentation / hard to estimate time and cost
Spiral: risk analysis and prototyping in each loop - suits high-risk, complex projects
Spiral can be expensive / time-consuming and needs risk-assessment expertise
RAD / prototypes involve users (clinicians) in design so the system fits how they work
RAD's speed risks lower quality / not enough testing for a safety-critical system
Extensive testing (alpha, beta, white box, black box) is needed because errors could harm patients
User involvement of hospital staff / feedback throughout to check the system meets their needs
A justified recommendation, e.g. spiral or agile (possibly with elements of both)

questions.model: Waterfall is sequential and well documented, but it is inflexible and the hospital staff would see nothing until the end, so with complex requirements likely to change it could be very costly if errors are only found late. Agile develops the system in short iterations with frequent working releases and feedback from clinicians, which copes well with changing requirements, but it can lead to poor documentation and makes time and cost hard to estimate. The spiral model uses prototyping and a risk analysis in every loop, which is ideal for a high-risk, complex project where errors could harm patients, although it is expensive and time-consuming and needs risk-assessment expertise. RAD would involve the hospital staff in prototyping, but the focus on speed could reduce quality, which is dangerous for a safety-critical system. Whatever is chosen, extensive alpha, beta, white box and black box testing is needed. Overall, I would recommend the spiral model, possibly using agile-style iterations within each loop, because it manages risk while allowing the requirements to change and giving users regular involvement.

1-2-4.title: 1.2.4 Types of programming language
1-2-4.blurb: Programming paradigms, assembly language and the Little Man Computer, addressing modes and object-oriented programming.

questions.q: What is a programming paradigm?
o: An approach or style of programming used to solve a problem
questions.e: Examples: procedural, object-oriented, functional and logic.

questions.q: Which pair are both imperative paradigms?
questions.e: Imperative = specify HOW to do it step by step. Declarative (functional, logic) = state WHAT is wanted.

questions.q: Which feature is typical of procedural programming?
o: Programs are built only from objects
A program is structured as a sequence of instructions grouped into procedures or subroutines
The program is a set of facts and rules
questions.e: Procedural code uses sequence, selection and iteration.

questions.q: Which paradigm is Prolog, which uses facts, rules and queries, an example of?
questions.e: A logic program states facts and rules, then queries are used to find answers.

questions.q: Which paradigm is based on the evaluation of functions, and is closely linked to maths?
questions.e: Functional languages (such as Haskell) build programs by combining functions.

questions.q: What is assembly language?
o: A high-level language with English-like commands
A language made of only 1s and 0s
A low-level language that uses mnemonics which map closely to machine code instructions
A language used only for web pages
questions.e: Assembly is translated by an assembler and is specific to a processor family.

questions.q: Why might assembly language be used to write a device driver or program for a small embedded system?
o: It gives direct control of the hardware and can be very efficient in speed and memory
It has no need to be translated
It is easy to read and write
It runs on any type of processor
questions.e: Disadvantages: hard to write and maintain, and not portable.

questions.q: In the Little Man Computer, what does the instruction LDA 10 do?
o: Loads the value stored at address 10 into the accumulator
questions.e: LDA = load. STA = store.

questions.q: In the Little Man Computer, what does STA 15 do?
o: Stores the value in the accumulator at address 15
Loads the value at address 15 into the accumulator
questions.e: STA copies the accumulator into the memory location.

questions.q: What does the LMC instruction BRP do?
o: Branches if the accumulator is negative
Branches if the accumulator is positive (zero or greater)
Branches only if the accumulator is zero
questions.e: BRZ = branch if zero; BRP = branch if positive or zero; BRA = branch always.

questions.q: An LMC program runs: INP, STA 10, INP, ADD 10, OUT, HLT. If the inputs are 4 then 5, what is output?
questions.e: The first input is stored at 10; the second is added to it, giving 9, which is then output.

questions.q: An LMC program is: INP, SUB ten, BRP big, LDA zero, OUT, HLT, big LDA one, OUT, HLT (ten = 10, zero = 0, one = 1). What is output for an input of 7?
questions.e: 7 - 10 = -3 is negative, so BRP does not branch and the program outputs 0. (An input of 10 or more outputs 1.)

questions.q: In which addressing mode is the operand the actual value to be used?
questions.e: Immediate addressing: the operand IS the data.

questions.q: In which addressing mode does the operand give the address of the memory location that holds the value?
questions.e: Direct addressing: operand = address of the data.

questions.q: Address 20 holds 35, and address 35 holds 7. Using INDIRECT addressing with operand 20, which value is used?
questions.e: Indirect: the operand (20) is the address of a location (holding 35) which is itself the address of the data (7).

questions.q: In indexed addressing, how is the address of the data found?
o: By using the operand directly as the data
By adding the operand to the value in an index register
By reading an address from the accumulator
questions.e: Indexed addressing is useful for working through arrays or lists.

questions.q: In object-oriented programming, what is a class?
o: A function that has no name
A single instance of an object
A template that defines the attributes and methods of objects
questions.e: An object is an instance of a class.

questions.q: What is an object?
o: A variable that can only hold a number
questions.e: For example, 'myCar' is an object of the class 'Car'.

questions.q: What is encapsulation?
o: A class inheriting from another class
Giving different classes methods with the same name
Compressing the code in a class
Keeping attributes private and only accessible through the object's methods
questions.e: Data hiding makes the code more secure and reliable, because attributes can only be changed in controlled ways.

questions.q: What is inheritance?
o: A subclass acquiring the attributes and methods of its parent class
Two classes sharing the same name
An object being deleted when its class is deleted
questions.e: For example, a Truck subclass inherits from Vehicle and adds its own attributes.

questions.q: What is polymorphism in OOP?
o: An object belonging to no class
Different classes having methods with the same name that behave differently
A method that can never be changed
questions.e: For example, Dog.speak() and Cat.speak() produce different output (method overriding).

questions.q: Explain the difference between imperative and declarative programming.

pts.p: Imperative programs specify the steps / how to do a task, in order
Declarative programs state what result is wanted / the problem, not how to achieve it
Examples: imperative - procedural / OOP; declarative - functional / logic

questions.model: Imperative programming specifies the sequence of steps that the computer must carry out to solve a problem (for example procedural and object-oriented programming). Declarative programming states what result is wanted, and the language works out how to obtain it (for example functional and logic programming, such as Prolog).

questions.q: Describe four addressing modes used in machine code instructions.

pts.p: Immediate: the operand is the actual value to be used
Direct: the operand is the address of the memory location holding the value
Indirect: the operand is the address of a location which holds the address of the value
Indexed: the operand is added to the value in an index register to give the address

questions.model: In immediate addressing the operand is the actual value to be used. In direct addressing the operand is the address of the memory location that holds the value. In indirect addressing the operand is the address of a location that contains the address of the value. In indexed addressing the operand is added to the contents of an index register to give the address of the value.

questions.q: Explain what is meant by encapsulation and why it is useful.

pts.p: Attributes are made private / hidden inside the object (data hiding)
They can only be accessed or changed through the object's methods (getters / setters)
This protects data from accidental / unauthorised change, making the code more secure / reliable / easier to maintain

questions.model: Encapsulation means that the attributes of an object are kept private inside the class and can only be accessed or changed through the object's methods (such as getters and setters). This protects the data from accidental or unauthorised changes, which makes the code more secure, reliable and easier to maintain.

questions.q: Explain what is meant by inheritance and polymorphism in object-oriented programming.

pts.p: Inheritance: a subclass (child) takes on the attributes and methods of its superclass (parent)
The subclass can add its own attributes / methods (so code is reused)
Polymorphism: methods with the same name behave differently in different classes
Example given of overriding / same method name in different classes (e.g. speak() in Dog and Cat)

questions.model: Inheritance is where a subclass takes on the attributes and methods of its parent class, and can add its own, so code is reused. For example, a Truck class inherits from Vehicle and adds a trailer attribute. Polymorphism is where methods with the same name behave differently in different classes; for example, a Dog class and a Cat class might both have a speak() method that produces different output.

questions.q: Give two reasons why a programmer might choose to write in assembly language rather than a high-level language.

pts.p: It gives direct control of the hardware / registers / memory
It can produce faster / smaller / more memory-efficient programs
Suitable for embedded systems / device drivers / systems with limited resources

questions.model: Assembly language gives the programmer direct control of the hardware, such as registers and memory locations. It can also produce faster, smaller programs, which is useful for embedded systems and device drivers with limited resources.

questions.q: Explain the main features of object-oriented programming, using a suitable example such as a Vehicle class.

pts.p: A class is a template / blueprint that defines attributes and methods
An object is an instance of a class (e.g. a specific car)
Attributes are the data / properties of an object (e.g. make, colour)
Methods are the actions / behaviours an object can carry out (e.g. start, brake)
Encapsulation: attributes are private and accessed only through methods (getters / setters)
Inheritance: a subclass (e.g. Truck) inherits attributes / methods from the superclass and can add its own
Polymorphism: the same method name behaves differently in different classes (overriding)
Benefits: reusable code, easier to maintain / update, more secure

questions.model: A class is a template that defines the attributes and methods of objects; for example, a Vehicle class. An object is an instance of a class, such as a particular car. Attributes are the data held about an object, such as its make, colour and registration, and methods are the actions it can carry out, such as start() or brake(). Encapsulation means the attributes are private and can only be accessed or changed using methods such as getters and setters. Inheritance allows a Truck subclass to inherit the attributes and methods of the Vehicle superclass and to add its own, such as a trailer attribute. Polymorphism means that different classes can have a method with the same name that behaves differently, such as a different version of calculateTax() in each class. These features make code reusable, easier to maintain and more secure.

1-3-1.title: 1.3.1 Compression, encryption and hashing
1-3-1.blurb: Lossy vs lossless compression, run length and dictionary coding, symmetric and asymmetric encryption, and hashing.

questions.q: What is the purpose of compressing a file?
o: To remove all errors from it
To make it easier to edit
To reduce its size so it takes less storage and can be transmitted faster
questions.e: Smaller files need less storage space and less bandwidth.

questions.q: Which statement describes LOSSY compression?
o: The file is split into packets
No data is lost and the original can be restored exactly
Some data is permanently removed to make the file smaller
questions.e: Lossy is used for images, audio and video where small losses are acceptable.

questions.q: Which statement describes LOSSLESS compression?
o: The original data can be restored exactly
It always gives a smaller file than lossy
It can only be used on images
questions.e: Lossless is needed for text, program files and data where every bit matters.

questions.q: Which file type should NOT be compressed using lossy compression?
questions.e: Losing any data from a program or document could corrupt it.

questions.q: Why is lossy compression often used for streaming music or video?
o: It makes the file larger but clearer
It gives much smaller files, so less buffering, and the loss of quality is hardly noticeable
questions.e: Lower bandwidth is needed, so streaming is smoother.

questions.q: Using run length encoding (RLE), what is AAAABBBCC compressed to?
questions.e: Each run of repeated characters is replaced by a count and the character.

questions.q: Decompress this run length encoded data: 3X2Y1Z
questions.e: 3 X's, then 2 Y's, then 1 Z.

questions.q: For which data is run length encoding LEAST effective?
o: Data with very little repetition, such as ABCDEFG
A fax of a mostly blank page
A black and white image with large blocks of one colour
questions.e: With no runs, each character gets a count added and the data can actually get larger.

questions.q: How does dictionary coding compress data?
o: Runs of repeated characters are replaced with a count
The data is encrypted with a key
Frequently repeated patterns are replaced by shorter codes held in a dictionary
questions.e: The dictionary must be stored or transmitted with the data so it can be decompressed.

questions.q: Which is true of dictionary coding?
o: The dictionary must be kept with the compressed data
questions.e: Without the dictionary the codes cannot be decoded.

questions.q: What is the purpose of encryption?
o: To make data unreadable to anyone who does not have the key
questions.e: Encryption does not stop interception - it makes intercepted data meaningless.

questions.q: In SYMMETRIC encryption, which keys are used?
o: Two different keys that are never shared
The same key to encrypt and decrypt
A public key to encrypt and a private key to decrypt
questions.e: The main problem is how to share the key securely.

questions.q: In ASYMMETRIC encryption, how does someone send a message that only the recipient can read?
o: They encrypt it with the recipient's private key
They encrypt it with the recipient's public key
They encrypt it with their own private key
questions.e: Only the recipient's private key can decrypt it.

questions.q: What is the main advantage of asymmetric encryption over symmetric encryption?
o: The decryption (private) key never has to be shared or sent
questions.e: This avoids the key distribution problem, but asymmetric encryption is slower and needs more processing power.

questions.q: Which is an advantage of symmetric encryption over asymmetric?
o: It does not need a key
It solves the key exchange problem
It is faster and needs less processing power
questions.e: That's why HTTPS uses asymmetric encryption to share a symmetric key, then uses the faster symmetric method.

questions.q: How does a digital signature help prove who sent a message?
o: The message is compressed using lossless compression
The sender encrypts (a hash of) the message with their private key, and the receiver decrypts it with the sender's public key
The receiver encrypts the message with their own public key
The sender encrypts the message with the receiver's private key
questions.e: Only the sender holds their private key, so a successful decryption proves where it came from.

questions.q: What is a hash function?
o: A way to compress data without loss
A function that sorts data into order
A one-way function that turns data of any size into a fixed-size value
A function that encrypts data so it can be decrypted later
questions.e: Hashes cannot be reversed to get the original data.

questions.q: Why are passwords stored as hashes rather than as plain text?
o: So they can be sent over the internet
So the original passwords cannot be read if the database is stolen
So they can be decrypted if the user forgets them
questions.e: When a user logs in, the entered password is hashed and compared to the stored hash.

questions.q: What is a hash 'collision'?
o: A file being corrupted during transmission
Two different inputs producing the same hash value
questions.e: A good hash function has a low chance of collisions.

questions.q: How can hashing be used to check that a file has not been altered during transmission?
o: Encrypt the file with a public key
Hash the file before and after sending and compare the two hash values
questions.e: If the hashes match, the data has not been changed.

questions.q: Compare lossy and lossless compression.

pts.p: Lossy permanently removes some data / detail
Lossless allows the original file to be restored exactly / no data is lost
Lossy gives a smaller file / greater reduction in size than lossless
Lossy is suitable for images / audio / video; lossless is needed for text / program files / data

questions.model: Lossy compression permanently removes some of the data, so the original cannot be restored exactly, but it gives a much smaller file; it suits images, audio and video where a small loss of quality is acceptable. Lossless compression allows the original file to be restored exactly, so no data is lost, but the file is not reduced as much; it is needed for text, program files and other data where every bit matters.

questions.q: Use run length encoding to compress the following data: AAAAABBBCCCCCCD

pts.p: 5A (or A5)
3B (or B3)
6C and 1D (or C6 and D1)

questions.model: 5A3B6C1D

questions.q: Explain how dictionary coding can be used to compress a text file.

pts.p: A dictionary is created of words or patterns that appear frequently
Each repeated word / pattern is replaced by a shorter code / index
The dictionary must be stored / sent with the compressed file so that it can be decompressed

questions.model: A dictionary is created of the words or patterns that appear frequently in the file. Each occurrence is replaced by a shorter code or index, which reduces the size of the file. The dictionary has to be stored or sent with the compressed file so it can be used to decompress it.

questions.q: Explain the difference between symmetric and asymmetric encryption.

pts.p: Symmetric uses the same key to encrypt and decrypt
Symmetric: the key must be shared / sent, so it could be intercepted
Asymmetric uses a pair of keys - a public key and a private key
Data encrypted with the public key can only be decrypted with the matching private key, which is never shared
Symmetric is faster / simpler; asymmetric is slower / needs more processing

questions.model: Symmetric encryption uses the same key to encrypt and decrypt the data, so the key must be shared with the receiver, and if it is intercepted the data can be read. Asymmetric encryption uses a pair of keys: a public key to encrypt and a private key to decrypt. The private key is never shared, so it is more secure, but asymmetric encryption is slower and needs more processing than symmetric.

questions.q: Describe two uses of hashing.

pts.p: Storing passwords: the hash is stored instead of the plain text password
Checking data integrity / verifying that a file or message has not been altered
Hash tables: a hash of the key gives the storage location for fast lookup
Digital signatures (a hash of the message is signed)

questions.model: Hashing is used to store passwords securely: only the hash is stored, so the original cannot be read if the database is stolen. It is also used to check that data has not been altered, by comparing the hash of the data before and after it is sent.

questions.q: Alice wants to send Bob a confidential message over the internet. Explain how asymmetric encryption can be used so that only Bob can read it, and how Bob can be sure that it came from Alice.

pts.p: Bob has a key pair: a public key and a private key
Bob's public key can be shared with anyone; his private key is kept secret
Alice encrypts the message with Bob's public key
Only Bob's private key can decrypt the message, so it cannot be read if intercepted
This avoids having to send a secret key (the key exchange problem of symmetric encryption)
Digital signature: Alice encrypts (a hash of) the message with her own private key
Bob decrypts it with Alice's public key; success proves it came from Alice and was not altered
Asymmetric encryption is slower, so is often used to exchange a symmetric key

questions.model: Bob has a pair of keys, a public key and a private key. He shares his public key with anyone but keeps his private key secret. Alice encrypts her message using Bob's public key, and only Bob's private key can decrypt it, so the message cannot be read if it is intercepted. This also means no secret key has to be sent across the network, which avoids the key exchange problem of symmetric encryption. To prove the message came from Alice, she can create a digital signature by encrypting a hash of the message with her own private key. Bob decrypts it using Alice's public key; if this works, it proves it came from Alice and that the message was not altered. Because asymmetric encryption is slower than symmetric encryption, it is often used just to exchange a symmetric key.

1-3-2.title: 1.3.2 Databases
1-3-2.blurb: Flat file vs relational, keys, ER modelling, normalisation to 3NF, SQL, referential integrity, ACID and record locking.

questions.q: What is a flat file database?
o: A database with many linked tables
A database that stores all of its data in a single table
A database that cannot be searched
questions.e: Flat files are simple, but contain a lot of repeated data (redundancy).

questions.q: What is a relational database?
o: A database with no primary keys
A database that only stores numbers
A database made of several tables that are linked using keys
A database stored in one text file
questions.e: Relationships reduce repeated data and make the data easier to maintain.

questions.q: What is a primary key?
o: A field that can contain repeated values
A field that is indexed for faster searching
A field that uniquely identifies each record in a table
A field that links to another table
questions.e: A primary key must be unique and not NULL.

questions.q: What is a foreign key?
o: A field that has been encrypted
A field that identifies each record in its own table
A key used to unlock the database
A field in one table that is the primary key of another table, used to link them
questions.e: Foreign keys create the relationships in a relational database.

questions.q: What is a composite key?
o: A key that is stored in two places
A primary key made from two or more fields combined
A key with a repeated value
A key that is used by two tables
questions.e: E.g. (OrderID, ProductID) together identify one line of an order.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a secondary key?
o: A field that is indexed to allow faster searching
questions.e: A secondary key may not be unique, but an index on it speeds up searches.
