questions.q: A teacher can teach many students, but each student has one form teacher. What type of relationship is this?
questions.e: One teacher (one) to many students (many).

questions.q: How can a many-to-many relationship be implemented in a relational database?
o: By storing both values in the same cell
By adding a second primary key to each table
By using a linking table with two one-to-many relationships
questions.e: For example, a Loan table linking Member and Book.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of normalisation?
o: To reduce data redundancy and improve data integrity
To make the database run on a network
questions.e: Normalisation organises tables to avoid repeated data and update/insert/delete anomalies.

questions.q: A table has a cell containing 'Maths, English, Physics'. Which normal form rule does this break?
o: 1NF - values must be atomic (one value per cell)
questions.e: 1NF: no repeating groups, atomic values and a primary key.

questions.q: What is a PARTIAL dependency (broken in 2NF)?
o: A table has no primary key
A non-key attribute depends on only part of a composite key
Two tables have the same name
A non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute
questions.e: Partial dependencies only happen with composite keys.

questions.q: What is a transitive (non-key) dependency (broken in 3NF)?
o: A foreign key has no matching primary key
A non-key attribute depends on only part of the primary key
A non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute
questions.e: E.g. in (StudentID, CourseID, TeacherName), TeacherName depends on CourseID, a non-key field.

questions.q: A table has a composite key (OrderID, ProductID) and the attribute ProductName. What problem does it have?
o: A partial dependency, because ProductName depends only on ProductID
questions.e: ProductName should be moved to a separate Product table.

questions.q: Which SQL keyword is used to choose which fields are displayed?
questions.e: SELECT names the fields, FROM names the table, WHERE filters records.

questions.q: Which SQL clause sorts the results?
questions.e: ORDER BY field ASC/DESC.

questions.q: What does SELECT Name FROM Student WHERE Age > 17 return?
o: The names of all students older than 17
questions.e: WHERE filters the rows; SELECT picks the column.

questions.q: Which SQL statement changes existing data in a record?
questions.e: UPDATE table SET field = value WHERE condition.

questions.q: Which JOIN returns only rows that have a match in both tables?
questions.e: LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table plus matches from the right.

questions.q: What is referential integrity?
o: Making sure every field has a value
Keeping a backup copy of every table
Ensuring that every foreign key value matches an existing primary key value
questions.e: It prevents orphaned records, e.g. a loan for a member who has been deleted.

questions.q: In ACID, what does 'Atomicity' mean?
o: A transaction is completed entirely or not at all
Data must obey the rules of the database
Transactions never run at the same time
questions.e: If a bank transfer fails halfway, it is rolled back.

questions.q: In ACID, what does 'Durability' mean?
o: Once a transaction is complete, its results are permanent, even after a crash or power loss
Transactions can't be run at the same time
questions.e: Committed data is written to non-volatile storage.

questions.q: In ACID, what does 'Isolation' mean?
o: Only one user can ever use the database
Concurrent transactions have the same result as if they had been run one after another
Each transaction is stored in a separate table
Data is hidden from other users
questions.e: Often implemented using record locking.

questions.q: What is the purpose of record locking?
o: To stop two users updating the same record at the same time
To stop users reading any data
questions.e: Prevents lost updates and keeps data consistent.

questions.q: Which is the best description of 'redundancy' as a protection for a database?
o: Keeping copies of the data (e.g. on another disk or server) so that it can be recovered
Having the same data repeated in many tables
questions.e: Redundancy in this sense is a backup/fail-safe. Don't confuse with redundant (repeated) data in tables, which normalisation removes.

questions.q: Explain two advantages of using a relational database rather than a flat file database.

pts.p: Less redundancy / data is not repeated
Because it only needs to be stored / updated once, it is more consistent / has fewer errors
Tables are linked using keys so data can be combined using queries / joins
Easier to search / maintain / add data without affecting other data; supports referential integrity / access rights

questions.model: A relational database reduces redundancy, because data such as a customer's address is stored once in its own table rather than repeated in every record. This also keeps the data consistent, because it only has to be updated in one place. Tables are linked by keys, so queries and joins can be used to bring related data together, and referential integrity can be enforced.

questions.q: Explain what is meant by referential integrity, giving an example of a problem it prevents.

pts.p: Every foreign key value must match a primary key value in the linked table
It prevents orphaned records, e.g. a loan for a member who has been deleted

questions.model: Referential integrity ensures that every foreign key value matches an existing primary key value in the linked table. It prevents orphaned records, for example a loan record that refers to a member who has been deleted.

questions.q: A table has the composite primary key (OrderID, ProductID) and the fields Quantity and ProductName. Explain why the table is not in 2NF and how to normalise it.

pts.p: ProductName depends only on ProductID (part of the key) - a partial dependency
A partial dependency means the table is not in 2NF
Move ProductName into a separate Product table (ProductID, ProductName) with ProductID as its primary key

questions.model: ProductName depends only on ProductID, which is part of the composite key, so there is a partial dependency and the table is not in 2NF. It should be split by moving ProductName into a separate Product table (ProductID as primary key), leaving OrderID, ProductID and Quantity in the original table.

questions.q: Write an SQL statement to display the Title of every book in the table Book that was written by the author 'Orwell', in alphabetical order of Title.

pts.p: SELECT Title FROM Book
WHERE Author = 'Orwell'
ORDER BY Title (ASC)

questions.model: SELECT Title FROM Book WHERE Author = 'Orwell' ORDER BY Title ASC;

questions.q: A bank transfers money from account A to account B. Explain how the ACID properties apply to this transaction.

pts.p: Atomicity: both the withdrawal and the deposit happen, or neither does (rolled back if it fails part-way)
Consistency: the data stays valid and obeys the rules (e.g. the total money is unchanged, no invalid account)
Isolation: other transactions at the same time do not interfere (e.g. record locking, so the result is as if they ran one after another)
Durability: once completed the transfer is permanent even if there is a power failure / crash

questions.model: Atomicity means the withdrawal from A and the deposit to B both happen, or neither does; if it fails half way it is rolled back. Consistency means the database stays valid and obeys its rules, so the total amount of money is unchanged. Isolation means that other transactions happening at the same time, which might be controlled by record locking, do not interfere, so the result is as if they ran one after the other. Durability means that once the transfer is complete it is permanently stored, even if there is a power failure.

questions.q: An online ticket-booking system is used by thousands of customers at the same time. Explain the meaning of ACID and why each property matters for this system.

pts.p: Atomicity: a transaction is completed in full or not at all
Example: payment is taken AND ticket reserved, or neither happens (rolled back if it fails)
Consistency: a transaction leaves the database in a valid state, following the rules (e.g. referential integrity, no seat booked that does not exist)
Isolation: transactions running at the same time give the same result as if run one after another
Example: two customers cannot book the same seat; record locking stops a lost update / double booking
Durability: once a transaction is complete it is permanent, even after a crash or power failure
Example: a confirmed booking is saved to non-volatile storage so is not lost
ACID together keep the data accurate / reliable and customers' trust

questions.model: ACID stands for atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability. Atomicity means a transaction is completed in full or not at all; for example, if payment is taken but the ticket cannot be reserved, the whole transaction is rolled back. Consistency means a transaction must leave the database in a valid state that obeys its rules, such as referential integrity, so a ticket cannot be booked for an event that does not exist. Isolation means that transactions happening at the same time give the same result as if they ran one after another, so record locking stops two customers booking the same seat. Durability means that once a transaction is complete it is permanent, so a confirmed booking is written to non-volatile storage and is not lost after a crash or power failure. Together they keep the data accurate and reliable.

questions.q: Explain the purpose of normalisation and describe the requirements for a table to be in first, second and third normal form.

pts.p: Normalisation organises data to reduce redundancy (repeated data)
It improves data integrity / avoids inconsistencies and anomalies when inserting, updating or deleting
1NF: atomic values - one value per cell, no repeating groups
1NF: the table has a primary key
2NF: in 1NF with no partial dependencies - every non-key field depends on the whole (composite) key
3NF: in 2NF with no non-key (transitive) dependencies - non-key fields depend only on the key
Tables are split and linked using foreign keys

questions.model: Normalisation organises a database to reduce redundancy and improve data integrity, avoiding inconsistencies when data is inserted, updated or deleted. For first normal form (1NF) the table must have a primary key and all values must be atomic, with one value per cell and no repeating groups. For second normal form (2NF) the table must be in 1NF and have no partial dependencies, meaning every non-key field depends on the whole of the composite key. For third normal form (3NF) the table must be in 2NF and have no transitive (non-key) dependencies, meaning non-key fields depend only on the primary key and not on other non-key fields. Tables are split up and linked using foreign keys to achieve this.

1-3-3.title: 1.3.3 Networks
1-3-3.blurb: Protocols and standards, the TCP/IP stack, DNS, ARP, LAN/WAN, switching, security, hardware, topologies and client-server vs peer-to-peer.

questions.q: What is a network protocol?
o: A set of rules that governs how data is communicated
A device that connects two networks
questions.e: Protocols allow different devices to communicate by agreeing on the format and rules.

questions.q: Why are standards important in networking?
o: They make networks free to use
They make the internet faster automatically
They let hardware and software from different manufacturers work together
questions.e: E.g. Ethernet and Wi-Fi standards.

questions.q: What is the difference between the internet and the World Wide Web?
o: The web is the hardware; the internet is the software
The internet is the global network of networks; the web is a service running on it, made of linked web pages
questions.e: The web uses HTTP/HTTPS on top of the internet.

questions.q: How many layers does the TCP/IP stack used at A Level have?
questions.e: Application, Transport, Internet and Link.

questions.q: At which layer of the TCP/IP stack does the TCP protocol operate?
questions.e: TCP (and UDP) operate at the transport layer, splitting data into segments and using port numbers.

questions.q: At which layer are IP addresses added?
questions.e: The internet layer adds source and destination IP addresses (making a packet) and routers use them.

questions.q: At which layer are MAC addresses added?
questions.e: At the link layer a packet is placed in a frame, with source and destination MAC addresses.

questions.q: Which protocol operates at the application layer?
questions.e: Others at this layer: HTTPS, FTP, SMTP, IMAP, POP3.

questions.q: What are the data units called at the transport, internet and link layers (in that order)?
questions.e: Data is encapsulated as it moves down the stack.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a port number?
o: To identify which application or service the data is for
To identify the computer on the internet
questions.e: E.g. port 80 for HTTP, 443 for HTTPS.

questions.q: What is a socket?
o: The MAC address of a device
A physical connector on a router
The combination of an IP address and a port number

questions.q: What is the role of the Domain Name System (DNS)?
o: To translate domain names into IP addresses
questions.e: DNS servers look up www.example.com and return the IP address.

questions.q: What does ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) do?
o: It finds the MAC address that matches an IP address on the local network
It routes packets across the internet
It encrypts data on the local network
It finds the IP address for a domain name
questions.e: ARP works at the link layer on a local network.

questions.q: What is the difference between a LAN and a WAN?
o: A LAN needs the internet; a WAN does not
A WAN is faster than a LAN
A LAN is wireless and a WAN is wired
A LAN covers a small area and is usually owned by one organisation; a WAN covers a large area
questions.e: The internet is the largest WAN. WANs often use leased telecom lines.

questions.q: Which statement describes PACKET switching?
o: A dedicated path is reserved for the whole communication
Data is split into packets that may take different routes and are reassembled at the destination
Each packet is sent to every device
All data travels in one continuous stream
questions.e: This uses the network efficiently, but packets can arrive out of order.

questions.q: Which statement describes CIRCUIT switching?
o: A dedicated connection with fixed bandwidth is set up for the duration of the communication
The connection is shared between all users
questions.e: Used by traditional phone calls. The connection is guaranteed but wastes bandwidth when it is idle.

questions.q: What is the main function of a firewall?
o: To increase the speed of the network
To monitor and filter network traffic according to a set of rules
To store frequently used web pages
questions.e: Firewalls can block traffic by port number, IP address or protocol.

questions.q: What is a proxy server?
o: A server that stores email only
A hardware device that connects LANs
A server that acts as an intermediary between a client and the internet
questions.e: Proxies can filter content, cache pages and hide the client's IP address.

questions.q: Which type of malware replicates itself across a network WITHOUT needing a user to run a program?
questions.e: A virus needs a host program and user action; a Trojan pretends to be legitimate software.

questions.q: What is SQL injection?
o: Sending a large number of requests to a server
Reading data from a network cable
Entering SQL code into a form field to attack the database behind a website
Tricking someone with a fake email
questions.e: Prevented by input sanitisation / validation and parameterised queries.

questions.q: What is the role of a router?
o: To connect devices within one LAN by MAC address
To forward packets between different networks using IP addresses
To broadcast every packet to all devices
questions.e: A switch connects devices within a LAN; a router connects networks.

questions.q: How does a switch differ from a hub?
o: A hub is faster than a switch
A switch sends data only to the device it is intended for; a hub sends it to all devices
A switch connects different networks; a hub does not
questions.e: Switches reduce unnecessary traffic and collisions.

questions.q: Which is a disadvantage of a star topology?
o: A single cable fault brings down the whole network
Adding a device affects all other devices
If the central switch fails, the whole network goes down
It is impossible to add new devices
questions.e: Star networks are easy to manage and a failure of one cable only affects one device.

questions.q: Which is an advantage of a client-server network over peer-to-peer?
o: It has no single point of failure
It is cheaper to set up
Centralised management of security, backups and resources
questions.e: A server must be bought and maintained, but data and users can be managed centrally.

questions.q: What is the difference between TCP and UDP?
o: TCP works at the link layer
TCP is reliable and ordered, using acknowledgements; UDP is faster but does not guarantee delivery
UDP is more reliable than TCP
questions.e: UDP is used where speed matters more than perfect delivery, e.g. video calls.

questions.q: Explain why protocols are important in network communication.

pts.p: A protocol is a set of rules for how data is sent / received
Defines the format / structure of the data (e.g. headers, packet size, error checking)
Allows different devices / manufacturers / systems to communicate with each other

questions.model: A protocol is a set of agreed rules that defines how data is formatted and sent, for example the structure of packets and how errors are checked. Using protocols means devices made by different manufacturers, running different systems, can communicate and understand each other's data.

questions.q: Describe how the Domain Name System (DNS) is used when a user types a web address into a browser.

pts.p: The browser sends the domain name to a DNS server (resolver)
The DNS server looks up (or asks other DNS servers) the domain name
The IP address is returned so the browser can contact the web server

questions.model: The browser sends the domain name to a DNS server. The DNS server looks the name up (querying other DNS servers if it does not know it) and returns the IP address of the web server, which the browser then uses to request the page.

questions.q: Explain two differences between packet switching and circuit switching.

pts.p: Packet switching splits data into packets which can take different routes; circuit switching uses one dedicated route
Circuit switching reserves a fixed bandwidth / connection for the whole communication; packet switching does not
Packet switching uses the network more efficiently / less bandwidth is wasted; circuit switching wastes bandwidth when idle
In packet switching, packets can arrive out of order and need reassembling; circuit switching data arrives in order with consistent quality

questions.model: In packet switching the data is split into packets which can each take a different route and are reassembled at the destination, whereas circuit switching sets up one dedicated route for the whole communication. Circuit switching reserves a fixed bandwidth, which guarantees quality but wastes capacity when it is idle, whereas packet switching uses the network more efficiently. In packet switching the packets can arrive out of order and need to be reassembled.

questions.q: Explain how a firewall helps to protect a network.

pts.p: It monitors / inspects incoming and outgoing network traffic (packets)
It compares traffic against a set of rules and blocks anything that does not meet them
It can block traffic by port / IP address / protocol, preventing unauthorised access

questions.model: A firewall monitors the packets entering and leaving the network and compares them with a set of rules. Traffic from unauthorised sources, or using ports or protocols that are not allowed, is blocked, preventing unauthorised access.

questions.q: Compare client-server and peer-to-peer networks.

pts.p: Client-server: clients request services / data from a central server
Client-server: easier to manage / back up / secure centrally
Peer-to-peer: all computers are equal and share resources directly with each other, with no central server
Peer-to-peer is cheaper / easier to set up; but harder to secure and manage, and has no central backup

questions.model: In a client-server network, clients make requests to a central server which provides the services and data, so security, backups and users can be managed centrally, although the server is expensive and a single point of failure. In a peer-to-peer network, all computers are equal and share their resources directly with each other without a server, which is cheaper and simpler to set up, but is harder to secure and manage and has no central backup.

questions.q: Describe how SQL injection can be used to attack a website and how it can be prevented.

pts.p: The attacker enters SQL code into an input field / form
The code is run by the database, allowing the attacker to read, change or delete data
Prevented by validating / sanitising inputs (or parameterised queries)

questions.model: The attacker types SQL code into a form field on the website. If the input is not checked, the database runs the code, allowing the attacker to read, change or delete data. It can be prevented by validating and sanitising all input, or by using parameterised queries.

questions.q: Describe how a message is sent from a user's computer to a web server using the TCP/IP stack.

pts.p: The application layer formats the data using an application protocol (e.g. HTTP)
At the transport layer the data is split into segments and port numbers are added (TCP)
TCP adds sequence numbers so the data can be put back in order / checked for missing segments
At the internet layer the source and destination IP addresses are added, making a packet
Routers use the destination IP address to forward the packet across networks
At the link layer source and destination MAC addresses are added, making a frame, which is sent over the physical medium
At the destination the process is reversed up the stack and the data is reassembled

questions.model: At the application layer the data is formatted using a protocol such as HTTP. At the transport layer TCP splits it into segments, adds port numbers to identify the application, and adds sequence numbers so the data can be put in order and missing segments detected and resent. At the internet layer source and destination IP addresses are added, creating packets, and routers use the destination IP address to forward each packet across the networks towards the web server. At the link layer MAC addresses are added, creating a frame which is sent over the physical medium (such as a cable or wireless link). At the destination the process is reversed up through the layers and the data is reassembled in the correct order.

questions.q: A company wants to protect its network and the data it holds from attack. Discuss the measures it could use.

pts.p: A firewall filters incoming and outgoing traffic using rules (ports, IP addresses)
A proxy server can filter content, hide internal IP addresses and cache pages
Encryption makes intercepted data unreadable without the key
Antivirus / anti-malware software detects and removes viruses, worms and Trojans
Keeping software and operating systems updated / patched to remove vulnerabilities
Strong passwords, access levels and user accounts limit who can access what
Staff training to spot phishing and social engineering
Input validation / sanitisation (and parameterised queries) prevents SQL injection and buffer overflow
Access logs and packet sniffers / network monitoring help detect suspicious activity
Backups allow recovery after an attack
Evaluation: no single measure is enough (layered defence) / costs, usability and human error must be considered

questions.model: The company should use a combination of measures. A firewall will filter traffic into and out of the network according to rules, blocking unauthorised ports and addresses, and a proxy server can filter content and hide internal IP addresses. Encryption makes any data that is intercepted unreadable without the key. Antivirus and anti-malware software will detect and remove viruses, worms and Trojans, and keeping the operating system and software updated patches known vulnerabilities. Strong passwords, access levels and user accounts limit who can reach sensitive data. Staff should be trained to spot phishing and social engineering. Input should be validated and sanitised to prevent SQL injection and buffer overflow attacks, and access logs and network monitoring will help detect suspicious activity. Backups allow recovery after an attack. No single measure is enough, because attackers use many methods, so a layered defence is best, balanced against cost and usability, and the weakest link is often human error, which makes training particularly important.

1-3-4.title: 1.3.4 Web technologies
1-3-4.blurb: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, search engine indexing, the PageRank algorithm, and client-side vs server-side processing.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of HTML?
o: To style the colours and fonts of a page
To define the structure and content of a web page
To store user data on the server
questions.e: HTML marks up elements such as headings, paragraphs, images and links.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of CSS?
o: To store data in a database
To define the structure of a web page
To run code on the server
To control the presentation of a web page, such as colours, fonts and layout
questions.e: CSS is separate from HTML so styling can be changed in one place.

questions.q: Which language is typically used to add interactivity to a web page in the browser?
questions.e: JavaScript runs client-side and can respond to events such as clicks.

questions.q: Which HTML tag correctly links an external CSS file called style.css?
questions.e: A <link> element uses the href attribute to point at the stylesheet. (<script src=...> uses src, but <link> uses href.)

questions.q: What does the CSS rule  p { color: blue; }  do?
o: Makes the background of the page blue
Makes one paragraph with the id 'p' blue
Makes the text in all paragraph elements blue
questions.e: The selector p applies to every paragraph element.

questions.q: What is a search engine index?
o: A program that blocks bad websites
A list of the most visited websites
A database of information about web pages that have been found by a web crawler
questions.e: Search queries are matched against the index, not the live web.

questions.q: What does a web crawler (spider) do?
o: Follows hyperlinks from page to page, collecting information to add to the index
questions.e: The crawler records details such as the URL, content/keywords and when the page was last updated.

questions.q: What is the main idea behind the PageRank algorithm?
o: A page is more important if it has more images
A page is more important if it is newer
A page is more important if many pages, especially important pages, link to it
A page is more important if it has more words
questions.e: Links are treated as 'votes', weighted by the importance of the page that links.

questions.q: In PageRank, what does the damping factor (often 0.85) represent?
o: The number of pages that link to a page
The size of a web page
The number of times the algorithm is repeated
The probability that a user continues clicking on links rather than stopping or jumping to a random page
questions.e: The (1 - d) part of the formula models the user choosing a random page.

questions.q: Pages A, B and C all start with a PageRank of 1 and d = 0.85. A links to B; B links to A and C; C links to A. Using PR = (1 - d) + d x (sum of PR/links from each linking page), what is A's PageRank after one iteration?
questions.e: A receives 1/2 from B (B has two links) and 1/1 from C: 0.15 + 0.85 x (0.5 + 1) = 1.425.

questions.q: For the same pages (A links to B; B links to A and C; C links to A; all start at 1; d = 0.85), what is C's PageRank after one iteration?
questions.e: C receives half of B's rank: 0.15 + 0.85 x (1/2) = 0.575.

questions.q: What is SERVER-SIDE processing?
o: Code that runs on the web server before the page is sent to the browser
Code that runs in the user's browser
Code that runs on a router
questions.e: Typical server-side tasks: checking logins, database queries, processing payments.

questions.q: What is CLIENT-SIDE processing?
o: Code that is stored in the database
Code that runs in the user's web browser
Code that runs on the ISP's DNS server
Code that runs on the web server
questions.e: Client-side code (e.g. JavaScript) can respond immediately without contacting the server.

questions.q: Which task is best done on the SERVER side?
o: Checking a username and password against a database
Checking that an email field is not empty before sending
Highlighting a field when the cursor is over it
questions.e: Sensitive operations must not be done in code the user can view or modify.

questions.q: Which is an advantage of client-side processing?
o: It works even if JavaScript is disabled
It gives immediate feedback and reduces the load on the server
It is more secure than server-side processing
It can access the database directly
questions.e: Disadvantages: the code can be viewed or altered by the user, and depends on the browser.

questions.q: Why should input be validated on the server even if it has been validated on the client?
o: The server is faster at validating
Client-side checks can be bypassed or altered by the user
Validation is only needed once per year
questions.e: Server-side validation is essential for security.

questions.q: Describe how a search engine uses a web crawler to create its index.

pts.p: The crawler (spider) visits a web page and follows the hyperlinks to other pages
It records information about each page (e.g. URL, keywords / content, when it was last updated)
This information is stored in the search engine's index (a database) which is searched when a user enters a query

questions.model: The web crawler visits a page and follows the hyperlinks on it to find other pages. It records information about each page, such as the URL, keywords or content and when it was last updated. This information is stored in the search engine's index, which is searched when a user enters a query.

questions.q: Explain how the PageRank algorithm decides the order in which search results are displayed.

pts.p: It ranks pages by the number of links (backlinks) pointing to them
A link from a page with a high rank is worth more than a link from a low-ranked page
Each page's rank is shared between its outgoing links and recalculated repeatedly (using a damping factor) until the values settle

questions.model: PageRank gives each page a score based on the number of links pointing to it. A link from a highly ranked page is worth more than one from a low-ranked page. The rank of each page is shared between its outgoing links and the calculation is repeated many times, using a damping factor, until the values settle. Pages with higher ranks are listed first.

questions.q: Explain the difference between client-side and server-side processing, giving an example task for each.

pts.p: Client-side code runs in the user's browser / on their computer
Example of client-side: form validation / animation / responding to a click (JavaScript)
Server-side code runs on the web server and only the result is sent to the browser
Example of server-side: database access / checking a login / payment processing (PHP, SQL)

questions.model: Client-side processing is done by code that runs in the user's browser, for example using JavaScript to validate a form or respond to a click straight away without contacting the server. Server-side processing is done on the web server and only the result is sent to the browser, for example checking a login against a database or processing a payment using PHP.

questions.q: A website has a booking form. Explain why the data entered should be validated on both the client side and the server side.

pts.p: Client-side validation (e.g. JavaScript) gives immediate feedback to the user
It reduces the load on the server / avoids a round trip for invalid data
But client-side code can be viewed, modified or disabled by the user, so it can be bypassed
Server-side validation cannot be tampered with by the user, so it is secure
It protects the database from malicious input such as SQL injection
Some checks can only be done on the server (e.g. username already in use, seat still available)
Using both gives a good user experience and security

questions.model: Client-side validation, using JavaScript in the browser, gives the user immediate feedback and reduces the load on the server because invalid data does not have to be sent. However, client-side code can be viewed, modified or disabled by the user, so it can be bypassed. Server-side validation cannot be tampered with by the user, so it is secure and protects the database from malicious input such as SQL injection. Some checks can only be done on the server, such as whether a username is already in use or a seat is still available. Using both gives a good user experience and good security.

1-4-1.group: 1.4 Data types, data structures and algorithms
1-4-1.title: 1.4.1 Data types
1-4-1.blurb: Primitive types, binary and hexadecimal, signed integers, floating point, bitwise operations and character encoding.

questions.q: Which type best stores whether an account is active?
questions.e: A Boolean stores true or false.

questions.q: Which type best stores a single letter?
questions.e: A character stores one symbol; a string stores a sequence of characters.

questions.q: What is unsigned binary 10110110 in denary?
What is hexadecimal 3A in denary?
What is denary 173 in hexadecimal?
What is −13 in 8-bit two’s complement?
questions.e: 13 is 00001101. Invert and add 1 to get 11110011.

questions.q: What is −13 in 8-bit sign and magnitude?
questions.e: The sign bit is 1 and the magnitude is 0001101.

questions.q: What is the range of an 8-bit two’s complement integer?
questions.e: The sign position has weight −128; the remaining bits total 127.

questions.q: Add unsigned binary 00101101 and 00010111.
Subtract unsigned 00001101 from 00101000.

questions.e: An AND mask keeps only positions that are 1 in both values.
OR sets a bit when either input has a 1.
XOR is 1 when the input bits differ.

questions.q: Logically shift 11000001 left by one, retaining eight bits.
questions.e: Discard the high bit and insert 0 on the right; overflow means this is not an exact doubling.

questions.q: Decode mantissa 01100000 and exponent 0010, using an 8-bit two’s complement fraction and 4-bit two’s complement exponent.
questions.e: The mantissa is 0.75; 0.75 × 2² = 3.

questions.q: Which pair normalises mantissa 00110000 with exponent 0011?
questions.e: Left-shift the mantissa once and decrease the exponent once, preserving the value.

questions.q: Why may a real number lose precision when stored in floating point?
o: There are finitely many mantissa bits
questions.e: Some values require more binary fractional digits than the mantissa can store.

questions.q: Which statement about Unicode and ASCII is correct?
o: Unicode represents a much wider range of characters
ASCII includes every world writing system
questions.e: Unicode assigns code points across many scripts; UTF encodings determine storage.

questions.q: Explain how to represent −18 in 8-bit two’s complement.

pts.p: Write positive 18 as 00010010.
Invert each bit to obtain 11101101.
Add one to obtain 11101110.

questions.model: Write positive 18 as 00010010. Invert each bit to obtain 11101101. Add one to obtain 11101110.

questions.q: Explain how mantissa length and exponent length affect a floating-point representation.

pts.p: More mantissa bits improve precision.
More exponent bits increase the range of representable magnitudes.
With a fixed total bit budget there is a trade-off between range and precision.

questions.model: More mantissa bits improve precision. More exponent bits increase the range of representable magnitudes. With a fixed total bit budget there is a trade-off between range and precision.

questions.q: Describe how a bit mask can test whether bit 3 is set in an unsigned byte; bit 0 is the least significant bit.

pts.p: Use the mask 00001000.
Apply bitwise AND to the byte and the mask.
A non-zero result means that bit 3 is set.

questions.model: Use the mask 00001000. Apply bitwise AND to the byte and the mask. A non-zero result means that bit 3 is set.

questions.q: A weather sensor records decimal temperatures, on/off status and text labels. Discuss appropriate data types and how the temperatures could be represented.

pts.p: Use a Boolean for the on/off status.
Use a string for a text label.
A real type supports fractional temperatures.
Floating point uses a mantissa and an exponent.
A signed representation allows negative temperatures.
Finite precision may cause rounding error, so choose enough bits for the required precision and range.

questions.model: Use a Boolean for the on/off status. Use a string for a text label. A real type supports fractional temperatures. Floating point uses a mantissa and an exponent. A signed representation allows negative temperatures. Finite precision may cause rounding error, so choose enough bits for the required precision and range. Compare each candidate type with the actual requirements of the sensor system. The measurement must preserve enough detail to distinguish small changes, while the status needs only two values. Text labels may include several characters and must be stored together. Representation choices should reflect the required temperature limits and the accuracy the application needs.

1-4-2.group: 1.4 Data types, data structures and algorithms
1-4-2.title: 1.4.2 Data structures
1-4-2.blurb: Arrays, records, lists, tuples, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, graphs and hash tables.

questions.q: How many elements are in an array with dimensions 3 × 4 × 2?
questions.e: Multiply the sizes of all three dimensions.

questions.q: What does a record typically group?
o: Related named fields that may have different types
questions.e: For example a student record can contain name, age and attendance.

questions.q: What characterises a tuple in languages where tuples are immutable?
o: Its elements cannot be changed after creation
It can only contain two values
questions.e: Immutable tuples provide a fixed grouping of values; exact language behaviour varies.

questions.q: How does a singly linked list connect its nodes?
o: Each node stores a pointer to the next node
Each node stores every other node
A hash function orders every node
questions.e: The final next pointer is null; traversal follows successive links.

questions.q: When inserting after a linked-list node P, what must be updated?
o: The new node’s next pointer and P’s next pointer
questions.e: Set new.next = P.next, then P.next = new.

questions.q: A stack receives A, B, C in that order. Which value is popped first?
questions.e: A stack is last in, first out.

questions.q: A queue receives A, B, C in that order. Which value is dequeued first?
questions.e: A queue is first in, first out.

questions.q: Which traversal visits a binary search tree’s keys in ascending order?
questions.e: Visit the left subtree, the node, then the right subtree.

questions.q: Insert 8, 3, 10, 6 into an empty binary search tree. Where is 6?
questions.e: 6 is below 8 but above 3, so it goes right from 3.

questions.q: What can replace a BST node with two children during deletion?
o: A null pointer without reconnecting children
questions.e: Reconnect the replacement and remove its old occurrence while preserving the ordering.

questions.q: What distinguishes a directed graph?
o: Every vertex has exactly two edges
questions.e: A→B need not imply B→A; undirected edges connect both ways.

questions.q: For a sparse graph, which representation often uses less space?
o: A stack of every possible edge
questions.e: Lists store existing neighbours, whereas a matrix reserves entries for all vertex pairs.

questions.q: What is a hash-table collision?
o: Different keys map to the same slot
questions.e: Resolve collisions using chaining or a suitable probing strategy.

questions.q: What is expected average lookup time in a well-managed hash table?
questions.e: A good hash distribution and controlled load factor support constant expected lookup; worst cases can be slower.

questions.q: Why does open-addressed deletion often use a tombstone?
o: To preserve the probe chain for later searches
questions.e: Stopping at a newly empty slot could hide a key stored later in the chain.

questions.q: Describe how to traverse a singly linked list.

pts.p: Start at the head pointer.
Visit the current node’s data.
Follow its next pointer to the next node.
Stop when the pointer is null.

questions.model: Start at the head pointer. Visit the current node’s data. Follow its next pointer to the next node. Stop when the pointer is null.

questions.q: Explain how to remove an item from a circular queue.

pts.p: Check whether the queue is empty before removing an item.
Read the item at the front index.
Advance the front index using modulo the capacity.
Decrease the number of stored items.

questions.model: Check whether the queue is empty before removing an item. Read the item at the front index. Advance the front index using modulo the capacity. Decrease the number of stored items.

questions.q: Describe how to find a key in a binary search tree.

pts.p: Compare the key with the current node.
Move left for a smaller key and right for a larger key.
Stop when the key is found or a null pointer is reached.

questions.model: Compare the key with the current node. Move left for a smaller key and right for a larger key. Stop when the key is found or a null pointer is reached.

questions.q: A school stores student records by ID and also processes help requests in arrival order. Evaluate suitable data structures.

pts.p: Records group named student fields.
A hash table can index records by student ID.
A suitable hash function gives fast expected lookup.
Collisions need chaining or probing.
A queue processes help requests in first-in, first-out order.
Check for an empty queue and consider capacity or dynamic storage when adding and removing requests.

questions.model: Records group named student fields. A hash table can index records by student ID. A suitable hash function gives fast expected lookup. Collisions need chaining or probing. A queue processes help requests in first-in, first-out order. Check for an empty queue and consider capacity or dynamic storage when adding and removing requests. Arrival order matters because an early request should not be overtaken merely because another student has a smaller ID. Separate storage for student information and pending requests avoids confusing these purposes. Maintain links or indices correctly when adding and removing items, and handle missing IDs and empty requests safely. Choose the allocation approach according to the expected number of users.

1-4-3.group: 1.4 Data types, data structures and algorithms
1-4-3.title: 1.4.3 Boolean algebra
1-4-3.blurb: Truth tables, gates, Boolean laws, Karnaugh maps, adders and D-type flip-flops.

questions.q: When is A AND B equal to 1?
o: When both A and B are 1
questions.e: AND requires both inputs to be true.

questions.q: When is A XOR B equal to 1?
questions.e: XOR is exclusive OR: exactly one input is true.

questions.q: What is NOT(A AND B) equivalent to?
questions.e: De Morgan’s law complements each input and swaps AND for OR.

questions.q: What is NOT(A OR B) equivalent to?
questions.e: This is the other De Morgan identity.

questions.q: Simplify A AND (A OR B).
questions.e: The absorption law gives A.

questions.q: Simplify NOT(NOT A).
questions.e: Double negation returns the original input.

questions.q: Which is the distributive expansion of A AND (B OR C)?
questions.e: AND distributes over OR.

questions.q: Which expression uses the commutative law?
o: A OR B = B OR A
questions.e: Commutation changes operand order without changing the result.

questions.q: Which expression uses the associative law?
o: (A OR B) OR C = A OR (B OR C)
A OR B = B OR A
questions.e: Association changes grouping within the same operation.

questions.q: How many rows are in a complete truth table with three inputs?
questions.e: There are 2³ combinations.

questions.q: What sizes of groups may be used for adjacent 1s in a Karnaugh map?
questions.e: Use rectangular groups of 1, 2, 4, 8, etc.; edges wrap and groups may overlap.

questions.q: Why do Karnaugh-map headings use Gray-code order?
o: Adjacent cells differ in exactly one input
questions.e: One-bit adjacency enables elimination of changing variables.

questions.q: For a half adder, what are sum and carry?
o: Sum = A AND B; carry = A OR B
Sum = A OR B; carry = NOT A
Sum = A XOR B; carry = A AND B
questions.e: Two true inputs give sum 0 and carry 1.

questions.q: For a full adder with A=1, B=1 and carry-in=1, what are sum and carry-out?
questions.e: Three ones represent binary 11.

questions.q: When does a positive-edge-triggered D-type flip-flop copy D to Q?
questions.e: It captures D at the triggering edge and holds Q between edges.

questions.q: A door unlocks if a valid card is presented AND either a PIN is correct OR a staff override is active. Define inputs and give a Boolean expression.

pts.p: Let C represent a valid card.
Let P represent a correct PIN and S a staff override.
The output is C AND (P OR S).

questions.model: Let C represent a valid card. Let P represent a correct PIN and S a staff override. The output is C AND (P OR S).

questions.q: Explain how to simplify an expression using a Karnaugh map.

pts.p: Fill cells with the truth-table outputs in Gray-code order.
Group adjacent 1s in rectangles whose sizes are powers of two.
Keep variables that remain constant within a group and remove variables that change.
OR the group terms together.

questions.model: Fill cells with the truth-table outputs in Gray-code order. Group adjacent 1s in rectangles whose sizes are powers of two. Keep variables that remain constant within a group and remove variables that change. OR the group terms together.

questions.q: Give equations for a full adder with inputs A, B and carry-in C.

pts.p: Sum is A XOR B XOR C.
Carry-out is (A AND B) OR (C AND (A XOR B)).
The carry-out is 1 when at least two inputs are 1.

questions.model: Sum is A XOR B XOR C. Carry-out is (A AND B) OR (C AND (A XOR B)). The carry-out is 1 when at least two inputs are 1.

questions.q: Explain how gates, half adders, full adders and D-type flip-flops contribute to arithmetic and storage circuits.

pts.p: Logic gates implement Boolean operations.
A half adder uses XOR for sum and AND for carry.
A full adder accepts a carry-in as a third input.
Full adders can be chained so carry-out feeds the next column.
A D-type flip-flop stores one bit by capturing D at a clock edge.
Several flip-flops can form a register that holds an arithmetic result.

questions.model: Logic gates implement Boolean operations. A half adder uses XOR for sum and AND for carry. A full adder accepts a carry-in as a third input. Full adders can be chained so carry-out feeds the next column. A D-type flip-flop stores one bit by capturing D at a clock edge. Several flip-flops can form a register that holds an arithmetic result. In a multi-bit addition circuit each column uses its own inputs and the incoming carry from the previous column. The stored output remains available after the inputs to the arithmetic circuit change. Clocked storage allows the next stage to use a stable result at the appropriate time. Registers collect bits into words so the processor can store a complete value.

1-5-1.group: 1.5 Legal, moral, cultural and ethical issues
1-5-1.title: 1.5.1 Computing legislation
1-5-1.blurb: The Data Protection Act 2018 (UK GDPR), Computer Misuse Act 1990, Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 and the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the Data Protection Act 2018 (which implements UK GDPR)?
o: To protect software from being copied
To regulate how personal data about living people is collected, stored and used
To allow police to monitor communications
questions.e: It gives individuals rights over their data and places duties on organisations that hold it.

questions.q: In data protection law, who is the 'data subject'?
o: The company that sells the data
The organisation that stores the data
The person whom the personal data is about
The person who enforces the law
questions.e: The data controller decides how and why the data is processed.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of 'special category' (sensitive) personal data?
o: A username with no other data
questions.e: Others: ethnicity, religion, political opinions, genetic and biometric data, sexual orientation.

questions.q: Which is one of the data protection principles?
o: Data must be kept accurate and up to date
Data may be used for any purpose
Data must be shared with other organisations
questions.e: Others: lawful, fair and transparent; purpose limitation; data minimisation; storage limitation; security; accountability.

questions.q: A company keeps customer records for 20 years after a customer closes their account, with no reason to do so. Which principle is broken?
o: Data should be kept no longer than necessary
questions.e: Storage limitation.

questions.q: A shop collects customers' email addresses for receipts and then sells them to advertisers. Which principle is MOST clearly broken?
o: Data must be deleted after a year
Data must only be used for the purpose it was collected for
questions.e: Purpose limitation.

questions.q: Which of these is a right of a data subject?
o: To delete data held by the government without a reason
To ask to see the personal data an organisation holds about them
questions.e: Rights include access, rectification, erasure, restriction, portability and objection.

questions.q: Which organisation enforces data protection law in the UK?
questions.e: The ICO can investigate and fine organisations.

questions.q: What does the Computer Misuse Act 1990 make illegal?
questions.e: It covers hacking and related offences.

questions.q: An employee guesses a colleague's password and reads their emails without permission. Which offence is this?
questions.e: Offence 1 of the CMA: even just viewing is enough.

questions.q: A person gains unauthorised access to a bank's system in order to commit fraud. Which CMA offence is this?
o: Failing to register with the ICO
Unauthorised access with intent to commit or facilitate further offences
questions.e: This is more serious than accessing without further intent.

questions.q: Which action would be an offence under the CMA's 'unauthorised modification' provision?
o: Deliberately spreading malware that deletes files
questions.e: This covers viruses, ransomware and altering or deleting data.

questions.q: What does the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 protect?
o: The creators of original works such as software, music, films and writing
questions.e: Copying or distributing without permission is an offence.

questions.q: A school buys one licence for a piece of software and installs it on 30 computers. Which law is being broken?
questions.e: Software is protected by copyright; the licence only allows installation as agreed.

questions.q: Which of these is illegal under the CDPA?
o: Downloading and sharing a film without the owner's permission
Buying a licensed copy of a game
Quoting a short passage with credit in an essay
questions.e: Piracy is copyright infringement.

questions.q: What does the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000 (RIPA) allow?
o: Public bodies to monitor communications and demand access to protected data, under certain conditions
Anyone to read other people's email
questions.e: E.g. the police and security services can intercept communications and ISPs can be required to provide access.

questions.q: What is the main criticism of RIPA?
o: It stops the police investigating crimes
It can threaten privacy and be used for excessive surveillance
questions.e: Concerns: invasion of privacy, mass surveillance and misuse of powers.

questions.q: Describe two principles of the Data Protection Act 2018.

pts.p: Data must be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently
Data must be collected for a specific purpose / only used for that purpose
Data must be accurate and kept up to date
Data must not be kept longer than necessary / only the minimum data collected
Data must be kept secure (protected from unauthorised access, loss or damage)

questions.model: Any two from: data must be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently; data must only be collected and used for a specific purpose; data must be accurate and up to date; data must not be kept longer than necessary; data must be kept secure.

questions.q: A hacker gains access to a company's network without permission and deletes some of its files. Explain which law has been broken.

pts.p: The Computer Misuse Act 1990
Unauthorised access to computer material (the hacker gained access without permission)
Unauthorised modification of data (deleting the files)

questions.model: The Computer Misuse Act 1990 has been broken. The hacker committed the offence of unauthorised access to computer material by entering the network without permission, and also the offence of unauthorised modification of data by deleting the files.

questions.q: Describe two ways in which the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 affects how people may use software.

pts.p: It is illegal to copy or distribute software without the copyright holder's permission (piracy)
Software must only be used according to its licence (e.g. the number of installations / users)
It is illegal to claim the work as your own / use code or content without crediting the owner
It protects creators' work, so they can profit from it

questions.model: It is illegal to copy or distribute software without the permission of the copyright holder, which is known as piracy. Software must also be used in line with the terms of its licence, for example only being installed on the number of computers that the licence covers.

questions.q: Explain how the Data Protection Act 2018, the Computer Misuse Act 1990 and the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 affect the way an organisation must use its computer systems.

pts.p: DPA: personal data must be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently
DPA: data must be accurate, kept secure and not kept longer than necessary
DPA: individuals (data subjects) have rights, e.g. to see or correct their data
CMA: unauthorised access to computer material is illegal (hacking), including by employees
CMA: unauthorised modification of data / spreading malware is illegal; so the organisation needs security measures
CDPA: software and other works must not be copied or used without the owner's permission
CDPA: organisations must hold the correct licences for the software they use
Penalties: fines or prison for breaking these laws

questions.model: Under the Data Protection Act 2018 an organisation must process personal data lawfully, fairly and transparently, keep it accurate and secure, and not keep it longer than necessary; individuals have rights such as seeing and correcting their data. Under the Computer Misuse Act 1990 it is illegal to gain unauthorised access to computer material or to modify data without permission, such as by spreading malware, so the organisation should have security measures such as passwords and firewalls and make sure that employees do not access data without authority. Under the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 the organisation must not copy software or other works without permission and must hold the correct licences for software it uses. Breaking these laws can lead to fines or prison.

questions.q: A company gathers and analyses large amounts of personal data about its customers, and also monitors its employees' emails and web use. Discuss the legal issues the company must consider.

pts.p: The Data Protection Act 2018 / UK GDPR applies to personal data about customers and employees
Data must be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently - people must be told what is collected and why
Data must only be used for the stated purpose and only the data needed collected (purpose limitation, minimisation)
Data must be accurate, not kept longer than necessary, and kept secure
Individuals have rights, e.g. to access, correct or request deletion of their data
The company must be accountable; the ICO can investigate and impose fines for breaches
Monitoring of communications: RIPA / employers must have a lawful reason and employees should be told (policy)
The Computer Misuse Act applies if staff or outsiders access or modify data without authority, so access controls are needed
Copyright law: the company must have licences for analysis software and must not misuse third-party data
Balance: business benefit vs privacy rights; concluding judgement

questions.model: The Data Protection Act 2018 (UK GDPR) applies because the company holds personal data about customers and employees. It must process this data lawfully, fairly and transparently, which means telling people what is collected and why, and usually obtaining consent. The data must only be used for the stated purpose and the company must not collect more than it needs. The data must be accurate, kept secure and not retained longer than necessary, and people have rights to access, correct or request deletion of their data. The company is accountable for this, and the ICO can investigate and fine it for breaches. Monitoring employees' emails and web use is also a legal issue: it should have a lawful reason, be proportionate, and employees should be told through a policy; RIPA regulates interception of communications. The Computer Misuse Act applies if anyone accesses or modifies the data without authority, so the company needs access controls. It must also hold licences for the software it uses under copyright law. Overall, the company has to balance its business interests against individuals' right to privacy.

1-5-2.group: 1.5 Legal, moral, cultural and ethical issues
1-5-2.title: 1.5.2 Moral, social, ethical and cultural issues
1-5-2.blurb: Computers in the workforce, automated decision making, AI, environmental effects, censorship, monitoring, privacy, piracy, accessibility and culture.

questions.q: What is the difference between a MORAL and an ETHICAL issue?
o: Moral issues are always illegal; ethical ones are always legal
Moral relates to personal beliefs about right and wrong; ethical relates to shared principles of a group or profession
Ethical issues only apply to computers
questions.e: Morals are personal; ethics are the agreed standards of a community or profession.

questions.q: What is the 'digital divide'?
o: The gap between people who have access to digital technology and those who do not
The difference between analogue and digital signals
The gap between two computer networks
The boundary between a LAN and a WAN
questions.e: It can be caused by cost, location, age, skills or disability.

questions.q: Which is a possible benefit of computers in the workplace?
o: No human employees are ever needed
Tasks can be automated, increasing efficiency and allowing 24-hour operation
questions.e: Risks include job losses, deskilling and dependence on systems.

questions.q: Which is a possible negative effect of automation on employment?
o: Some jobs may be replaced, causing unemployment unless people are retrained
questions.e: New technology also creates new jobs, but workers may need new skills.

questions.q: A company uses an algorithm to shortlist job applicants. It was trained on past hiring data that favoured one group. What is the main ethical concern?
o: It will use too much storage
The algorithm may be biased and discriminate unfairly
questions.e: Training data can contain bias, which an AI system learns and repeats.

questions.q: Which is an ethical concern about decisions made by AI systems?
o: AI systems never make mistakes, so they cannot be questioned
It can be hard to explain how a decision was reached or to say who is accountable for a mistake
AI systems always explain every decision in plain English
AI decisions can only be made by the person who owns the computer
questions.e: Lack of transparency and accountability is a key ethical issue: should responsibility lie with the developer, the company using it, or the user?

questions.q: Which is an environmental concern about digital technology?
o: Digital technology always reduces energy use
Large amounts of energy are used by data centres and devices, and e-waste is hard to dispose of
questions.e: Positives: remote working can reduce travel; smart systems can improve efficiency.

questions.q: Which is an argument FOR internet censorship?
o: It can protect children from harmful content
It reduces the need for laws
questions.e: Arguments against: it restricts freedom of speech and who decides what is censored?

questions.q: Which is an argument AGAINST internet censorship?
o: It is easy to apply fairly
It can restrict freedom of speech and access to information
questions.e: Censorship raises questions about who decides what is acceptable.

questions.q: A company uses CCTV and software to monitor employees' computer use. Which is the main concern for employees?
questions.e: Benefits for employers include security, productivity and protecting data.

questions.q: Which is a benefit of analysing customers' personal data?
o: Organisations can offer personalised, targeted products and services
questions.e: Concerns: privacy, data security and how the data might be sold or misused.

questions.q: What is meant by 'piracy' in the context of digital content?
o: Illegally copying or distributing copyrighted material
questions.e: Piracy harms creators' income and is illegal under the CDPA.

questions.q: Which law makes it illegal to send indecent or offensive messages online?
questions.e: Online communication can also lead to bullying and harassment.

questions.q: Which of these helps to make a website ACCESSIBLE to people with visual impairments?
o: Using only images with no text
Alternative text for images and good colour contrast
questions.e: Other measures: transcripts or captions for audio and video, clear navigation, and adjustable text size. The Equality Act 2010 requires services not to discriminate.

questions.q: Why should designers of an international website think about colour choices?
o: All cultures interpret colours the same
Colours can have different meanings in different cultures
Colours cannot be used on websites
questions.e: E.g. white is associated with purity in some cultures and mourning in others.

questions.q: Why is Unicode recommended for international websites?
o: It can represent the characters of many different languages
It makes files smaller than any other encoding
questions.e: A limited character set such as ASCII cannot display many languages.

questions.q: Describe two ethical issues that arise from the use of automated decision-making (e.g. algorithms to approve loans or shortlist job applicants).

pts.p: The algorithm may be biased / discriminate (e.g. because of biased training data)
It may treat people unfairly or make mistakes with no human to review or challenge
It is difficult to know who is accountable / decisions can be hard to explain (lack of transparency)
It can lead to loss of jobs / de-humanises decisions / uses large amounts of personal data (privacy)

questions.model: One issue is bias: the algorithm may discriminate unfairly if it was trained on biased data, so some groups could be treated less favourably. Another is accountability and transparency: it can be hard to know who is responsible if the system makes a wrong decision, and people may be unable to understand or challenge a decision made without any human review. There are also concerns about privacy because large amounts of personal data are used, and jobs may be lost.

questions.q: Describe three ways in which a website designer could make a website more accessible to users.

pts.p: Alternative text for images (for screen readers)
Good colour contrast / option to change colours or text size
Transcripts / captions / subtitles for audio and video
Simple, consistent layout / easy navigation / clear language
Support for different languages (e.g. Unicode) / avoid culture-specific symbols or colours
Keyboard / voice control as alternatives to a mouse

questions.model: The designer could provide alternative text for images so that screen readers can describe them, use high colour contrast and allow the text size to be changed, and provide captions or transcripts for audio and video content.

questions.q: Describe two ways in which the increased use of digital technology can affect the environment.

pts.p: Data centres and devices use large amounts of electricity (increased energy use / carbon emissions)
Manufacturing devices uses raw materials / rare minerals and causes pollution / habitat damage
E-waste: devices are discarded quickly and can release toxic substances when disposed of (often exported)
Positive effects: reduced travel (remote working), paperless offices, smart systems that save energy

questions.model: Data centres and devices use large amounts of electricity, which increases energy use and carbon emissions unless the power is renewable. Manufacturing devices uses raw materials such as rare minerals and causes pollution. Devices also have a short lifespan, so large amounts of e-waste are created, which can release toxic substances if it is not disposed of or recycled properly. On the positive side, remote working and paperless systems can reduce travel and paper use.

questions.q: A school plans to install software that monitors and filters students' internet use, and analyses browsing data to identify students who may be at risk. Discuss the legal, moral, social and ethical issues the school should consider.

pts.p: Legal: the Data Protection Act 2018 / GDPR - browsing data is personal data, must be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently, kept secure and not kept longer than needed
Legal: students (and parents) should be informed about what is monitored and why / consent
Legal: RIPA / rules on interception of communications and the school's duty to safeguard children
Moral / ethical: monitoring invades students' privacy and may feel like constant surveillance
Moral / ethical: it can protect students from harmful content and identify those who are at risk (safeguarding)
Social: could affect trust between students and staff / stop students asking for help online
Social / ethical: filtering is a form of censorship that may block useful sites / limit freedom of access to information
Ethical: the software may be inaccurate / biased (false alarms or missing real problems)
Data security: the sensitive data collected could be hacked / misused if not kept secure
Balanced judgement: benefits vs privacy; safeguards (limit access to data, human review) to make it acceptable

questions.model: Legally, the browsing data is personal data, so the school must comply with the Data Protection Act 2018: it must process it lawfully, fairly and transparently, keep it secure, and not keep it longer than necessary. Students and parents should be told what is monitored and why, and the school has a legal duty to safeguard children. Morally and ethically, monitoring invades students' privacy and can feel like constant surveillance, but it could protect students from harmful content and identify those at risk of harm, which is a strong argument in its favour. Socially, it could damage trust between students and staff and stop students looking for help online. Filtering is a form of censorship and may block useful sites or limit access to information, and the software may be inaccurate, giving false alarms or missing real problems. The sensitive data could be hacked or misused if it is not kept secure. Overall, the benefits for safeguarding need to be balanced against privacy, and the school should use safeguards such as limiting who can see the data and having a human review any alerts.

questions.q: Discuss the social and environmental impacts of the increasing use of digital technology.

pts.p: Social: communication across the world, easier to keep in touch, share ideas and culture
Social: the digital divide - some people lack access, skills or money for technology
Social: automation / computers in the workplace can improve efficiency but replace jobs
Social: concerns about privacy, cyberbullying, addiction or less face-to-face contact
Environmental: energy use of data centres and devices (carbon emissions)
Environmental: e-waste and the extraction of raw materials
Environmental benefit: remote working / video calls / paperless reduce travel and paper
A reasoned judgement / balance of benefits and drawbacks

questions.model: Socially, digital technology allows people to communicate across the world, share ideas and keep in touch, and it creates new ways of working. However, there is a digital divide between people who have access and skills and those who do not, automation may replace jobs, and there are concerns about privacy, cyberbullying, addiction and less face-to-face contact. Environmentally, data centres and devices use a lot of energy and so contribute to carbon emissions, and manufacturing devices uses raw materials while old devices become e-waste which can be toxic if disposed of badly. On the other hand, remote working, video calls and paperless systems can reduce travel and paper use. Overall, the technology has major benefits, but the drawbacks need to be managed.

h446-02.title: Algorithms and programming
h446-02.notice: Original Paper 2 practice aligned to the supplied OCR specification. Written marking is approximate: review the scheme and credit equivalent answers. Programming tasks have their own Python / pseudocode lab. Paper 2 also builds on Paper 1 knowledge.

2-1-1.title: 2.1.1 Thinking abstractly
2-1-1.blurb: Models, essential detail, simplification and limitations in context.

questions.q: A route planner represents roads as weighted edges. What is being abstracted?
o: Real roads are simplified to connections and costs
The problem is divided among processors
questions.e: The graph retains useful connectivity and cost, omitting irrelevant physical detail.

questions.q: Which detail is most relevant in a model that predicts queue waiting time?
questions.e: Arrival rate affects queue length and waiting time.

questions.q: Why might a journey-time model give an inaccurate prediction?
o: It omits the paint colour of cars
It omits a road closure that changes the real route
questions.e: An abstraction can omit a factor that matters for its intended purpose.

questions.q: Which statement best distinguishes abstraction from decomposition?
o: Abstraction removes unnecessary detail; decomposition splits a problem
Abstraction always splits programs into files
questions.e: The two techniques can be used together, but have different purposes.

questions.q: A school attendance model stores pupil ID and presence. Which addition is most useful for identifying repeated lateness?
questions.e: Relevant details depend on the questions the model must answer.

questions.q: Which is a benefit of abstraction?
o: A simpler model is easier to reason about
questions.e: Reducing unnecessary detail makes a problem more manageable.

questions.q: Describe an abstract model for finding the cheapest rail journey.

pts.p: Stations represented as nodes
Routes represented as edges
Ticket costs used as weights

questions.model: Represent stations as nodes and direct routes as edges. Use ticket costs as edge weights so a minimum-cost path can be found.

questions.q: Explain one limitation of modelling every road with a fixed travel time.

pts.p: Real travel time varies with traffic
The predicted journey may be inaccurate

questions.model: Real travel time varies with traffic during the day. A fixed value can therefore produce an inaccurate predicted journey time.

questions.q: A hospital models its emergency department to predict waiting times. Discuss the details it should retain, what it can omit, and how it should validate the model.

pts.p: Retain patient arrival rates
Retain treatment duration
Retain staff capacity
Omit irrelevant visual detail
Compare with observed waiting times
Revise assumptions when conditions change

questions.model: The model should retain patient arrival rates because busy periods produce longer queues. Treatment duration must be represented because patients occupy staff and rooms for different amounts of time. Staff capacity limits how many people can receive care together. Visual detail such as the colour of chairs can be omitted because it does not affect waiting time. Compare predicted waiting times with observed hospital records to judge whether the simplification is useful. Revise assumptions when staffing or demand changes; the model is a useful estimate rather than an exact copy of reality.

2-1-2.title: 2.1.2 Thinking ahead
2-1-2.blurb: Inputs, outputs, preconditions, caching and reusable components.

questions.q: Which precondition does binary search normally require?
o: The sequence has an odd length
questions.e: Sorted order allows half of the remaining candidates to be discarded.

questions.q: For a function returning mean rainfall, which is a useful precondition?
o: The collection contains at least one numeric measurement
questions.e: An empty collection would cause division by zero in a simple mean calculation.

questions.q: Which is an output of a fare-calculation function?
questions.e: Inputs are received; the result is returned as output.

questions.q: A cache hit means that…
o: The result must always be recomputed
The requested result is already in the cache
questions.e: A stored result can be reused without repeating the expensive operation.

questions.q: What is a risk of caching a product price?
o: A cached price may become stale
Reading a cache always changes the price
questions.e: The underlying price may change after the result was cached.

questions.q: When is caching least likely to help?
o: Many users request the same page
Reading the result is cheaper than recomputing it
Almost every request is unique and never repeated
questions.e: Low reuse may not justify lookup and storage overhead.

questions.q: Explain two benefits of using a tested validation component in several forms.

pts.p: Reuse reduces duplicated code
Existing tests reduce repeated testing work

questions.model: Reuse reduces duplicated code across the forms. Existing tests reduce repeated testing work, although integration into each form should still be checked.

questions.q: Explain a benefit and a drawback of caching search results.

pts.p: Repeated requests can be answered faster
Cached results consume memory
Results can become stale

questions.model: Repeated requests can be answered faster without repeating a search. Cached results consume memory, and the results can become stale if the source changes.

questions.q: A function divides total cost by passenger count. State a suitable input precondition and distinguish it from the output.

pts.p: Passenger count is a positive integer
Output is cost per passenger

questions.model: Passenger count must be a positive integer, preventing division by zero. The output is the calculated cost per passenger, not a condition on the input.

questions.q: Which is a useful decomposition of an online booking system?
o: Check availability, take payment, issue confirmation
questions.e: Each component has a distinct responsibility.

questions.q: A receipt includes a calculated total. Which dependency matters?
o: Print the receipt before reading prices
Send the receipt before payment details exist
Sort item names after shutting down
Calculate the total before producing the receipt
questions.e: A step must have its required data before it can run.

questions.q: Which subroutine design best supports reuse?
o: Include all interface drawing in every calculation
Use a different undocumented input format each time
Accept the needed inputs as parameters and return a documented result
questions.e: A clear interface makes the component easier to use elsewhere.

questions.q: Why split a large program into sub-procedures?
o: Each component can be developed and tested separately
questions.e: Modularity helps testing and maintenance, but does not guarantee runtime speed.

questions.q: Which order is sensible for a file-processing task?
o: Open file, read records, calculate summary, close file
Read records, close file, open file, calculate summary
Close file, read records, open file, calculate summary
Calculate summary, read records, open file, close file
questions.e: Operations must respect resource and data dependencies.

questions.q: Which component should usually handle a changed tax formula?
questions.e: Keeping a responsibility in one module reduces scattered changes.

questions.q: Decompose a system that imports marks and produces student reports into three sub-procedures.

pts.p: Read and validate marks
Calculate grades
Generate reports

questions.model: Read and validate the imported marks. Calculate grades using the grade boundaries. Generate reports containing each student and the calculated grade.

questions.q: Explain why validation should happen before calculating a mean from user input.

pts.p: Reject invalid or nonnumeric input
Avoid calculation errors or misleading results

questions.model: Validation can reject invalid or nonnumeric input before arithmetic begins. This avoids calculation errors and misleading results from unsuitable data.

questions.q: Explain how decomposition helps a team develop a program.

pts.p: Allocate separate components to team members
Test individual components
Agree interfaces for integration

questions.model: Allocate separate components to team members so work can proceed independently. Test individual components in isolation. Agree interfaces in advance so the components can be integrated correctly.

2-1-4.title: 2.1.4 Thinking logically
2-1-4.blurb: Boolean conditions, decisions, boundaries and program flow.

questions.q: Entry requires age >= 16 AND a valid ticket. Which person is admitted?
questions.e: Both conditions must be true; 16 is included by >=.

questions.q: Which condition accepts x in the inclusive range 1 to 10?
questions.e: AND requires both bounds to hold, including the endpoints.

questions.q: Which condition detects a value outside the inclusive range 1 to 10?
questions.e: Either an underflow or an overflow makes the value invalid.

questions.q: What is NOT (p AND q) equivalent to?
questions.e: De Morgan’s law negates each operand and changes AND to OR.

questions.q: An if / elseif / else chain executes how many branches for one evaluation?
questions.e: With an else present, the first true branch is selected or else runs.

questions.q: A loop continues while attempts < 3 AND NOT success. When does it stop?
o: Only when both conditions become false
