When attempts reaches 3 or success is true
questions.e: Negating the continuation condition gives attempts >= 3 OR success.

questions.q: Explain why x >= 0 OR x <= 100 is unsuitable for validating a percentage.

pts.p: Every numeric value satisfies at least one side
Use AND to enforce both limits

questions.model: Every numeric value satisfies at least one side, so invalid percentages are accepted. Use AND so the lower and upper limits must both hold.

questions.q: A discount applies at age 18 or below. Give two boundary tests and their expected outcomes.

pts.p: Age 18 receives discount
Age 19 does not receive discount

questions.model: Age 18 receives the discount because the endpoint is included. Age 19 does not receive the discount because it is immediately above the boundary.

questions.q: Explain the difference between two independent if statements and an if / else selection.

pts.p: Independent conditions can both execute
If / else chooses one alternative

questions.model: Two independent if conditions can both be true and both execute. An if / else selection chooses one alternative, so only one of its branches executes.

2-1-5.title: 2.1.5 Thinking concurrently
2-1-5.blurb: Independent work, dependencies, shared state and trade-offs.

questions.q: Which tasks are most suitable for concurrent processing?
o: Reading a total before calculating it
Using a password before it is entered
Printing a result before receiving its inputs
questions.e: Independent tasks have fewer coordination dependencies.

questions.q: Does concurrency necessarily mean instructions run at exactly the same instant?
o: Yes; it always requires two processors
Yes; each task requires its own computer
No; only one task may ever make progress
No; tasks may be interleaved on one core
questions.e: Concurrency allows overlapping progress; parallelism involves simultaneous execution.

questions.q: What can cause a race condition?
o: A loop has a base case
Unsynchronised tasks update the same shared value
questions.e: The result may depend on the timing of overlapping reads and writes.

questions.q: Which can reduce a race condition on a shared counter?
o: Protect the update using suitable synchronisation
Give the counter a shorter name
questions.e: A lock or another suitable atomic coordination mechanism protects the update.

questions.q: Why may concurrent execution be slower for very small tasks?
o: Scheduling and communication overhead can outweigh saved time
questions.e: Parallel or concurrent organisation has costs as well as benefits.

questions.q: Two tasks each read counter=4, then each writes 5. What happened?
questions.e: Both tasks read the same old value, so one update overwrote the other.

questions.q: Give a benefit and a drawback of downloading independent files concurrently.

pts.p: Downloads can overlap and reduce elapsed time
They share bandwidth and coordination resources

questions.model: Downloads can overlap and reduce total elapsed time. They share limited bandwidth and require coordination, so extra downloads do not guarantee proportionate speed gains.

questions.q: Explain why report printing cannot always run before report calculation finishes.

pts.p: Printing depends on calculated data
Synchronisation is needed before consuming results

questions.model: Printing depends on the calculated data, so it may use incomplete values. Synchronisation is needed before printing consumes the finished results.

questions.q: A game runs input handling, world updates and saving concurrently. Discuss the benefits and the problems the programmer must handle.

pts.p: Input remains responsive
Independent tasks can overlap
Shared game state creates race risks
Synchronise saving with state changes
Coordination adds overhead
Dependent tasks limit speed-up

questions.model: Input handling can remain responsive while another task saves the game. Independent tasks can overlap, and multiple cores may allow parallel execution. However, shared game state creates a risk that saving reads some old and some new values. Synchronise access or save a consistent snapshot to avoid a corrupt save. Coordination adds overhead and can introduce delays, so very small tasks may gain little. Dependent tasks still need results from earlier steps; adding more workers cannot remove those dependencies. The design should therefore separate independent work and protect shared state carefully.

2-2-1.title: 2.2.1 Programming techniques
2-2-1.blurb: Constructs, recursion, scope, parameters, IDE tools and object-oriented programming.

questions.q: Which construct repeats a block until a condition changes?
questions.e: Iteration repeats operations; sequence performs them in order.

questions.q: What is essential to a terminating recursive solution?
o: A different name for each call
A reachable base case and progress towards it
questions.e: Calls must eventually reach a case that does not recurse.

questions.q: Compared with a simple iterative loop, deep recursion can require extra space for…
questions.e: Each active call retains parameters, local state and a return location.

questions.q: A local variable is normally accessible…
o: From every program on the machine
questions.e: Local scope limits where the identifier can be used.

questions.q: Under pass-by-value semantics, reassigning a scalar parameter normally…
o: Does not reassign the caller’s variable
questions.e: The subroutine receives a copy of the value, not the caller’s variable itself.

questions.q: Under pass-by-reference semantics, assigning through the parameter can…
questions.e: The parameter refers to the caller’s storage. Language-specific details matter.

questions.q: Which IDE tool pauses execution at a chosen line?
questions.e: A breakpoint pauses execution so state can be inspected.

questions.q: What is inheritance?
o: A subclass derives attributes or behaviour from a superclass
Every object shares the same values
questions.e: Inheritance allows a class to extend or specialise another class.

questions.q: What is encapsulation?
o: Bundling state and operations with controlled access
Copying every object into a database
questions.e: Controlled access helps maintain the object’s invariants.

questions.q: What does a constructor typically do?
questions.e: The constructor establishes the new instance’s initial attributes.

questions.q: A subclass supplies a different implementation of an inherited method. This is…
questions.e: Overriding supports specialised behaviour through a common interface.

questions.q: In Python, a function receives a list and appends an item to it. What can the caller observe?
o: Python always copies the entire list
questions.e: Python passes object references by assignment: mutation can be visible, but rebinding a parameter is different.

questions.q: Describe how breakpoints and a variable watch can help find a faulty loop.

pts.p: Pause execution near the loop
Inspect changing variable values
Step through iterations to locate the error

questions.model: Pause execution at a breakpoint near the loop. Inspect the changing variable values in a watch window. Step through iterations to locate the incorrect update or condition.

questions.q: Explain why a recursive factorial function needs a base case.

pts.p: Stop recursive calls at a defined input
Return a value to start unwinding
Without it calls may continue until stack exhaustion

questions.model: A base case stops recursive calls at a defined input such as zero. It returns a value so pending calls can unwind. Without it the call stack may be exhausted.

questions.q: Distinguish a class from an object, using a library book example.

pts.p: Class defines attributes and methods
Object is an instance
Each book object has its own state

questions.model: A Book class defines attributes and methods for books. A particular book object is an instance of that class. Each book object can hold its own title and loan state.

questions.q: Explain how a validated setter supports encapsulation.

pts.p: Controls access to an attribute
Checks proposed values
Preserves valid object state

questions.model: A setter controls access to an attribute. It checks proposed values before accepting changes. This preserves valid object state, such as a capacity that cannot become negative.

questions.q: Compare recursion and iteration for processing a tree. Consider clarity, termination and memory.

pts.p: Recursion matches recursive tree structure
Base case handles an empty subtree
Recursive calls move to smaller subtrees
Active calls consume stack space
Iteration may use an explicit stack
Choice depends on depth and clarity

questions.model: Recursion closely matches the structure of a tree because each subtree can be processed by the same procedure. A base case handles an empty subtree, and recursive calls move towards smaller subtrees so the traversal terminates. Active calls consume stack space, which may become a problem for a very deep tree. Iteration can replace the call stack with an explicit stack of nodes, making storage more directly controlled without necessarily eliminating it. The best choice depends on expected depth and implementation clarity. A shallow balanced tree may be easy to express recursively, while a deep skewed tree may favour an iterative traversal.

2-2-2.title: 2.2.2 Computational methods
2-2-2.blurb: Recognition, decomposition, divide and conquer, backtracking, heuristics, modelling and visualisation.

questions.q: Which problem is most directly computable?
o: Calculate a fare from explicit distance and tariff rules
Decide an undefined idea of beauty with no criteria
Solve a task with no inputs or rules specified
questions.e: Well-defined inputs, rules and outputs support an algorithmic solution.

questions.q: Divide and conquer typically involves…
o: Putting every operation into one statement
Splitting into smaller subproblems, solving them, then combining results
questions.e: Merge sort is a standard example.

questions.q: What is backtracking?
o: Running a program backwards at machine-code level
Undoing a choice and trying another when a path fails
questions.e: Backtracking explores alternatives after rejecting an unsuitable partial solution.

questions.q: What is a heuristic?
o: A complete list of every possible input
A practical estimate or rule that guides a search
A guarantee of optimality in every problem
questions.e: Heuristics can reduce search effort, but their guarantees depend on the method and assumptions.

questions.q: What is data mining used for?
o: Discovering useful patterns in large datasets
Replacing all data with random values
questions.e: Patterns can support decisions, but correlation alone does not establish causation.

questions.q: What is performance modelling used to estimate?
o: The exact future regardless of assumptions
How a system behaves under different loads
questions.e: A model can estimate bottlenecks, throughput and response times before deployment.

questions.q: In a processing pipeline, different stages can…
o: Guarantee lower latency for a single item
Work on different items at the same time
questions.e: Pipelining can improve throughput by overlapping stages.

questions.q: Why visualise a large dataset?
o: Patterns and outliers may become easier to identify
questions.e: Visual presentation can reveal relationships, but must be interpreted critically.

questions.q: Explain how backtracking can solve a maze.

pts.p: Choose and explore a route
Detect dead ends
Return to a previous choice and try an alternative

questions.model: Choose and explore a route through the maze. Detect a dead end when no unvisited continuation remains. Return to a previous choice and try an alternative route.

questions.q: Explain how merge sort illustrates divide and conquer.

pts.p: Divide the list into halves
Recursively sort the smaller lists
Merge sorted results

questions.model: Divide the list into halves until small base cases are reached. Recursively sort the smaller lists. Merge the sorted results to produce the final ordered list.

questions.q: A company mines sales records. Explain why an observed association requires careful interpretation.

pts.p: Correlation does not prove causation
Data may contain bias or missing context
Validate findings against other evidence

questions.model: Correlation does not prove causation. The records may contain bias or omit relevant context. Validate the findings against other evidence before changing business decisions.

questions.q: A three-stage pipeline takes 2 ms, 5 ms and 3 ms per stage with one worker per stage. Ignore transfer costs. Give latency for one item and steady-state output interval.

pts.p: One item takes 10 ms
Slowest stage limits output to one item every 5 ms

questions.model: One item takes 10 ms to pass through all three stages. Once filled, the slowest stage limits output to one item every 5 ms.

questions.q: A delivery company uses a heuristic to plan routes. Discuss why it might prefer this to evaluating every possible route.

pts.p: Number of routes grows rapidly
Exhaustive search may take too long
Heuristic guides selection
May sacrifice optimality
Compare results against known cases
Consider deadline and route quality trade-off

questions.model: The number of possible routes grows rapidly as more destinations are added, so exhaustive search may take too long for practical dispatch decisions. A heuristic guides selection towards promising routes and can produce a useful answer quickly. It may sacrifice optimality, however, so a faster answer can still use more fuel than the best route. Compare its results against known cases where the best route can be calculated, and check performance under realistic loads. The decision should consider the deadline for dispatch as well as route quality. A timely good route may be more useful than a perfect route produced after the vehicles should have left.

2-3-1.title: 2.3.1 Algorithm analysis and Big O
2-3-1.blurb: Time and space, cases, growth rates and algorithm suitability.

questions.q: What does Big O normally describe?
o: An asymptotic upper bound on growth
The exact running time in seconds
questions.e: Big O expresses how a resource requirement grows with input size.

questions.q: Indexing an array by a known position is normally…
questions.e: The number of access operations does not grow with array length.

questions.q: A loop visits n items once with constant work per item. Its time complexity is…
questions.e: The amount of work grows linearly with n.

questions.q: Two nested loops each run n times. The inner body is constant time. Complexity is…
questions.e: The body runs n × n times.

questions.q: A search halves the remaining range at each step. Its worst-case comparisons are…
questions.e: Repeated halving requires logarithmically many steps.

questions.q: Which grows fastest for sufficiently large n?
questions.e: Exponential growth eventually exceeds these polynomial and logarithmic functions.

questions.q: If n doubles, an n² operation count changes by approximately…
questions.e: (2n)² = 4n².

questions.q: An algorithm keeps a new array of length n. Its auxiliary space is…
questions.e: The extra storage scales with the input size.

questions.q: Why can an O(n²) algorithm beat an O(n log n) algorithm on a tiny input?
o: Constants and overhead matter for small inputs
Quadratic growth is always slower at every size
The faster algorithm must be incorrect
questions.e: Asymptotic growth does not specify absolute times for every input.

questions.q: Which statement about linear search is correct?
o: Best and worst cases are always O(log n)
Best case O(1), worst case O(n)
questions.e: The first item may match; an absent or last item may require checking all n items.

questions.q: Explain why a benchmark on one machine is not the same as a Big O analysis.

pts.p: Benchmark measures actual time for particular conditions
Hardware and implementation affect measured time
Big O describes growth with input size

questions.model: A benchmark measures actual time under particular conditions. Hardware and implementation affect the measured time. Big O instead describes how work grows as the input size increases.

questions.q: Explain a time-space trade-off using a lookup table.

pts.p: Precompute and store results
Use extra memory
Avoid repeated calculation to save time

questions.model: Precompute and store results in a lookup table. This uses extra memory, but avoids repeated calculation so later lookups can save time.

questions.q: An algorithm does n operations followed by n squared operations. Give and justify its Big O complexity.

pts.p: O(n²)
Quadratic term dominates for large n

questions.model: The complexity is O(n²). The quadratic term dominates the linear term as n becomes large, so lower-order growth is omitted.

2-3-1-structures.title: 2.3.1 Data structures and traversals
2-3-1-structures.blurb: Stacks, queues, linked lists, binary search trees and tree traversals.

questions.q: A stack uses which removal order?
questions.e: The most recently pushed item is popped first.

questions.q: Push A, push B, pop, push C, pop on an empty stack. Which values are popped?
questions.e: B is on top at the first pop, then C at the second.

questions.q: Enqueue A, enqueue B, dequeue, enqueue C, dequeue. What is the second dequeued value?
questions.e: A leaves first; B remains ahead of C.

questions.q: In a circular queue of capacity 5, how is index 4 advanced?
questions.e: Modulo wraps the next position back to index zero.

questions.q: What does a linked-list head pointer identify?
o: The first node in the logical list
questions.e: Logical order follows links, not necessarily physical array order.

questions.q: What does a null next pointer usually indicate?
questions.e: For an ordinary singly linked list, null marks the end of the chain.

questions.q: A BST contains unique keys. Where is a key smaller than the root searched next?
questions.e: The BST ordering property eliminates the opposite subtree.

questions.q: Insert 40, 20, 60, 30 into an initially empty BST. Where is 30?
questions.e: 30 is less than 40 and greater than 20.

questions.q: For root A, left child B and right child C, what is left-to-right post-order?
questions.e: Post-order visits left subtree, right subtree, then the root.

questions.q: Which data structure naturally supports breadth-first tree traversal?
questions.e: FIFO processing visits the earliest discovered level first.

questions.q: Why can a BST search degrade to O(n)?
o: The tree may become a chain
All balanced trees require linear search
questions.e: Without balancing, sorted insertion can produce linear height.

questions.q: In-order traversal of a BST with unique keys produces…
questions.e: Left, root, right follows the BST ordering property.

questions.q: Describe insertion at the head of a singly linked list.

pts.p: Create or allocate a node
Set new node’s next pointer to old head
Set head to the new node

questions.model: Create or allocate a node containing the new data. Set the new node’s next pointer to the old head. Set head to the new node, preserving the rest of the chain.

questions.q: Explain how to detect queue underflow and why the check is necessary.

pts.p: Check whether the queue is empty
Reject dequeue when no item exists

questions.model: Check whether the queue is empty before dequeuing. Reject the operation when no item exists, preventing an invalid read and an incorrect pointer update.

questions.q: A tree has root 8, children 3 and 10; node 3 has children 1 and 6. Give breadth-first and left-to-right post-order traversals.

pts.p: Breadth-first: 8, 3, 10, 1, 6
Post-order: 1, 6, 3, 10, 8

questions.model: Breadth-first is 8, 3, 10, 1, 6 because nodes are visited level by level. Post-order is 1, 6, 3, 10, 8 because each subtree is processed before its root.

questions.q: Compare an array and a linked list for a collection with frequent insertions and position-based reads.

pts.p: Arrays support direct indexing
Linked lists require traversal for indexed reads
Array insertion may shift many items
Linked insertion can update pointers after locating position
Links require extra storage
Choice depends on access and insertion pattern

questions.model: An array supports direct indexing, making position-based reads efficient. A linked list normally requires traversal from the head to reach a numbered position, which can take linear time. Inserting into the middle of an array may shift many items, while a linked insertion can update a small number of pointers after the insertion position is found. Finding that position can still require traversal, so linked insertion is not always constant time overall. Links also require extra storage. The choice depends on the access and insertion pattern: frequent indexed reads favour arrays, while insertions at already-known nodes may favour linked lists.

2-3-1-sorting.title: 2.3.1 Searching and sorting
2-3-1-sorting.blurb: Linear and binary search; bubble, insertion, merge and quick sort.

questions.q: Which search works directly on an unsorted list?
questions.e: Linear search checks items without relying on sorted order.

questions.q: Binary search examines a middle value smaller than the target in ascending data. What happens next?
questions.e: All values at or below that middle position can be discarded.

questions.q: One left-to-right ascending bubble pass over [5, 1, 4, 2] gives…
questions.e: Adjacent swaps move the maximum to the right-hand end during this pass.

questions.q: Insertion sort maintains…
o: A sorted prefix into which the next item is inserted
Two fully sorted equal halves at all times
A random pivot on every comparison
questions.e: Each step extends the sorted part by one item.

questions.q: Which input often suits insertion sort particularly well?
o: Only a graph with negative weights
Only a linked list with cycles
questions.e: Few shifts are needed when items are already close to their correct positions.

questions.q: Standard merge sort has worst-case time complexity…
questions.e: There are logarithmically many levels with linear merging work per level.

questions.q: Why can basic quick sort take O(n²) time?
o: It always allocates n squared arrays
Repeated pivots split into extremely unbalanced partitions
It always performs a breadth-first traversal
questions.e: Repeated splits of sizes zero and n−1 produce quadratic work.

questions.q: A stable sort preserves…
o: Original relative order of equal-key items
The original order of every item
questions.e: Stability matters when records have equal sort keys.

questions.q: An optimised bubble sort records whether any swap occurred. Why?
o: A pass with no swaps permits early termination
A swap means the whole list is sorted
It makes worst-case time O(log n)
questions.e: No swaps in a full pass shows that adjacent pairs are ordered.

questions.q: Binary search uses low=0 and high=7. With mid=(low+high) DIV 2, mid is…
questions.e: Integer division rounds 7/2 down to 3.

questions.q: Explain why binary search cannot safely discard half of an unsorted array.

pts.p: Middle value does not establish where target lies
Discarded half could contain the target

questions.model: The middle value does not establish where the target lies in an unsorted array. The discarded half could contain the target, causing an incorrect not-found result.

questions.q: Merge [2, 7, 9] and [1, 7, 8] into ascending order. Explain how equal values are handled in a stable merge.

pts.p: Merged list is 1, 2, 7, 7, 8, 9
Choose equal key from left input first

questions.model: The merged list is 1, 2, 7, 7, 8, 9. Choose an equal key from the left input first to preserve the original relative order.

questions.q: Explain a drawback of sorting a list solely to perform one search.

pts.p: Sorting has a preprocessing cost
One linear search may cost less overall

questions.model: Sorting has a preprocessing cost before the search can begin. For one query, a linear search may cost less overall than sorting the entire list and then performing binary search.

questions.q: A system repeatedly searches a mostly unchanged list of one million IDs. Compare repeated linear search with sorting once and using binary search.

pts.p: Linear search can inspect every ID
Binary search requires sorted data
Sorting adds an initial cost
Each binary search halves the range
Repeated queries amortise sorting cost
Updates may require maintaining order

questions.model: Linear search can inspect every ID on each unsuccessful lookup, so repeated queries on one million IDs can be costly. Binary search requires sorted data, adding an initial sorting cost. Once ordered, each comparison halves the remaining range, giving logarithmic search growth rather than linear growth. Repeated queries can amortise the one-off sorting cost, especially because this list changes infrequently. Updates may still require maintaining order or rebuilding the sorted version, which adds work. For this workload, sorting once and using binary search is likely suitable, but the total decision should include the number of queries and the cost of future changes.

2-3-1-paths.title: 2.3.1 Dijkstra and A*
2-3-1-paths.blurb: Weighted graphs, tentative distances, relaxation, heuristics and path reconstruction.

questions.q: Dijkstra’s standard shortest-path algorithm assumes…
o: Every edge has a negative weight
The graph is a binary search tree
questions.e: Negative edges can invalidate the usual settled-node argument.

questions.q: At the start of Dijkstra’s algorithm, the source distance is…
questions.e: The distance from the source to itself is zero; other distances begin at infinity.

questions.q: Which unsettled node does Dijkstra’s algorithm select next?
o: The one with the largest edge
An arbitrary leaf of a tree
The one with the smallest tentative distance
The one with the largest label
questions.e: With nonnegative weights, the smallest tentative distance can be settled.

questions.q: A settled node has distance 6 and an outgoing edge has weight 4. The neighbour’s old distance is 13. Its new distance is…
questions.e: Relaxation compares 13 with 6 + 4 and keeps 10.

questions.q: In A*, f(n) is usually calculated as…
questions.e: g is known path cost so far; h estimates remaining cost.

questions.q: What does an admissible heuristic do?
o: Never overestimates the true remaining minimum cost
questions.e: Admissibility supports optimality under the appropriate A* search conditions.

questions.q: If h(n)=0 everywhere, A* behaves like…
questions.e: Only known path cost g determines priority.

questions.q: Why store predecessor information in shortest-path search?
o: To turn the graph into a stack
To reconstruct the route after finding distances
To change every edge to zero
questions.e: Follow predecessors from destination to source, then reverse the sequence.

questions.q: A* has g=8 and h=5 for node X, and g=10 and h=2 for node Y. Which has lower f?
questions.e: X has f=13; Y has f=12, so Y has the lower priority value.

questions.q: In graph-search A* that never reopens closed nodes, which heuristic condition supports optimality?
o: Using negative g values for every node
Consistency, along with the usual nonnegative-cost assumptions
questions.e: A consistent heuristic obeys h(u) ≤ cost(u,v) + h(v), avoiding the need to reopen settled nodes.

questions.q: Explain the difference between g and h in A*.

pts.p: g is actual cost of the current path from the start
h estimates remaining cost to the goal

questions.model: The value g is the actual cost of the current path from the start. The value h estimates the remaining cost from that node to the goal.

questions.q: An undirected graph has edges A–B=4, A–C=1, C–B=2, B–D=1, C–D=5. Give the shortest A-to-D path and cost.

pts.p: Path is A, C, B, D
Total cost is 4

questions.model: The shortest path is A, C, B, D. Its total cost is 1 + 2 + 1 = 4, lower than A, B, D at cost 5.

questions.q: Explain why straight-line distance can be useful as a heuristic for road distance.

pts.p: Estimates the remaining distance to the destination
Cannot exceed the actual road distance under the same distance units
Can guide exploration towards promising routes

questions.model: Straight-line distance estimates the remaining distance to the destination. Under the same distance units it cannot exceed the actual road distance. It can guide exploration towards promising routes; it is not automatically valid for a travel-time cost.

questions.q: Compare Dijkstra and A* for finding a route to one destination. Consider correctness and the quality of the heuristic.

pts.p: Both track path costs
Dijkstra uses cost so far
A* adds estimated remaining cost
Good heuristic can reduce explored nodes
Poor overestimating heuristic can lose optimality
Zero heuristic gives Dijkstra-like ordering

questions.model: Both algorithms track path costs and improve tentative routes through relaxation. Dijkstra prioritises cost so far, without guidance towards one destination. A* adds an estimated remaining cost, which can reduce the number of explored nodes when the heuristic is informative. Correctness depends on the assumptions: Dijkstra normally requires nonnegative edges, while A* also needs an appropriate heuristic and handling of repeated states. An overestimating heuristic can lose optimality. A zero heuristic gives Dijkstra-like ordering and removes the directional benefit. For one destination with a useful consistent distance estimate, A* can be attractive; without such an estimate, Dijkstra provides a straightforward alternative.

parts.work: Stopping distance: initial kinetic energy ÷ 65 = 6.78 m.

pts.p: Initial kinetic energy: ½ × 18 × 7² = 441 J.
Stopping distance: initial kinetic energy ÷ 65 = 6.78 m.

questions.model: Initial kinetic energy: ½ × 18 × 7² = 441 J. Stopping distance: initial kinetic energy ÷ 65 = 6.78 m.

questions.q: A 35 kg cart travelling at 12 m/s stops on a level track due to constant resistance 140 N. Find the initial kinetic energy and stopping distance using energy. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: Stopping distance
parts.work: Stopping distance: initial kinetic energy ÷ 140 = 18 m.

pts.p: Initial kinetic energy: ½ × 35 × 12² = 2.52e+03 J.
Stopping distance: initial kinetic energy ÷ 140 = 18 m.

questions.model: Initial kinetic energy: ½ × 35 × 12² = 2.52e+03 J. Stopping distance: initial kinetic energy ÷ 140 = 18 m.

questions.q: A 58 kg cart travelling at 9.5 m/s stops on a level track due to constant resistance 180 N. Find the initial kinetic energy and stopping distance using energy. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: Stopping distance
parts.work: Stopping distance: initial kinetic energy ÷ 180 = 14.5 m.

pts.p: Initial kinetic energy: ½ × 58 × 9.5² = 2.62e+03 J.
Stopping distance: initial kinetic energy ÷ 180 = 14.5 m.

questions.model: Initial kinetic energy: ½ × 58 × 9.5² = 2.62e+03 J. Stopping distance: initial kinetic energy ÷ 180 = 14.5 m.

questions.q: Where does mechanical energy go when a brake stops a wheel?
o: It all becomes gravitational potential energy
It remains entirely as kinetic energy
Mostly to thermal energy in the brake and surroundings
questions.e: Friction converts mechanical energy primarily to thermal energy.

questions.q: Explain how to include constant friction in an energy balance for a cart moving downhill.

pts.p: Calculate the gravitational potential energy lost from weight times vertical drop.
Subtract work against friction, given by friction force times distance along the path.
The balance is the gain in kinetic energy if there are no other transfers.

questions.model: Calculate the gravitational potential energy lost from weight times vertical drop. Subtract work against friction, given by friction force times distance along the path. The balance is the gain in kinetic energy if there are no other transfers.

questions.q: Two carts of masses 5 kg and 4 kg have signed velocities 6 m/s and -3 m/s. They stick together. Find the total initial momentum and signed common velocity. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Total momentum: 5 × 6 + 4 × (-3) = 18 kg m/s.
Common velocity: total momentum ÷ (5 + 4) = 2 m/s.

questions.model: Total momentum: 5 × 6 + 4 × (-3) = 18 kg m/s. Common velocity: total momentum ÷ (5 + 4) = 2 m/s.

questions.q: Two carts of masses 8 kg and 3 kg have signed velocities 7 m/s and -4 m/s. They stick together. Find the total initial momentum and signed common velocity. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Total momentum: 8 × 7 + 3 × (-4) = 44 kg m/s.
Common velocity: total momentum ÷ (8 + 3) = 4 m/s.

questions.model: Total momentum: 8 × 7 + 3 × (-4) = 44 kg m/s. Common velocity: total momentum ÷ (8 + 3) = 4 m/s.

questions.q: Two carts of masses 6 kg and 9 kg have signed velocities 3 m/s and -4 m/s. They stick together. Find the total initial momentum and signed common velocity. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Total momentum: 6 × 3 + 9 × (-4) = -18 kg m/s.
Common velocity: total momentum ÷ (6 + 9) = -1.2 m/s.

questions.model: Total momentum: 6 × 3 + 9 × (-4) = -18 kg m/s. Common velocity: total momentum ÷ (6 + 9) = -1.2 m/s.

questions.q: A 3 kg cart moving at 6 m/s collides elastically head-on with a stationary 5 kg cart. Positive is the initial direction. Using momentum conservation and equal relative speeds before and after, find both final velocities. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Second cart: 2 × 3 × 6 ÷ (3 + 5) = 4.5 m/s.

questions.q: A 2 kg cart moving at 9 m/s collides elastically head-on with a stationary 4 kg cart. Positive is the initial direction. Using momentum conservation and equal relative speeds before and after, find both final velocities. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Second cart: 2 × 2 × 9 ÷ (2 + 4) = 6 m/s.

questions.q: A 8 kg cart moving at 5 m/s collides elastically head-on with a stationary 3 kg cart. Positive is the initial direction. Using momentum conservation and equal relative speeds before and after, find both final velocities. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

A 4 kg cart moving at 8 m/s strikes a stationary 6 kg cart in one dimension. The first cart continues at 2 m/s. Find the signed velocity of the second cart and the kinetic energy lost. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: Energy lost
parts.work: Energy lost: ½ × 4 × 8² − ½ × 4 × 2² − ½ × 6 × (second cart velocity)² = 72 J.

pts.p: Second cart velocity: 4 × (8 − 2) ÷ 6 = 4 m/s.
Energy lost: ½ × 4 × 8² − ½ × 4 × 2² − ½ × 6 × (second cart velocity)² = 72 J.

questions.model: Second cart velocity: 4 × (8 − 2) ÷ 6 = 4 m/s. Energy lost: ½ × 4 × 8² − ½ × 4 × 2² − ½ × 6 × (second cart velocity)² = 72 J.

questions.q: A 6 kg cart moving at 12 m/s strikes a stationary 9 kg cart in one dimension. The first cart continues at 4 m/s. Find the signed velocity of the second cart and the kinetic energy lost. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: Energy lost
parts.work: Energy lost: ½ × 6 × 12² − ½ × 6 × 4² − ½ × 9 × (second cart velocity)² = 256 J.

pts.p: Second cart velocity: 6 × (12 − 4) ÷ 9 = 5.33 m/s.
Energy lost: ½ × 6 × 12² − ½ × 6 × 4² − ½ × 9 × (second cart velocity)² = 256 J.

questions.model: Second cart velocity: 6 × (12 − 4) ÷ 9 = 5.33 m/s. Energy lost: ½ × 6 × 12² − ½ × 6 × 4² − ½ × 9 × (second cart velocity)² = 256 J.

questions.q: A 8 kg cart moving at 6 m/s strikes a stationary 12 kg cart in one dimension. The first cart continues at 3 m/s. Find the signed velocity of the second cart and the kinetic energy lost. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: Energy lost
parts.work: Energy lost: ½ × 8 × 6² − ½ × 8 × 3² − ½ × 12 × (second cart velocity)² = 84 J.

pts.p: Second cart velocity: 8 × (6 − 3) ÷ 12 = 2 m/s.
Energy lost: ½ × 8 × 6² − ½ × 8 × 3² − ½ × 12 × (second cart velocity)² = 84 J.

questions.model: Second cart velocity: 8 × (6 − 3) ÷ 12 = 2 m/s. Energy lost: ½ × 8 × 6² − ½ × 8 × 3² − ½ × 12 × (second cart velocity)² = 84 J.

questions.q: Which quantity is conserved in both elastic and perfectly inelastic collisions in an isolated system?
questions.e: Only an elastic collision also conserves kinetic energy.

questions.q: Explain how to classify an isolated collision using velocities and kinetic energies before and afterwards.

pts.p: Total momentum must be conserved across the collision.
Equal total kinetic energy identifies an elastic collision.
Identical final velocity because the objects stick identifies a perfectly inelastic collision.

questions.model: Total momentum must be conserved across the collision. Equal total kinetic energy identifies an elastic collision. Identical final velocity because the objects stick identifies a perfectly inelastic collision.

3.1.1.title: 3.1.1 · DC quantities, resistance and circuits
3.1.1.blurb: Practise dC quantities, resistance and circuits.

questions.q: A DC load takes 0.85 A for 42 s from a 12 V supply. Find the charge transferred, the power and the energy transferred. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.
A DC load takes 2.4 A for 15 s from a 9 V supply. Find the charge transferred, the power and the energy transferred. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.
A DC load takes 0.35 A for 80 s from a 24 V supply. Find the charge transferred, the power and the energy transferred. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.
A wire has resistance 0.65 Ω, length 22 m and diameter 0.85 mm. Find its cross-sectional area in m² and the material resistivity. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Resistivity: 0.65 × cross-sectional area ÷ 22 = 1.68e-08 Ω m.

questions.model: Area: π × (0.85 ÷ 2000)² = 5.67e-07 m². Resistivity: 0.65 × cross-sectional area ÷ 22 = 1.68e-08 Ω m.

questions.q: A wire has resistance 1.3 Ω, length 35 m and diameter 0.74 mm. Find its cross-sectional area in m² and the material resistivity. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Resistivity: 1.3 × cross-sectional area ÷ 35 = 1.6e-08 Ω m.

questions.model: Area: π × (0.74 ÷ 2000)² = 4.3e-07 m². Resistivity: 1.3 × cross-sectional area ÷ 35 = 1.6e-08 Ω m.

questions.q: A wire has resistance 0.42 Ω, length 18 m and diameter 1.2 mm. Find its cross-sectional area in m² and the material resistivity. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Resistivity: 0.42 × cross-sectional area ÷ 18 = 2.64e-08 Ω m.

questions.model: Area: π × (1.2 ÷ 2000)² = 1.13e-06 m². Resistivity: 0.42 × cross-sectional area ÷ 18 = 2.64e-08 Ω m.

questions.q: A 12 Ω resistor is in series with a parallel pair of 30 Ω and 20 Ω across 18 V DC. Find equivalent resistance, total current and current in the 20 Ω branch. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Equivalent resistance: 12 + 1 ÷ (1/30 + 1/20) = 24 Ω.
Total current: 18 ÷ equivalent resistance = 0.75 A.
Branch current: total current × 30 ÷ (30 + 20) = 0.45 A.

questions.model: Equivalent resistance: 12 + 1 ÷ (1/30 + 1/20) = 24 Ω. Total current: 18 ÷ equivalent resistance = 0.75 A. Branch current: total current × 30 ÷ (30 + 20) = 0.45 A.

questions.q: A 8 Ω resistor is in series with a parallel pair of 15 Ω and 30 Ω across 12 V DC. Find equivalent resistance, total current and current in the 30 Ω branch. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Equivalent resistance: 8 + 1 ÷ (1/15 + 1/30) = 18 Ω.
Total current: 12 ÷ equivalent resistance = 0.667 A.
Branch current: total current × 15 ÷ (15 + 30) = 0.222 A.

questions.model: Equivalent resistance: 8 + 1 ÷ (1/15 + 1/30) = 18 Ω. Total current: 12 ÷ equivalent resistance = 0.667 A. Branch current: total current × 15 ÷ (15 + 30) = 0.222 A.

questions.q: A 33 Ω resistor is in series with a parallel pair of 22 Ω and 44 Ω across 24 V DC. Find equivalent resistance, total current and current in the 44 Ω branch. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Equivalent resistance: 33 + 1 ÷ (1/22 + 1/44) = 47.7 Ω.
Total current: 24 ÷ equivalent resistance = 0.503 A.
Branch current: total current × 22 ÷ (22 + 44) = 0.168 A.

questions.model: Equivalent resistance: 33 + 1 ÷ (1/22 + 1/44) = 47.7 Ω. Total current: 24 ÷ equivalent resistance = 0.503 A. Branch current: total current × 22 ÷ (22 + 44) = 0.168 A.

questions.q: Three resistors 10 Ω, 20 Ω and 30 Ω are connected in parallel across 12 V DC. Calculate total current and power dissipated by the 20 Ω resistor. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Power in branch: 12² ÷ 20 = 7.2 W.

questions.model: Total current: 12/10 + 12/20 + 12/30 = 2.2 A. Power in branch: 12² ÷ 20 = 7.2 W.

questions.q: Three resistors 12 Ω, 18 Ω and 36 Ω are connected in parallel across 9 V DC. Calculate total current and power dissipated by the 18 Ω resistor. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Power in branch: 9² ÷ 18 = 4.5 W.

questions.model: Total current: 9/12 + 9/18 + 9/36 = 1.5 A. Power in branch: 9² ÷ 18 = 4.5 W.

questions.q: Three resistors 8 Ω, 24 Ω and 48 Ω are connected in parallel across 16 V DC. Calculate total current and power dissipated by the 24 Ω resistor. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Power in branch: 16² ÷ 24 = 10.7 W.

questions.model: Total current: 16/8 + 16/24 + 16/48 = 3 A. Power in branch: 16² ÷ 24 = 10.7 W.

questions.q: Which source best maintains a set DC voltage on a test bench as load changes within its rating?
questions.e: A stabilised supply regulates its DC output within its rating.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a semiconductor from a typical insulator?
o: It must have zero resistance at room temperature
It has no mobile charges under any condition
It conducts identically to a metal
Its conductivity can be deliberately controlled, for example by doping
questions.e: Semiconductor conductivity is controllable, making it useful in electronic components.

questions.q: Explain why the current–voltage graph for a filament lamp curves, while that for a metallic resistor at fixed temperature is a straight line.

pts.p: Filament current heats the filament and increases its resistance.
The fixed-temperature resistor has constant resistance, so current is proportional to voltage.

questions.model: Filament current heats the filament and increases its resistance. The fixed-temperature resistor has constant resistance, so current is proportional to voltage.

questions.q: In the usual cell symbol, which terminal does the longer of the two parallel lines represent?
o: The polarity cannot be read from the symbol
questions.e: The short line is negative; repeated cell pairs indicate a battery.

questions.q: Describe the IEC resistor symbol, and explain how an ammeter and a voltmeter are placed to measure its current and voltage.

pts.p: The fixed resistor is a rectangle in the circuit line.
An ammeter goes in series with the resistor.
A voltmeter goes in parallel across the resistor.

questions.model: The fixed resistor is a rectangle in the circuit line. An ammeter goes in series with the resistor. A voltmeter goes in parallel across the resistor.

questions.q: A 220 μF capacitor charged to 12 V is discharged through a 15 kΩ resistor. Find its initial charge, stored energy and discharge time constant. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Stored energy: ½ × 220 × 10⁻⁶ × 12² × 1000 = 15.8 mJ.

questions.q: A 470 μF capacitor charged to 9 V is discharged through a 22 kΩ resistor. Find its initial charge, stored energy and discharge time constant. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Stored energy: ½ × 470 × 10⁻⁶ × 9² × 1000 = 19 mJ.

questions.model: Charge: 470 × 9 = 4.23e+03 μC. Stored energy: ½ × 470 × 10⁻⁶ × 9² × 1000 = 19 mJ. Time constant: (22 × 10³) × (470 × 10⁻⁶) = 10.3 s.

questions.q: A 100 μF capacitor charged to 24 V is discharged through a 47 kΩ resistor. Find its initial charge, stored energy and discharge time constant. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Stored energy: ½ × 100 × 10⁻⁶ × 24² × 1000 = 28.8 mJ.

questions.model: Charge: 100 × 24 = 2.4e+03 μC. Stored energy: ½ × 100 × 10⁻⁶ × 24² × 1000 = 28.8 mJ. Time constant: (47 × 10³) × (100 × 10⁻⁶) = 4.7 s.

questions.q: Parallel plates of overlap area 80 cm² are separated by 0.25 mm. The dielectric has relative permittivity 25; use ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F/m. Find capacitance in air approximated as vacuum and with the dielectric, both in pF. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Dielectric capacitance: air capacitance × 25 = 7.08e+03 pF.

questions.model: Air capacitance: 8.85 × (80 × 10⁻⁴) ÷ (0.25 × 10⁻³) = 283 pF. Dielectric capacitance: air capacitance × 25 = 7.08e+03 pF.

questions.q: Parallel plates of overlap area 120 cm² are separated by 0.45 mm. The dielectric has relative permittivity 25; use ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F/m. Find capacitance in air approximated as vacuum and with the dielectric, both in pF. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Dielectric capacitance: air capacitance × 25 = 5.9e+03 pF.

questions.model: Air capacitance: 8.85 × (120 × 10⁻⁴) ÷ (0.45 × 10⁻³) = 236 pF. Dielectric capacitance: air capacitance × 25 = 5.9e+03 pF.

questions.q: Parallel plates of overlap area 45 cm² are separated by 0.16 mm. The dielectric has relative permittivity 25; use ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F/m. Find capacitance in air approximated as vacuum and with the dielectric, both in pF. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Dielectric capacitance: air capacitance × 25 = 6.22e+03 pF.

questions.model: Air capacitance: 8.85 × (45 × 10⁻⁴) ÷ (0.16 × 10⁻³) = 249 pF. Dielectric capacitance: air capacitance × 25 = 6.22e+03 pF.

pts.p: Initial current: 6 ÷ 15 = 0.4 mA.
Voltage after one time constant: 0.368 × 6 = 2.21 V.
Current after one time constant: 0.368 × initial current = 0.147 mA.

Voltage after one time constant: 0.368 × 18 = 6.62 V.
Current after one time constant: 0.368 × initial current = 0.301 mA.

questions.model: Initial current: 18 ÷ 22 = 0.818 mA. Voltage after one time constant: 0.368 × 18 = 6.62 V. Current after one time constant: 0.368 × initial current = 0.301 mA.

questions.q: What must you check when fitting a polarised capacitor to a DC circuit?
o: It is wired in series with every resistor
Its capacitance is expressed in henries
It will only ever charge to half supply voltage
Its positive and negative terminals face the correct way
questions.e: The marked terminals must match the intended voltage polarity.

questions.q: Describe the shape of voltage and current-magnitude graphs during capacitor discharge through a resistor.

pts.p: Both start at a maximum and decrease towards zero.
The fall is initially steep and then flattens as the capacitor discharges.

questions.model: Both start at a maximum and decrease towards zero. The fall is initially steep and then flattens as the capacitor discharges.

questions.q: Describe the circuit symbols for a non-polarised capacitor and a polarised capacitor. State why a capacitor might be connected across a DC supply.

pts.p: A non-polarised capacitor is two parallel separated plates.
A polarised version indicates polarity, for example with a plus sign.
The capacitor stores charge and can supply brief current to help smooth changes in supply voltage.

questions.model: A non-polarised capacitor is two parallel separated plates. A polarised version indicates polarity, for example with a plus sign. The capacitor stores charge and can supply brief current to help smooth changes in supply voltage.

questions.q: A DC source of 12 V feeds a 4 Ω series resistor. The next node returns to ground through a 12 Ω and a 6 Ω branch in parallel. Use Kirchhoff’s laws to find node voltage and both currents leaving that node. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: Node voltage
parts.work: Node voltage: KCL gives (12 − V)/4 = V/12 + V/6, so V = 12 ÷ (1 + 4/12 + 4/6) = 6 V.

parts.label: First branch current
parts.work: First branch current: node voltage ÷ 12 = 0.5 A.

parts.label: Second branch current
parts.work: Second branch current: node voltage ÷ 6 = 1 A.

pts.p: Node voltage: KCL gives (12 − V)/4 = V/12 + V/6, so V = 12 ÷ (1 + 4/12 + 4/6) = 6 V.
First branch current: node voltage ÷ 12 = 0.5 A.
Second branch current: node voltage ÷ 6 = 1 A.

questions.model: Node voltage: KCL gives (12 − V)/4 = V/12 + V/6, so V = 12 ÷ (1 + 4/12 + 4/6) = 6 V. First branch current: node voltage ÷ 12 = 0.5 A. Second branch current: node voltage ÷ 6 = 1 A.

questions.q: A DC source of 18 V feeds a 6 Ω series resistor. The next node returns to ground through a 18 Ω and a 9 Ω branch in parallel. Use Kirchhoff’s laws to find node voltage and both currents leaving that node. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: Second branch current

pts.p: Node voltage: KCL gives (18 − V)/6 = V/18 + V/9, so V = 18 ÷ (1 + 6/18 + 6/9) = 9 V.
First branch current: node voltage ÷ 18 = 0.5 A.
Second branch current: node voltage ÷ 9 = 1 A.

questions.model: Node voltage: KCL gives (18 − V)/6 = V/18 + V/9, so V = 18 ÷ (1 + 6/18 + 6/9) = 9 V. First branch current: node voltage ÷ 18 = 0.5 A. Second branch current: node voltage ÷ 9 = 1 A.

questions.q: A DC source of 24 V feeds a 8 Ω series resistor. The next node returns to ground through a 16 Ω and a 16 Ω branch in parallel. Use Kirchhoff’s laws to find node voltage and both currents leaving that node. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: First branch current

parts.label: Second branch current
parts.work: Second branch current: node voltage ÷ 16 = 0.75 A.

pts.p: Node voltage: KCL gives (24 − V)/8 = V/16 + V/16, so V = 24 ÷ (1 + 8/16 + 8/16) = 12 V.
First branch current: node voltage ÷ 16 = 0.75 A.
Second branch current: node voltage ÷ 16 = 0.75 A.

questions.model: Node voltage: KCL gives (24 − V)/8 = V/16 + V/16, so V = 24 ÷ (1 + 8/16 + 8/16) = 12 V. First branch current: node voltage ÷ 16 = 0.75 A. Second branch current: node voltage ÷ 16 = 0.75 A.

questions.q: Ideal sources at 18 V and 6 V relative to ground feed a node X through 6 Ω and 9 Ω respectively. X connects to ground through 12 Ω. Find X’s voltage and the signed current from each source towards X. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

parts.work: Current from first source: (18 − X) ÷ 6 = 1.31 A.

parts.label: Current from second source
parts.work: Current from second source: (6 − X) ÷ 9 = -0.462 A.

pts.p: Current from first source: (18 − X) ÷ 6 = 1.31 A.
Current from second source: (6 − X) ÷ 9 = -0.462 A.

questions.model: Voltage at X: from KCL, X = (18/6 + 6/9) ÷ (1/6 + 1/9 + 1/12) = 10.2 V. Current from first source: (18 − X) ÷ 6 = 1.31 A. Current from second source: (6 − X) ÷ 9 = -0.462 A.

parts.label: Current from second source

Current from second source: (8 − X) ÷ 12 = -0.462 A.

questions.q: Ideal sources at 15 V and 5 V relative to ground feed a node X through 5 Ω and 10 Ω respectively. X connects to ground through 15 Ω. Find X’s voltage and the signed current from each source towards X. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: Current from second source
parts.work: Current from second source: (5 − X) ÷ 10 = -0.455 A.

Current from second source: (5 − X) ÷ 10 = -0.455 A.

questions.q: A loop contains opposing ideal supplies of 14 V clockwise and 5 V anticlockwise, plus series resistors of 6 Ω and 9 Ω. Find signed clockwise current and the signed clockwise voltage drop across the 9 Ω resistor. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Loop current: (14 − 5) ÷ (6 + 9) = 0.6 A.
Voltage drop: loop current × 9 = 5.4 V.

questions.model: Loop current: (14 − 5) ÷ (6 + 9) = 0.6 A. Voltage drop: loop current × 9 = 5.4 V.

questions.q: A loop contains opposing ideal supplies of 24 V clockwise and 12 V anticlockwise, plus series resistors of 10 Ω and 5 Ω. Find signed clockwise current and the signed clockwise voltage drop across the 5 Ω resistor. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Voltage drop: loop current × 5 = 4 V.

questions.model: Loop current: (24 − 12) ÷ (10 + 5) = 0.8 A. Voltage drop: loop current × 5 = 4 V.

questions.q: A loop contains opposing ideal supplies of 9 V clockwise and 15 V anticlockwise, plus series resistors of 4 Ω and 8 Ω. Find signed clockwise current and the signed clockwise voltage drop across the 8 Ω resistor. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Voltage drop: loop current × 8 = -4 V.

questions.model: Loop current: (9 − 15) ÷ (4 + 8) = -0.5 A. Voltage drop: loop current × 8 = -4 V.

questions.q: If a Kirchhoff calculation gives a negative branch current, what does the sign mean?
o: Current cannot flow through that branch
The voltage source stores negative energy
The current is opposite to the chosen positive direction
questions.e: Current directions can be assumed before solving and interpreted afterwards.

questions.q: State Kirchhoff’s current and voltage laws and identify where you apply each.

pts.p: At a node total current entering equals total current leaving.
Around a closed loop the signed voltage changes sum to zero.

questions.model: At a node total current entering equals total current leaving. Around a closed loop the signed voltage changes sum to zero.

questions.q: A coil of 450 turns has 0.18 mWb of flux linking each turn at current 1.2 A. Find its inductance and stored magnetic energy. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Stored energy: ½ × inductance × 1.2² = 0.0486 J.

questions.model: Inductance: 450 × 0.18 × 10⁻³ ÷ 1.2 = 0.0675 H. Stored energy: ½ × inductance × 1.2² = 0.0486 J.

questions.q: A coil of 800 turns has 0.09 mWb of flux linking each turn at current 0.7 A. Find its inductance and stored magnetic energy. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

questions.model: Inductance: 800 × 0.09 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.7 = 0.103 H. Stored energy: ½ × inductance × 0.7² = 0.0252 J.

questions.q: A coil of 650 turns has 0.24 mWb of flux linking each turn at current 2.1 A. Find its inductance and stored magnetic energy. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

questions.q: Which rule finds the direction of conventional current induced when a conductor moves across a magnetic field?
questions.e: The right-hand rule is for generators; the left-hand rule relates field and current to force in a motor.

questions.q: Explain how a simple motor differs from a simple generator in its use of a magnetic field.

pts.p: In a motor, current in the field produces force and movement.
In a generator, movement across the field induces a voltage, and a current if a circuit is closed.

questions.model: In a motor, current in the field produces force and movement. In a generator, movement across the field induces a voltage, and a current if a circuit is closed.

questions.q: Which component is normally represented by a sequence of loops in a circuit diagram?
questions.e: The loops represent the coil of an inductor.

questions.q: A source follows v = 24 sin(2π × 50t) V with t in seconds. Find the period in ms, RMS voltage and signed instantaneous voltage at 3 ms. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Period: 1000 ÷ 50 = 20 ms.
RMS voltage: 24 ÷ √2 = 17 V.
Instantaneous voltage: 24 × sin(2π × 50 × 3 ÷ 1000) = 19.4 V.

questions.model: Period: 1000 ÷ 50 = 20 ms. RMS voltage: 24 ÷ √2 = 17 V. Instantaneous voltage: 24 × sin(2π × 50 × 3 ÷ 1000) = 19.4 V.

questions.q: A source follows v = 15 sin(2π × 60t) V with t in seconds. Find the period in ms, RMS voltage and signed instantaneous voltage at 4 ms. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

Instantaneous voltage: 15 × sin(2π × 60 × 4 ÷ 1000) = 15 V.

questions.model: Period: 1000 ÷ 60 = 16.7 ms. RMS voltage: 15 ÷ √2 = 10.6 V. Instantaneous voltage: 15 × sin(2π × 60 × 4 ÷ 1000) = 15 V.

questions.q: A source follows v = 36 sin(2π × 80t) V with t in seconds. Find the period in ms, RMS voltage and signed instantaneous voltage at 9 ms. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

Instantaneous voltage: 36 × sin(2π × 80 × 9 ÷ 1000) = -35.4 V.

questions.model: Period: 1000 ÷ 80 = 12.5 ms. RMS voltage: 36 ÷ √2 = 25.5 V. Instantaneous voltage: 36 × sin(2π × 80 × 9 ÷ 1000) = -35.4 V.

parts.label: Voltage across pair

Current in branch: parallel voltage ÷ 6 = 2 A.

questions.q: A 30 V RMS AC source feeds a 5 Ω resistor in series with a parallel pair of 15 Ω and 10 Ω. Find total RMS current, RMS voltage across the pair and RMS current in the 10 Ω branch. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

parts.work: Voltage across pair: total current × parallel equivalent resistance = 16.4 V.

parts.label: Current in branch

questions.q: A 18 V RMS AC source feeds a 3 Ω resistor in series with a parallel pair of 9 Ω and 18 Ω. Find total RMS current, RMS voltage across the pair and RMS current in the 18 Ω branch. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: Voltage across pair
parts.work: Voltage across pair: total current × parallel equivalent resistance = 12 V.

parts.label: Current in branch
parts.work: Current in branch: parallel voltage ÷ 18 = 0.667 A.

pts.p: Voltage across pair: total current × parallel equivalent resistance = 12 V.
Current in branch: parallel voltage ÷ 18 = 0.667 A.

questions.model: Total current: 18 ÷ [3 + 1/(1/9 + 1/18)] = 2 A. Voltage across pair: total current × parallel equivalent resistance = 12 V. Current in branch: parallel voltage ÷ 18 = 0.667 A.

questions.q: A sinusoidal supply repeats every 25 ms and has 36 V peak-to-peak. Find the angular frequency and RMS voltage. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Angular frequency: 2π × 1000 ÷ 25 = 251 rad/s.
RMS voltage: 36 ÷ (2√2) = 12.7 V.

questions.model: Angular frequency: 2π × 1000 ÷ 25 = 251 rad/s. RMS voltage: 36 ÷ (2√2) = 12.7 V.

questions.q: A sinusoidal supply repeats every 16 ms and has 48 V peak-to-peak. Find the angular frequency and RMS voltage. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

RMS voltage: 48 ÷ (2√2) = 17 V.

questions.model: Angular frequency: 2π × 1000 ÷ 16 = 393 rad/s. RMS voltage: 48 ÷ (2√2) = 17 V.

questions.q: A sinusoidal supply repeats every 40 ms and has 60 V peak-to-peak. Find the angular frequency and RMS voltage. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Angular frequency: 2π × 1000 ÷ 40 = 157 rad/s.
RMS voltage: 60 ÷ (2√2) = 21.2 V.

questions.model: Angular frequency: 2π × 1000 ÷ 40 = 157 rad/s. RMS voltage: 60 ÷ (2√2) = 21.2 V.

questions.q: What does the RMS voltage of a sinusoidal supply mean for an ideal resistor?
o: The peak voltage reached once each cycle
The signed mean voltage over a full cycle
The difference between positive and negative peaks
The DC voltage giving the same average heating power
questions.e: RMS measures effective heating power in a resistor.

questions.q: Give one advantage of AC for distribution and one reason a battery-powered electronic circuit uses DC.

pts.p: AC voltage can readily be stepped up or down for transmission using transformers.
A battery naturally provides a steady polarity suitable for DC electronics.

questions.model: AC voltage can readily be stepped up or down for transmission using transformers. A battery naturally provides a steady polarity suitable for DC electronics.

questions.q: What does the small sine wave inside a circular source symbol indicate?
questions.e: The sine wave represents an alternating supply.

questions.q: A DC drive takes 3 A at 24 V and delivers useful power of 54 W for 2.5 h. Find loss power, efficiency and total electrical energy used. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Loss power: 24 × 3 − 54 = 18 W.
Energy input: 24 × 3 × 2.5 ÷ 1000 = 0.18 kWh.

questions.model: Loss power: 24 × 3 − 54 = 18 W. Efficiency: 100 × 54 ÷ (24 × 3) = 75 %. Energy input: 24 × 3 × 2.5 ÷ 1000 = 0.18 kWh.

questions.q: A DC drive takes 2.2 A at 48 V and delivers useful power of 78 W for 4 h. Find loss power, efficiency and total electrical energy used. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Energy input: 48 × 2.2 × 4 ÷ 1000 = 0.422 kWh.

questions.q: A DC drive takes 5 A at 12 V and delivers useful power of 42 W for 1.8 h. Find loss power, efficiency and total electrical energy used. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Loss power: 12 × 5 − 42 = 18 W.
Energy input: 12 × 5 × 1.8 ÷ 1000 = 0.108 kWh.

questions.q: A battery has rated capacity 2400 mAh. A device draws 180 mA for 25% of the time and 30 mA otherwise. Estimate average current and ideal battery life. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Battery life: 2400 ÷ average current = 35.6 h.

questions.model: Average current: [180 × 25 + 30 × (100 − 25)] ÷ 100 = 67.5 mA. Battery life: 2400 ÷ average current = 35.6 h.

questions.q: A battery has rated capacity 1800 mAh. A device draws 160 mA for 40% of the time and 20 mA otherwise. Estimate average current and ideal battery life. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Battery life: 1800 ÷ average current = 23.7 h.

questions.model: Average current: [160 × 40 + 20 × (100 − 40)] ÷ 100 = 76 mA. Battery life: 1800 ÷ average current = 23.7 h.

questions.q: A battery has rated capacity 3200 mAh. A device draws 240 mA for 10% of the time and 15 mA otherwise. Estimate average current and ideal battery life. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Battery life: 3200 ÷ average current = 85.3 h.

questions.model: Average current: [240 × 10 + 15 × (100 − 10)] ÷ 100 = 37.5 mA. Battery life: 3200 ÷ average current = 85.3 h.

questions.q: A supply lead of total resistance 0.4 Ω carries 5 A for 600 s. Find its power loss and the energy dissipated. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Power loss: 5² × 0.4 = 10 W.
Energy dissipated: 5² × 0.4 × 600 = 6e+03 J.

questions.model: Power loss: 5² × 0.4 = 10 W. Energy dissipated: 5² × 0.4 × 600 = 6e+03 J.

questions.q: A supply lead of total resistance 0.8 Ω carries 3.5 A for 420 s. Find its power loss and the energy dissipated. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Power loss: 3.5² × 0.8 = 9.8 W.
Energy dissipated: 3.5² × 0.8 × 420 = 4.12e+03 J.

questions.model: Power loss: 3.5² × 0.8 = 9.8 W. Energy dissipated: 3.5² × 0.8 × 420 = 4.12e+03 J.

questions.q: A supply lead of total resistance 0.22 Ω carries 8 A for 300 s. Find its power loss and the energy dissipated. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Power loss: 8² × 0.22 = 14.1 W.
Energy dissipated: 8² × 0.22 × 300 = 4.22e+03 J.

questions.model: Power loss: 8² × 0.22 = 14.1 W. Energy dissipated: 8² × 0.22 × 300 = 4.22e+03 J.

questions.q: Which unit measures energy rather than power?
questions.e: A kilowatt-hour is power multiplied by time.

questions.q: Explain why reducing a battery-powered device’s waste heating can increase run time for the same useful output.

pts.p: Higher efficiency means less electrical input for the same useful output.
At the same voltage, lower input power means lower battery current, so capacity lasts longer.

questions.model: Higher efficiency means less electrical input for the same useful output. At the same voltage, lower input power means lower battery current, so capacity lasts longer.

questions.q: An analogue stage takes 0.3 V and 0.4 mA and produces 2.4 V and 2 mA. Find voltage gain in dB, current gain in dB and power gain in dB. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Voltage gain: 20 log₁₀(2.4/0.3) = 18.1 dB.
Current gain: 20 log₁₀(2/0.4) = 14 dB.

questions.model: Voltage gain: 20 log₁₀(2.4/0.3) = 18.1 dB. Current gain: 20 log₁₀(2/0.4) = 14 dB. Power gain: 10 log₁₀[(2.4/0.3) × (2/0.4)] = 16 dB.

questions.q: An analogue stage takes 0.15 V and 0.5 mA and produces 1.5 V and 4 mA. Find voltage gain in dB, current gain in dB and power gain in dB. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Voltage gain: 20 log₁₀(1.5/0.15) = 20 dB.
Current gain: 20 log₁₀(4/0.5) = 18.1 dB.

questions.model: Voltage gain: 20 log₁₀(1.5/0.15) = 20 dB. Current gain: 20 log₁₀(4/0.5) = 18.1 dB. Power gain: 10 log₁₀[(1.5/0.15) × (4/0.5)] = 19 dB.

questions.q: An analogue stage takes 0.8 V and 2 mA and produces 0.4 V and 1.6 mA. Find voltage gain in dB, current gain in dB and power gain in dB. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Voltage gain: 20 log₁₀(0.4/0.8) = -6.02 dB.
Current gain: 20 log₁₀(1.6/2) = -1.94 dB.

questions.model: Voltage gain: 20 log₁₀(0.4/0.8) = -6.02 dB. Current gain: 20 log₁₀(1.6/2) = -1.94 dB. Power gain: 10 log₁₀[(0.4/0.8) × (1.6/2)] = -3.98 dB.

questions.q: A signal of 0.12 V enters three cascaded stages with voltage ratios 8, 0.25 and 12. Find the overall voltage ratio, gain in dB and output voltage. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Voltage ratio: 8 × 0.25 × 12 = 24.
Overall gain: 20 log₁₀(8 × 0.25 × 12) = 27.6 dB.
Output voltage: 0.12 × overall ratio = 2.88 V.

questions.model: Voltage ratio: 8 × 0.25 × 12 = 24. Overall gain: 20 log₁₀(8 × 0.25 × 12) = 27.6 dB. Output voltage: 0.12 × overall ratio = 2.88 V.

questions.q: A signal of 0.2 V enters three cascaded stages with voltage ratios 5, 0.4 and 6. Find the overall voltage ratio, gain in dB and output voltage. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Voltage ratio: 5 × 0.4 × 6 = 12.
Overall gain: 20 log₁₀(5 × 0.4 × 6) = 21.6 dB.
Output voltage: 0.2 × overall ratio = 2.4 V.

questions.model: Voltage ratio: 5 × 0.4 × 6 = 12. Overall gain: 20 log₁₀(5 × 0.4 × 6) = 21.6 dB. Output voltage: 0.2 × overall ratio = 2.4 V.

questions.q: A signal of 0.35 V enters three cascaded stages with voltage ratios 10, 0.1 and 3. Find the overall voltage ratio, gain in dB and output voltage. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Voltage ratio: 10 × 0.1 × 3 = 3.
Overall gain: 20 log₁₀(10 × 0.1 × 3) = 9.54 dB.
Output voltage: 0.35 × overall ratio = 1.05 V.

questions.model: Voltage ratio: 10 × 0.1 × 3 = 3. Overall gain: 20 log₁₀(10 × 0.1 × 3) = 9.54 dB. Output voltage: 0.35 × overall ratio = 1.05 V.

questions.q: An ideal inverting amplifier has input resistor 10 kΩ, feedback resistor 47 kΩ and input 0.2 V. Its output is within supply limits. Find signed voltage gain and signed output voltage. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Voltage gain: −47 ÷ 10 = -4.7.
Output voltage: voltage gain × 0.2 = -0.94 V.

questions.model: Voltage gain: −47 ÷ 10 = -4.7. Output voltage: voltage gain × 0.2 = -0.94 V.

questions.q: An ideal inverting amplifier has input resistor 4.7 kΩ, feedback resistor 22 kΩ and input 0.3 V. Its output is within supply limits. Find signed voltage gain and signed output voltage. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Voltage gain: −22 ÷ 4.7 = -4.68.
Output voltage: voltage gain × 0.3 = -1.4 V.

questions.model: Voltage gain: −22 ÷ 4.7 = -4.68. Output voltage: voltage gain × 0.3 = -1.4 V.

questions.q: An ideal inverting amplifier has input resistor 15 kΩ, feedback resistor 68 kΩ and input 0.12 V. Its output is within supply limits. Find signed voltage gain and signed output voltage. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Voltage gain: −68 ÷ 15 = -4.53.
Output voltage: voltage gain × 0.12 = -0.544 V.

questions.model: Voltage gain: −68 ÷ 15 = -4.53. Output voltage: voltage gain × 0.12 = -0.544 V.

questions.q: An ideal non-inverting amplifier has 8 kΩ from its inverting input to ground and feedback resistor 40 kΩ. Its input is 0.35 V and it operates linearly. Find gain and output voltage. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Voltage gain: 1 + 40 ÷ 8 = 6.
Output voltage: 0.35 × voltage gain = 2.1 V.

questions.model: Voltage gain: 1 + 40 ÷ 8 = 6. Output voltage: 0.35 × voltage gain = 2.1 V.

questions.q: An ideal non-inverting amplifier has 6.8 kΩ from its inverting input to ground and feedback resistor 33 kΩ. Its input is 0.22 V and it operates linearly. Find gain and output voltage. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Voltage gain: 1 + 33 ÷ 6.8 = 5.85.
Output voltage: 0.22 × voltage gain = 1.29 V.

questions.model: Voltage gain: 1 + 33 ÷ 6.8 = 5.85. Output voltage: 0.22 × voltage gain = 1.29 V.

questions.q: An ideal non-inverting amplifier has 15 kΩ from its inverting input to ground and feedback resistor 56 kΩ. Its input is 0.4 V and it operates linearly. Find gain and output voltage. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Voltage gain: 1 + 56 ÷ 15 = 4.73.
Output voltage: 0.4 × voltage gain = 1.89 V.

questions.model: Voltage gain: 1 + 56 ÷ 15 = 4.73. Output voltage: 0.4 × voltage gain = 1.89 V.

questions.q: An amplifier has midband gain 24 dB, with the lower and upper −3 dB points at 150 Hz and 5400 Hz. Find the gain at either cutoff and the bandwidth. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Cutoff gain: 24 − 3 = 21 dB.
Bandwidth: 5400 − 150 = 5.25e+03 Hz.

questions.model: Cutoff gain: 24 − 3 = 21 dB. Bandwidth: 5400 − 150 = 5.25e+03 Hz.

questions.q: An amplifier has midband gain 30 dB, with the lower and upper −3 dB points at 220 Hz and 8250 Hz. Find the gain at either cutoff and the bandwidth. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Cutoff gain: 30 − 3 = 27 dB.
Bandwidth: 8250 − 220 = 8.03e+03 Hz.

questions.model: Cutoff gain: 30 − 3 = 27 dB. Bandwidth: 8250 − 220 = 8.03e+03 Hz.

questions.q: An amplifier has midband gain 18 dB, with the lower and upper −3 dB points at 95 Hz and 3700 Hz. Find the gain at either cutoff and the bandwidth. Give non-exact results to 3 significant figures.

pts.p: Cutoff gain: 18 − 3 = 15 dB.
Bandwidth: 3700 − 95 = 3.6e+03 Hz.

questions.model: Cutoff gain: 18 − 3 = 15 dB. Bandwidth: 3700 − 95 = 3.6e+03 Hz.

questions.q: A voltage stage gives a negative gain in dB. What follows about the magnitude of its voltage ratio?
questions.e: A negative logarithmic gain means attenuation.

questions.q: Describe a block diagram for an analogue temperature measuring system.

pts.p: A temperature sensor produces a varying analogue electrical signal.
An amplifier conditions or increases the signal for a display or meter.

questions.model: A temperature sensor produces a varying analogue electrical signal. An amplifier conditions or increases the signal for a display or meter.

questions.q: Which gate has output 1 only when its two inputs are different?
questions.e: Exclusive OR is true for 01 or 10 only.

questions.q: What does a small inversion bubble at the output of an AND gate indicate?
questions.e: The bubble negates the AND result.

questions.q: Which gate has output 1 only when both inputs are 0?
questions.e: NOR negates OR, so any high input makes its output low.

questions.q: Which gate has an output of 0 only when both inputs are 1?
questions.e: NAND negates the AND result.

questions.q: For Q = (A AND B) OR (NOT C), state the intermediate outputs and Q for inputs A = 1, B = 0, C = 0. Explain which stage sets Q.

pts.p: The AND output is 0 because B is 0.
NOT C is 1 and makes the OR output 1.

questions.model: The AND output is 0 because B is 0. NOT C is 1 and makes the OR output 1.

questions.q: An alarm sounds when an armed switch A is 1 and either door sensor D or window sensor W is 1. Describe a two-gate circuit.

pts.p: Feed D and W to an OR gate.
Feed the OR result and A to an AND gate to produce the alarm signal.

questions.model: Feed D and W to an OR gate. Feed the OR result and A to an AND gate to produce the alarm signal.

questions.q: For Q = (A XOR B) AND C, list the 3-bit inputs ABC that give Q = 1 and explain the test.

pts.p: The high-output rows are 011 and 101.
C must be 1 and exactly one of A and B must be 1.

questions.model: The high-output rows are 011 and 101. C must be 1 and exactly one of A and B must be 1.

questions.q: Construct the truth table for Q = (A NAND B) NOR C. Write the output values for ABC from 000 through 111, and explain your result.

pts.p: The sequence is 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0. Only row 110 gives 1.
NAND is 0 only when A and B are both high. The NOR also requires C = 0.

questions.model: The sequence is 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0. Only row 110 gives 1. NAND is 0 only when A and B are both high. The NOR also requires C = 0.

questions.q: An output must be high for AB = 01 only. Give the Boolean expression using one NOT gate and one AND gate, and describe their connections.

pts.p: The expression is Q = (NOT A) AND B.
Feed A into NOT, then connect its output and B to the AND inputs.

questions.model: The expression is Q = (NOT A) AND B. Feed A into NOT, then connect its output and B to the AND inputs.

questions.q: A quality alarm uses five gates: X = A XOR B, Y = NOT C, Z = X AND Y, W = B AND C, Q = Z OR W. Compare the two intermediate paths for ABC = 101 and ABC = 011.

pts.p: For 101, Z = 0 because Y = 0 and W = 0 because B = 0, giving Q = 0.
For 011, Z = 0 because Y = 0 and W = 1 because B and C are high, giving Q = 1.

questions.model: For 101, Z = 0 because Y = 0 and W = 0 because B = 0, giving Q = 0. For 011, Z = 0 because Y = 0 and W = 1 because B and C are high, giving Q = 1.

questions.q: Sketch standard AND and OR gate symbols on paper, then describe how to distinguish them and how to convert OR into the NOR symbol.

pts.p: The conventional AND symbol has a flat input side and a rounded output side.
The OR symbol has a curved input side and tapered output side.
Put an inversion bubble at the OR output to represent NOR.

questions.model: The conventional AND symbol has a flat input side and a rounded output side. The OR symbol has a curved input side and tapered output side. Put an inversion bubble at the OR output to represent NOR.
